senses.definition: Abdominal muscle.
senses.example: He strengthened his abs with crunches three times a week.

senses.definition: An abscess caused by injecting an illegal drug, usually heroin.
senses.example: The emergency room treated him for an ab on his arm from injecting heroin.

senses.definition: The expulsion from the womb of a fetus or embryo before it is fully developed, with loss of the fetus; either naturally as a spontaneous abortion (now usually called a miscarriage), or deliberately as an induced abortion.
senses.example: After the ab in the eighth week, the couple grieved quietly for months.

senses.definition: An aborted fetus; an abortus.
A misshapen person or thing; a monstrosity.
senses.example: Critics called the new stadium design an ab of modern architecture.

senses.definition: Failure or abandonment of a project, promise, goal etc.
senses.example: The ab of the merger left both companies scrambling for new partners.

senses.definition: Arrest of development of any organ, so that it remains an imperfect formation or is absorbed.
senses.example: The biopsy showed an ab of the embryonic structure, leaving only a vestigial remnant.

senses.definition: The cessation of an illness or disease at a very early stage.
senses.example: Early treatment led to the ab of the infection before it spread.

senses.definition: The early stages of; the beginning process; the start.
senses.example: We are still in the ab of the project, so nothing is final yet.

senses.definition: To abseil.
senses.example: The climbers ab down the cliff face using a rope anchored at the top.

senses.definition: To cause a premature termination of (a fetus); to end a pregnancy before term.
senses.example: The clinic will ab the pregnancy only before the twelfth week.

senses.definition: To end prematurely; to stop in the preliminary stages; to turn back.
senses.example: The board decided to ab the trial after two weeks of disappointing results.

senses.definition: To stop or fail at something in the preliminary stages.
senses.example: Several startups ab in the first year when their funding dries up.

senses.definition: To become checked in normal development, so as either to remain rudimentary or shrink away wholly; to cease organic growth before maturation; to become sterile.
senses.example: Some embryonic tissues ab during development, shrinking away before birth.

senses.definition: To cause an organism to develop minimally; to cause rudimentary development to happen; to prevent maturation.
senses.example: Researchers used the drug to ab the growth of the seedlings' roots.

senses.definition: To abandon a mission at any point after the beginning of the mission and prior to its completion.
senses.example: NASA chose to ab the mission after the spacecraft lost power.

senses.definition: To terminate a mission involving a missile or rocket; to destroy a missile or rocket prematurely.
senses.example: The defense crew had to ab the interceptor missile once it veered off course.

senses.definition: To terminate a process prior to completion.
(now rare outside medicine) To miscarry; to bring forth (non-living) offspring prematurely.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: On all sides; around.
senses.example: I looked about at the scenery that surrounded me.

senses.definition: Here and there; around; in one place and another; up and down.
senses.example: Bits of old machinery were lying about.

senses.definition: From one place or position to another in succession; indicating repeated movement or activity.
senses.example: walking about;  rushing about;  jumping about;  thrashing about

senses.definition: Indicating unproductive or unstructured activity.
senses.example: messing about;   fooling about;  loafing about

senses.definition: Nearly; approximately; with close correspondence in quality, manner, degree, quantity, or time; almost.
senses.example: Dinner's about ready.

senses.definition: Near; in the vicinity.
To a reversed order; half round; facing in the opposite direction; from a contrary point of view.
senses.example: to face about;  to turn oneself about

senses.definition: In succession; one after another; in the course of events.
In circuit; circularly; by a circuitous way; around the outside; in circumference.
senses.example: a mile about, and a third of a mile across

senses.definition: In a circle around; all round; on every side of; on the outside of.
senses.example: The snake was coiled about his ankle.

senses.definition: Over or upon different parts of; through or over in various directions; here and there in; to and fro in; throughout.
senses.example: He was well known about town.

senses.definition: Indicates that something will happen very soon; indicates a plan or intention to do something.
Concerning; with regard to; on account of; on the subject of; to affect.
senses.example: He talked a lot about his childhood.

senses.definition: Concerned with; engaged in; intent on.
senses.example: to be about one's business

senses.definition: Within or in the immediate neighborhood of; in contiguity or proximity to; near, as to place.
senses.example: I can't find my reading glasses, but they must be somewhere about the house.

senses.definition: On one's person; nearby the person.
senses.example: I had no weapon about me but a stick.

senses.definition: In or near, as in mental faculties or in the possession of; under the control of; at one's command; in one's makeup.
senses.example: He has his wits about him.

core.definition: Short for abortion: the ending of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive, either as a miscarriage or as an induced abortion.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short a as in 'cat' and say it as one quick syllable. Do not read the letters A and B as ay-bee, which is a common mistake with this short form.

nuance.connotation: Negative or sensitive in many contexts, and politically charged; it is clinical in medical settings.
nuance.usage_note: In American English ab is a clipped clinical or informal form, and most people prefer abortion or miscarriage. In everyday gym talk, ab usually means the abdominal muscles, so do not confuse the two senses. Use the term carefully and with clear context, especially around sensitive topics.

distinctions.note: Miscarriage is a spontaneous loss, while ab can refer to either spontaneous or induced termination.
Abort is a verb meaning to end something early, including a pregnancy or a process, while ab is a noun for the pregnancy event.
Abs means abdominal muscles in everyday talk, and it is the more common use of this short form in the United States.

examples.everyday: The nurse told her that an ab in the first trimester is more common than most people realize.
examples.professional: The clinic's quarterly report counts each ab separately from miscarriages in its outcome data.
examples.analytical: Clinical writers sometimes use ab for both spontaneous and induced losses, which can blur the distinction in the data.

nuance.analogy: Ab is like a shorthand label on a file: it points to the same content but hides the details.
nuance.etymology: Clipped from abortion, from Latin abortio, from aboriri, to miscarry.
common_mistakes: Using ab in everyday talk to mean abs, which can confuse listeners in a gym or medical context.
Pronouncing ab as the letters ay-bee instead of the short word ab.

senses.definition: The act of abating, or the state of being abated; a lessening, diminution, or reduction; a moderation; removal or putting an end to; the suppression.
senses.example: The abatement of a nuisance is the suppression thereof.

senses.definition: The deduction of minor revenues incidental to an operation in calculating the cost of the operation.
senses.example: The accountant netted the abatement of minor incidental revenues against the plant's operating costs for the quarter.

senses.definition: The action of a person that abates, or without proper authority enters a residence after the death of the owner and before the heir takes possession.
senses.example: Her cousin's abatement of the empty house, before the heirs ever received keys, ended in a messy lawsuit.

senses.definition: The reduction of the proceeds of a will, when the debts have not yet been satisfied; the reduction of taxes due.
senses.example: The estate lawyer warned that the abatement of legacies would apply because the debts were still unpaid.

senses.definition: An amount abated; that which is taken away by way of reduction; deduction; decrease; a rebate or discount allowed; in particular from a tax.
senses.example: The city granted a property tax abatement of four hundred dollars for the new roof.

senses.definition: A beating down, a putting down.
senses.example: The general's abatement of the rebellion took weeks, as the rebels regrouped in the hills.

senses.definition: A quashing, a judicial defeat, the rendering abortive by law.
senses.example: The appeals court's abatement of the indictment ended the prosecution before trial began.

senses.definition: Forcible entry of a stranger into an inheritance when the person seized of it dies, and before the heir or devisee can take possession; ouster.
senses.example: The nephew's forcible abatement of the farm, before the widow's heirs arrived, shocked the whole county.

senses.definition: Rebatement, real or imaginary marks of disgrace affixed to an escutcheon.
senses.example: The herald pointed out an abatement on the escutcheon, a mark that disgraced the family's knight.

senses.definition: A mark of dishonor on an escutcheon; any figure added to the coat of arms tending to lower the dignity or station of the bearer.
senses.example: The heralds granted the traitor's coat of arms a dishonoring abatement that followed every generation of his line.

core.definition: A lessening or reduction of something unpleasant, such as pain, noise or pollution; also a reduction or cancellation of a fee or tax.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, BAYT, and the final -ment is weak. Don't stress the last syllable or pronounce the first vowel as 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes something getting smaller or being reduced, and is usually a positive development for the person affected.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use abatement in formal, legal, environmental and government writing, as in noise abatement or tax abatement. In everyday speech they say 'the pain is easing up' or 'it's letting up'. The phrase 'tax abatement' appears in local news about city incentives for developers.

distinctions.note: Reduction is the common, general word for making something smaller. Abatement usually describes a lessening of something harmful or a formal cancellation of a charge.
Relief describes the feeling of being freed from pain or worry, while abatement describes the thing itself becoming less.

examples.everyday: The pain shows some abatement after I take the medicine, so I can finally sleep.
examples.professional: The company reported a tax abatement for the new facility, which lowered its operating costs for the next five years.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of the abatement of disordered desire describes a gradual cooling of the passions rather than their sudden disappearance.

nuance.analogy: Like a tide going out: the water is still there, but each wave reaches a little less far up the shore.
nuance.etymology: From the verb abate, from Old French abattre, meaning to beat down, from Latin battuere, to beat.
common_mistakes: Using abatement as a verb; the verb is 'abate'.
Confusing it with abandonment, which is about leaving someone or something behind.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the second.

abatement.etymology: From Middle English *abatement*, from Anglo-Norman *abatre* (“to abate”) (from Old French *abatre*), + *-ment*; equivalent to *abate* + *-ment*.

core.definition: In Jesus's parable in Luke 16, the place of comfort and honor where the righteous dead rest beside Abraham.

pronunciation.tip: Both 'Abraham' and 'bosom' are stressed. 'Bosom' rhymes with 'woozum', with the short 'oo' of 'book', not like 'bossom' or 'bows-um'. The 'h' in Abraham is pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Warm, comforting, and tender.
nuance.usage_note: This is a religious or literary phrase, known to Bible readers and in older hymns. It is not used in ordinary speech, and 'bosom' itself sounds old-fashioned. Americans sometimes use 'bosom' for a woman's chest, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A more general term for the blessed state; Abraham's bosom is the image from one parable.
Heaven is the usual term; this phrase is a Jewish image of rest with the patriarch.
In the parable, the rich man is in Hades and sees Lazarus in Abraham's bosom across a chasm.

examples.everyday: My grandmother loved the old line about being carried to Abraham's bosom.
examples.professional: In my lesson on Luke 16, I will explain what Abraham's bosom meant for Jesus's Jewish hearers.
examples.analytical: The image of Abraham's bosom evokes a banquet setting in which the poor man Lazarus reclines at the patriarch's side.

nuance.analogy: Like a child resting against a father's chest, or a guest at the place of honor at a feast.
nuance.etymology: Phrase from the English Bible rendering of Greek 'kolpos Abraam', 'the lap or bosom of Abraham'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'bosom' as 'BOH-zum'.
Taking it as a literal location in the New Testament outside this parable.
Dropping the 'h' in Abraham's.
nuance.biblical_note: Luke 16:19-31 tells of a poor man, Lazarus, who dies and is carried by angels to Abraham's bosom (Greek 'kolpos', bosom or lap), while the rich man suffers in Hades. A great chasm separates them. The point is reversal and the need to heed Moses and the prophets. The image of reclining at Abraham's side matches a banquet setting.

senses.definition: The measurement of a specific substance's ability to absorb radiant energy; absorptivity.

core.definition: A number showing what fraction of incoming radiant energy a substance absorbs, used in physics and engineering.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAWRP in the first word and on FAK in the second. The final -or is pronounced as a weak r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'tuhr.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It appears in engineering and physics contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use absorption factor in technical writing, especially in heat transfer, building physics, and radiation calculations. It is rarely used in ordinary conversation. Engineers may also say absorptivity or absorptance, depending on the standard.

distinctions.note: Absorptivity is the standard term for the property of a surface in thermal physics, while absorption factor is a broader phrase that may refer to a specific measured value.
Emissivity describes how well a surface emits radiation, while absorption factor describes how much incoming radiation it takes in.

examples.everyday: The engineer said the new roof panel has a high absorption factor, so it should keep the attic cooler in summer.
examples.professional: Plug the measured absorption factor into the energy balance to estimate the heat gain through the wall.
examples.analytical: Because the absorption factor depends on both material and wavelength, comparing surfaces requires a common spectral basis.

nuance.analogy: An absorption factor is like a sponge's share of water: it tells you what fraction of the incoming energy the surface keeps.
nuance.etymology: From absorption (Latin absorptio) and factor (Latin factor, maker or doer).
common_mistakes: Confusing absorption factor with absorption coefficient, which measures a material property per unit thickness.
Stressing the final syllable of factor instead of FAK.

senses.definition: Cleansing; purging; abstergent.
(rare) Something cleansing; detergent; abstergent.
senses.example: The old-fashioned recipe called for an abstersive of soap and wood ash to scrub the pots.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Cleansing or purging, especially used for a substance that removes dirt or impurities from a wound or the skin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STUR, the second syllable, and the 'ur' is a strong r-colored vowel in American speech. The final syllable is short, like 'siv.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. It describes a cleansing effect and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word found mainly in medical, pharmaceutical, or cosmetic writing. Americans would normally say 'cleansing' or 'detergent' in everyday speech. Use it only when you need a precise technical term.

distinctions.note: Abstergent is a near-synonym that is also used as a noun for a cleansing agent; abstersive is the more common adjective.
Detergent usually refers to household or industrial cleaning products; abstersive is mostly used in medical or cosmetic contexts.

examples.everyday: The pharmacist said this soap is abstersive, which is just a fancy way of saying it cleans really well.
examples.professional: The dermatology team tested several abstersive solutions to see which one best removed debris from the wound without irritating it.
examples.analytical: The author describes the essay's style as abstersive, scouring away vague sentiment to leave only the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a good dish soap that lifts grease off a pan so the surface is clean again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abstergere, 'to wipe away,' from abs- 'away' plus tergere 'to wipe.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress; it is ab-STUR-siv, not AB-ster-siv.
Using it as an everyday word; ordinary speakers would say 'cleansing' instead.

core.definition: A valley near Jericho where Achan was stoned for taking devoted goods, later a symbol of hope in the prophet Hosea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AY, and keep the final r. Do not say AY-kur, which sounds like the word acre.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a place name from Scripture.
nuance.usage_note: You will hear Achor in Bible study, sermons on Joshua or Hosea, or discussions of Jericho. Americans use it only in religious or geographic contexts.
collocations: Achor as a door of hope
the valley of Achor in Joshua

examples.everyday: Our pastor mentioned the valley of Achor, which is where Achan was stoned, and that story stuck with me.
examples.professional: For the sermon series, I'll use Achor in Hosea to show how God turns a place of trouble into a door of hope.
examples.analytical: Hosea's use of the valley of Achor depends on a word-play with the Hebrew root 'akar, to trouble, which Joshua 7 already exploits.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Akhor, linked to the root 'akar meaning to trouble, a pun in Joshua 7:26.
common_mistakes: Saying AY-kur, which sounds like the unit acre.
Confusing Achor with Achbor, the father of Elnathan in Jeremiah.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Akhor, linked to 'akar, to trouble. Key passages: Joshua 7:24-26, where Achan and his family are stoned in the valley and the place is named for the trouble he caused; Hosea 2:15, where the valley of Achor becomes a door of hope; Isaiah 65:10, where the valley of Achor becomes a pasture for herds.

senses.definition: To encourage development or induce increased activity; to stimulate.
senses.example: activate the economy

senses.definition: To put a device, mechanism (alarm etc.) or system into action or motion; to trigger, to actuate, to set off, to enable.
senses.example: The pranksters activated the fire alarm by spraying deodorant next to it.

senses.definition: To remove the limitations of demoware by providing a license; to unlock.
senses.example: The software was demoware until I bought a license to activate all of its features.

senses.definition: To aerate in order to aid decomposition of organic matter.
senses.example: Turning the compost pile every week helps to activate the organic matter and speeds decomposition.

senses.definition: To enter an active state.
senses.example: The burglar alarm activates automatically.

senses.definition: To render more reactive; excite.
senses.example: The new manager's arrival seemed to activate the sleepy team and spark real creativity.

senses.definition: To render a molecule reactive, active, or effective in performing its function.
senses.example: The liver enzyme must activate the prodrug before it can bind to its target.

senses.definition: To render a substance radioactive.
senses.example: Researchers used neutron bombardment to activate the sample so it could be tracked in the body.

senses.definition: To hasten a chemical reaction, especially by heating.
senses.example: Adding a few drops of acid will activate the reaction, so heat the flask gently.

senses.definition: To organize or create a military unit or station.
senses.example: A new squadron was activated.

senses.definition: To bring a player back after an injury.
senses.example: The coach hoped to activate the veteran linebacker after his hamstring injury healed.

core.definition: To turn on or start a device, system or feature, or to make something begin working, often through a setup step.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the middle vowel a short ih. Do not stress the final syllable as in ak-tih-VAYT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds precise and businesslike, and it is common in instructions and automated phone menus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use activate for devices, bank cards, phone plans, software features and accounts, especially in instructions such as 'Activate your card by calling this number.' In casual talk, people often say turn on or get it working. The word also appears figuratively, as in activate your muscles or activate a community.

distinctions.note: Turn on is casual and everyday, while activate suggests a formal setup or licensing step.
Enable means to make something possible or permitted, whereas activate means actually starting it to work.
Trigger implies a response to a signal, often automatic, while activate can be a deliberate action by a person.

examples.everyday: You need to activate your new credit card by calling the number on the sticker before you can use it.
examples.professional: Please activate the new feature flag for the pilot group, then watch the error rates for the next two hours.
examples.analytical: Whether a sermon can activate a congregation's conscience depends less on doctrine than on the practices that follow it.

nuance.analogy: Activating a system is like turning the key in an ignition: the engine is ready, but it runs only once the key starts it.
nuance.etymology: From active, from Latin activus, with the verb suffix -ate.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in ak-tih-VAYT; the stress falls on AK.
Confusing activate with activity; the related noun for activate is activation.

senses.definition: Synonym of hole (“solitary confinement”).

core.definition: The practice of isolating a prisoner from the general population for security or management reasons, usually in a separate unit; solitary confinement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MIN in administrative and GAY in segregation, and reduce the first syllable to a weak 'uh'. Don't stress the -tive ending; it sounds like 'tiv', not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The term is a formal, bureaucratic euphemism for solitary confinement, and it softens how harsh the practice feels.
nuance.usage_note: Corrections officers, lawyers, journalists and policy writers use this term in the United States. Prisoners and the public more often say solitary, the hole, or the SHU (special housing unit). Using the formal term in conversation signals that you are speaking as an official or a reporter.

distinctions.note: Solitary confinement is the everyday public term, while administrative segregation names the reason for the isolation as a management decision rather than a punishment.

Protective custody isolates a prisoner to keep them safe from others, often at their own request, whereas administrative segregation can be imposed for security reasons regardless of the prisoner's wishes.

examples.everyday: My cousin got moved to administrative segregation after the fight, and now we can only talk to him on the phone.
examples.professional: The memo says the inmate was moved to administrative segregation pending the investigation into the assault.
examples.analytical: Courts have debated whether prolonged administrative segregation amounts to cruel and unusual punishment, since it is imposed without a criminal sentence.

nuance.analogy: Like a quarantine room inside a building: people are separated not as punishment for a crime but to manage a risk to everyone else.
nuance.etymology: Administrative comes from Latin administrare, to manage; segregation comes from Latin segregare, to separate from the flock.
common_mistakes: Saying 'administrative isolation' or 'administrative solitary' instead of the set phrase 'administrative segregation'.
Stressing the first syllable of administrative as 'AD-min-is-tray-tive' with a strong final -tive, instead of stressing MIN and reducing the other syllables.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being admissible or allowable.

core.definition: The quality of being allowed or acceptable, especially whether evidence or a claim can be accepted in a legal, formal, or technical setting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BIL, the third syllable from the start of the stressed part, and reduce the vowels in the earlier syllables. The -ity ending is pronounced 'ih-tee', with a short i and a long e at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes whether something may be accepted under rules, without judging its truth or value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use admissibility mostly in law, especially in discussions of evidence in court, and also in academic, scientific, and regulatory contexts. Casual conversation usually uses 'whether it can be used' or 'whether it counts'. In legal settings, people often speak of 'the admissibility of evidence' or an 'admissibility hearing'.

distinctions.note: Admission means either entry into a place or a confession, while admissibility refers to whether evidence or a claim is allowed to be used.
Validity refers to whether an argument or test is logically or scientifically sound, whereas admissibility refers to whether it is allowed under the rules of a process.

examples.everyday: My lawyer friend says the judge will decide the admissibility of that text message at the hearing.
examples.professional: Before we rely on the survey results in the regulatory filing, we need to check their admissibility under the agency's standards.
examples.analytical: The admissibility of expert testimony depends less on its conclusions than on whether the method behind it is reliable and tested.

nuance.analogy: Like a bouncer checking names against a guest list: the question is whether you are allowed in, not whether you are a good guest.
nuance.etymology: From admissible plus the suffix -ity; admissible comes from Latin admittere, to admit.
common_mistakes: Confusing admissibility with admission, which has a different meaning in everyday English.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'ad-MISS-ih-bil-ih-tee', instead of stressing BIL.

senses.definition: In or into a drifting condition; moved (especially on water by waves and wind) without being propelled or steered.
senses.example: After the engine failed, our small boat stayed adrift for two days.

senses.definition: Not in the expected or usual place or position; awry; also, not following the expected or usual course; astray, off course.
senses.example: Without clear goals, the project quickly went adrift and missed every milestone.

senses.definition: In an unattached or unfastened condition; apart, loose, off.
senses.example: The storm tore a bracket loose, and the sign came adrift.

senses.definition: Drifting (especially on water) without being propelled or steered.
senses.example: The coast guard reported an adrift sailboat about forty miles offshore.

senses.definition: Of a person or group of people: having no aim or direction; aimless, lost.
senses.example: The team were six points adrift of their rivals.

senses.definition: Of a sailor: absent without leave or permission.
senses.example: The navy listed him as adrift after he missed muster for three days.

senses.definition: Of an object: no longer attached in position; detached, loose, unattached, unfastened; also, lost, missing.
senses.example: The rear wheel was adrift after the bolts had worked loose on the trailer.

core.definition: Floating without control on water or wind; or, lost and without direction, especially in one's life or plans.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, DRIFT, and keep the short i like the vowel in 'ship', not the long 'ee'. The final t is a clear, unreleased t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for boats and objects; often sad or negative when used for people who lack direction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adrift for boats, objects and people. For a person, it suggests a loss of direction, often after a breakup, job loss or move, as in 'I felt a bit adrift after college.' Cut adrift means to abandon someone without support, and set adrift means to send something out to float away.

distinctions.note: Lost means you don't know where you are or how to proceed; adrift suggests being carried along without control or purpose over time.
Aimless describes a lack of goals; adrift often describes a feeling or state of drifting after loss or change.
Afloat means staying on top of water or staying financially solvent; adrift means moving without control.

examples.everyday: After she moved to a new city, she felt a bit adrift for a few months.
examples.professional: Without a clear roadmap, the project team felt adrift and kept changing priorities every sprint.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's writing often describes the self adrift, struggling to find a secure foundation for meaning.

nuance.analogy: Adrift is like a rowboat that has lost its oars: it still moves, but it goes wherever the current takes it.
nuance.etymology: From a- (in a state of) plus drift, from Old Norse drift 'a driving, snowdrift'.
common_mistakes: Using adrift for an object that is just in the wrong place; it implies movement with no control.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long 'ee', as in uh-DREEFT.

adrift.etymology: The is derived from *a-* + *drift*, probably modelled after *afloat*.

senses.definition: In an affected manner; hypocritically; with more show than reality.

core.definition: In a pretentious or insincere way, showing feelings or manners that are more show than real.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, FEK. The middle syllable is a short 'id' sound, and the final -ly is a quick 'lee', not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes someone for putting on airs or pretending to feel or be something they are not.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use affectedly mostly in writing, reviews, and literary criticism, and it is less common in speech. In casual talk people more often say someone is 'putting on' a voice or acting 'fake'. Describing a person as speaking affectedly is a sharp criticism, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Sincerely describes genuine feeling; affectedly describes a show of feeling that is not genuine.
Affectionately means warmly and lovingly; affectedly means in a fake or showy way, and the two are easily confused.

examples.everyday: She kept saying 'darling' to the waiter, and she laughed so affectedly that my friend and I couldn't stop smirking.
examples.professional: During the offsite, the new director spoke affectedly about 'synergy,' and the team could tell he didn't believe a word of it.
examples.analytical: The narrator describes the aristocrat's manners as affectedly refined, which signals to the reader that his civility is a performance rather than a virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a plastic flower that looks real from across the room but has no life when you touch it.
nuance.etymology: From affected plus -ly; affect comes from Latin affectare, 'to aim at, strive after'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with effectively (in a successful way) or affectionately (warmly).
Stressing the last syllable; the stress belongs on FEK.

senses.definition: Emotional detachment; a lack of feeling.

core.definition: Emotional detachment; a lack of feeling or emotional response to people or events.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FEKT. Each reduced syllable is quick: -less becomes 'luhs' and -ness becomes 'nuhs'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an emotional flatness that is often seen as troubling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use affectlessness mostly in psychology, psychiatry, and literary criticism. In everyday conversation people say 'he seems cold' or 'she shows no feeling.' The word is precise and clinical, so it works best in professional writing about detachment.

distinctions.note: Apathy means lack of interest or motivation; affectlessness means lack of emotional response.
Detachment can be calm and chosen; affectlessness suggests a deeper, often troubling absence of feeling.

examples.everyday: After the accident he seemed to show no feeling at all, and his family said the affectlessness scared them.
examples.professional: The HR report noted a pattern of affectlessness in the manager's feedback, which the team found unsettling.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator shows a chilling affectlessness, recounting murder with the same tone he uses for the weather.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio tuned to a station with no music, all static and no feeling.
nuance.etymology: From affectless plus -ness; affect comes from Latin affectus, 'state of mind or feeling'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on FEKT, not on -less.
Confusing it with apathy, which refers to a lack of interest rather than feeling.

senses.definition: Eagerness; liveliness; enthusiasm.
senses.example: She accepted the invitation with alacrity, already picking out a dress.

senses.definition: Promptness; speed.
senses.example: The support team responded to our ticket with remarkable alacrity.

core.definition: Cheerful, eager readiness to do something, often shown by quick action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LAK. The a is short, as in 'cat', not 'lay', and the final -ty is a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests enthusiasm and prompt, willing action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alacrity in formal writing and occasionally in speech to describe eagerness, as in 'She accepted the offer with alacrity.' It sounds a bit formal, so in casual talk people say 'right away' or 'super quick' instead. The phrase 'with alacrity' is the usual pattern.

distinctions.note: Enthusiasm is a general strong interest; alacrity specifically means prompt, willing action in response to a request or opportunity.
Eagerness is common and everyday; alacrity is more formal and adds an emphasis on speed.

examples.everyday: When I asked if she could pick up the kids, she said yes with real alacrity.
examples.professional: The vendor responded with alacrity once we escalated the issue to their account manager.
examples.analytical: On Aristotle's account, virtue shows itself in a readiness to act well with alacrity rather than with reluctance.

nuance.analogy: Like a sprinter who leaps off the starting block the moment the gun sounds.
nuance.etymology: From Latin alacritas, from alacer, meaning brisk or lively.
common_mistakes: Using alacrity to mean speed alone; it also implies eagerness and willingness.
Pronouncing the a as in 'lay'; it is short, as in 'cat'.

alacrity.etymology: Mid-15th century; from Middle English *alacrite*, from Latin *alacritās*, from *alacer* (“brisk”) + *-itās* (“-ity”).

senses.definition: A branch of mathematics that studies algebraic varieties (solution sets of polynomial equations) and their generalizations, using techniques from both algebra (chiefly commutative algebra) and geometry.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that studies solution sets of polynomial equations, combining methods from algebra and geometry.

pronunciation.tip: There are two main stresses, on BRAY and AH. The g in geometry is a j sound, the first o is a short ee sound, and the final -try is -tree.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise name for an advanced mathematical field.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the term in university mathematics, mostly in graduate courses and research seminars. It names a field, so say I study algebraic geometry rather than an algebraic geometry. Outside mathematics, people will not recognize the term without context.

distinctions.note: Differential geometry uses calculus to study smooth curved spaces, while algebraic geometry uses polynomial equations and commutative algebra.
Algebra is the broader study of operations and structures; algebraic geometry applies algebra to shapes defined by equations.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law is a mathematician, and he says algebraic geometry is the most beautiful subject he ever studied.
examples.professional: Our data group is working with an algebraic geometry team to test a new method for nonlinear model fitting.
examples.analytical: Algebraic geometry studies varieties over fields, showing that the geometry of a solution set is encoded in the algebra of the polynomials that define it.

nuance.analogy: The polynomial equations are the blueprint, and the shape formed by their solutions is the building.
nuance.etymology: Algebra comes from Arabic al-jabr; geometry comes from Greek geōmetria, earth measurement.
common_mistakes: Saying an algebraic geometry when naming the field
Confusing it with the ordinary high school geometry of triangles and circles
Putting the stress on the second syllable of geometry, as in al-juh-bray-ik juh-OM-uh-tree

senses.definition: The plea or mode of defense under which a person on trial for a crime proves or attempts to prove being in another place when the alleged act was committed.
senses.example: to set up an alibi

senses.definition: An excuse, especially one used to avoid responsibility or blame.
senses.example: Her alibi for missing the meeting was a flat tire, which her coworkers found hard to believe.

senses.definition: To provide an alibi for.
senses.example: Her roommate was willing to alibi her for the night of the party.

senses.definition: To provide an excuse for.
senses.example: She tried to alibi her late arrival with a story about the subway breaking down.

core.definition: Proof or a claim that you were somewhere else when a crime happened, so you could not have committed it; also an excuse for not being responsible.

pronunciation.tip: Put the stress on the first syllable, and make the middle syllable a weak 'uh'. Do not say uh-LIE-bye or ah-LAH-bee, which are common learner errors.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the legal sense. In everyday speech it is often negative, since it suggests someone is making up an excuse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know this word mainly from courtroom dramas and crime shows. In everyday conversation, people use it jokingly for a made-up excuse, as in 'Do you have an alibi for being late?' A natural reply is to give your real reason or say 'Fair enough, I was stuck in traffic.'

distinctions.note: An alibi specifically places you somewhere else at the time of an event; an excuse can be any reason, such as being sick or tired.
A defense is any argument against a charge, while an alibi is one specific kind of defense that claims the defendant was elsewhere.

examples.everyday: Don't give me that traffic alibi again, you've used it three times this month!
examples.professional: Please stop using the 'my laptop crashed' alibi every time a deadline slips, and just tell us what happened.
examples.analytical: A credible alibi forces the prosecution to explain how the defendant could have been present at the scene despite the evidence of absence.

nuance.analogy: Like a store receipt proving you were across town when the item was stolen, so you could not have been the person who took it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin alibi, meaning 'elsewhere', from alius, meaning 'other'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it uh-LIE-bye with stress on the second syllable.
Using alibi for any small reason for being late, which can sound sarcastic or accusatory.
Assuming alibi is a common verb in everyday speech; as a verb it is rare and mostly legal.

alibi.etymology: From the 18th century, from Latin *alibī* (“elsewhere, at another place”).

senses.definition: The quality of being alienable.
An alienable transfer or sale.
senses.example: The contract's clause on alienability barred any sale of the land for ten years.

core.definition: The quality of property or a right being able to be legally transferred or sold to another owner.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the -bil- syllable, in the same position as in 'ability', not on the first syllable. The -ity ending becomes a reduced 'uh-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise legal or philosophical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in law, property, finance, and philosophy. In everyday business talk they more often say 'transferability' or 'can be sold'. Lawyers may use it to describe restrictions on selling land, shares, or rights.

distinctions.note: Transferability is the broader and more common everyday term, while alienability focuses on the legal power to transfer ownership.
Alienation means emotional estrangement or isolation, which has no connection to legal transfer.

examples.everyday: Our lawyer said the land has limited alienability because the family trust forbids selling it.
examples.professional: The bylaws restrict the alienability of founders' shares until the lockup period ends.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that human dignity places limits on the alienability of certain rights.

nuance.analogy: Alienability is like the 'for sale' sign on a house: it shows whether ownership can legally pass to someone else.
nuance.etymology: From alienable, from Latin alienare 'to transfer to another', with the suffix '-ability'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'alienation', which refers to emotional isolation.
Putting the main stress on the first syllable instead of the -bil- syllable.

senses.definition: Very great or powerful, used for emphasis ("the almighty dollar", "an almighty crash").

core.definition: Having unlimited power over all things; used as a title for God in religious speech, and in everyday use for something that seems overwhelmingly powerful.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MY, and the t in 'mighty' is a flap, so it sounds like 'MY-dee'. The gh is silent, and the first syllable is the 'aw' of 'all'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or reverent in religious speech; in everyday talk it can be ironic, as in 'the almighty dollar' or 'the almighty boss'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Almighty mainly in prayer, sermons and religious talk, as in 'Almighty God', and it is capitalized when it refers to God. In casual speech, 'God Almighty!' is a strong exclamation of surprise or frustration, and in humor 'the almighty' can mock a powerful person or institution. A natural reply to an exclamation is simply to laugh or ask what happened.

distinctions.note: Mighty means very strong or powerful, while almighty means having unlimited power; a mighty river is not almighty.
Omnipotent is the technical term in philosophy and theology for unlimited power; almighty is the everyday and biblical term.
Powerful is a neutral, everyday word for strength or influence, while almighty suggests absolute and unlimited power.

examples.everyday: After the flight was delayed for six hours, my brother said, 'God Almighty, what now?'
examples.professional: The old approval process treated the legacy system as almighty, so every new feature was blocked until it was rewritten.
examples.analytical: Christian theology affirms that God is almighty, yet it also holds that God freely limits divine power by entering covenant with creatures.

nuance.analogy: Almighty is like a power switch with no upper limit: there is nothing it cannot reach, and nothing that can override it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ælmihtig, from all 'all' and mihtig 'mighty'.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'all mighty', in formal writing; the standard form is one word, 'Almighty'.
Pronouncing the gh as a sound, or saying the t clearly instead of the American flap in 'mighty'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name El Shaddai is often rendered God Almighty, and the Greek pantokratōr, meaning ruler of all, is used for God in Revelation. Genesis 17:1 records God revealing himself to Abram as God Almighty, and Revelation 4:8 presents God Almighty as the one who is holy and sovereign. Ruth 1:20 has Naomi say that the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her in her grief.

almighty.etymology: From Middle English *almyghty*, *almighty*, from Old English *ælmihtiġ* (“all-powerful”), from Proto-Germanic **alamahtīgaz*, equivalent to *al-* + *might* + *-y*.

senses.definition: Synonym of alter ego.

core.definition: A rare, nonstandard Latin-style variant of alter ego, meaning another self; in English, the standard form is alter ego.

pronunciation.tip: Treat idem as Latin, pronounced with a short 'i' like 'ID-em', with the main stress on the first word. Do not confuse it with 'idea' or 'ID'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a rare variant that may look like a mistake to most readers.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will not recognize alter idem, and in ordinary speech it may sound like a mistake for alter ego. It appears occasionally in older or Latin-influenced writing, so use alter ego in conversation, email and academic writing. If you see it in a text, understand it as another self.

distinctions.note: Alter ego is the standard English phrase and the one Americans use, while alter idem is rare and may seem like a mistake.
Persona means a social role, while alter idem, like alter ego, means a second self or identity.

examples.everyday: I've seen alter idem written somewhere, but people usually just say alter ego.
examples.professional: Please use alter ego in the report, since alter idem looks nonstandard to most readers.
examples.analytical: The phrase alter idem appears in some older Latin-inspired writing, though modern English has standardized on alter ego.

nuance.analogy: Like a typo that survived long enough to look like a word.
nuance.etymology: Latin alter, 'other', plus idem, 'the same'; a nonstandard combination.
common_mistakes: Using alter idem in ordinary conversation, where most Americans will think it is a mistake.
Confusing it with the standard form alter ego.

senses.definition: A kind of car in drag racing, usually with a partial body situated behind the exposed engine.
senses.example: On Saturday night, the altered in the far lane pulled a huge wheelie off the line.

senses.definition: Having been changed from an original form.
Neutered; having had testicles or uterus and ovaries removed to prevent procreation.
senses.example: The veterinarian said the altered cat would be calmer and less likely to roam.

core.definition: Changed from its original form, shape, state, or meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Say two syllables, not three: AWL-terd. The t is a light flap, and the ending is a plain d sound after the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it simply reports a change. It can imply something was deliberately or significantly changed, as in an altered photo or altered plans.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use altered for things that have been changed from their original state: altered plans, an altered schedule, an altered state of consciousness, or a photo that has been edited. For minor adjustments, changed or adjusted is more natural. In a casual conversation, 'the plans changed' is more common than 'the plans were altered'. The car sense, a drag-racing vehicle, is specialized and rare in everyday use.

distinctions.note: Changed is broader and more everyday; altered suggests a noticeable change to something's form or character.
Modified implies a deliberate, usually limited adjustment to a design or system; altered can describe any noticeable change, including unplanned ones.

examples.everyday: The plans were altered at the last minute because of the rain.
examples.professional: The project scope was altered after the client changed its requirements in March.
examples.analytical: Locke argues that a person's identity is not altered merely because the body that houses it is replaced.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that moves its bed after a flood: the land is still there, but its course is no longer the same.
nuance.etymology: From alter, from Latin alter, other.
common_mistakes: Spelling it alterated; the past participle is altered.
Using altered when changed is more natural in everyday conversation.
Saying it as three syllables; it is two: AWL-terd.

senses.definition: Any of various herbs of the genus Amaranthus.
senses.example: The garden center sold amaranth seedlings with bright red plumes that attract hummingbirds.

senses.definition: The characteristic purplish-red color of the flowers or leaves of these plants.
senses.example: amaranth:

senses.definition: A red to purple azo dye used as a biological stain, and in some countries in cosmetics and as a food coloring. See Amaranth (dye).
senses.example: The lab used amaranth as a red biological stain to highlight the cell walls.

senses.definition: The seed of these plants, used as a cereal.
senses.example: For breakfast she mixed amaranth into her oatmeal for extra protein and fiber.

senses.definition: (dated, poetic) An imaginary flower that does not wither.
senses.example: The poet promised that their love would bloom like amaranth, forever untouched by winter.
senses.label: dated, poetic

core.definition: A purplish-red color, or a plant whose flowers or leaves have this color.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AM. The 'r' is pronounced clearly, and the 'th' at the end is unvoiced, as in 'thin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to poetic. It is usually a color word in descriptions, sometimes with a literary or symbolic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use amaranth mostly in fashion, design, botany or poetry. In everyday talk, people usually say 'deep purple' or 'reddish-purple'. The word is less common than the color names people use daily.

distinctions.note: Magenta is a bright purplish-red used in printing and digital design. Amaranth is a deeper, more muted purplish-red.
Maroon is a dark brownish red. Amaranth is more purple and brighter.

examples.everyday: She painted the bedroom a deep amaranth that looks almost purple at night.
examples.professional: The design team chose amaranth as the accent color for the error banner.
examples.analytical: The poet's images of amaranth and gold evoke both mortality and glory.

nuance.analogy: Like a plum seen in dim evening light: rich, deep, and between red and purple.
nuance.etymology: From Latin amarantus, from Greek amarantos, 'unfading'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying am-AIR-anth.
Confusing amaranth the plant with amaranthine, the adjective meaning unfading.

amaranth.etymology: Borrowed from French *amarante*, or directly from its etymon Latin *amarantus* (the word ending influenced by plant names derived from *ἄνθος* (“a bloom, blossom, flower”)), from Ancient Greek *ἀμάραντος* (“eternal, undying, unfading, unwilting; amaranth;…

senses.definition: In an amorous or loving manner.

core.definition: In a loving or romantic way, often with sexual desire or flirtation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AM, and the second syllable is a weak schwa. The r in the middle is pronounced clearly, and the final syllable is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing affection, but it can sound suggestive or intrusive if used about someone without their consent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'amorously' mostly in writing and descriptions of romance, such as in a novel or a movie review. In everyday talk, people often say 'romantically' or 'flirtatiously' instead. The word can sound a little formal or dated in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: 'Romantically' is the everyday word for a loving or romantic relationship, while 'amorously' emphasizes physical desire or flirtation.
'Flirtatiously' suggests playful, teasing behavior, while 'amorously' can be more intense and sensual.

examples.everyday: He looked at her amorously across the table, and everyone at the restaurant noticed.
examples.professional: The brand's video shows the couple gazing amorously at the product, which might come across as too suggestive for a family audience.
examples.analytical: The novel describes the protagonist's desire amorously, but the narrative voice increasingly questions the nature of her love.

nuance.analogy: An amorous glance is like a warm lamp left on in a window: it signals that someone is inside and interested.
nuance.etymology: From amorous, from Old French amoreus, from Medieval Latin amorosus, from Latin amor 'love'.
common_mistakes: Using 'amorously' to mean 'lovingly' in every situation; it often suggests romance or desire, not just affection.
Using the adjective 'amorous' where you need the adverb 'amorously'.

core.definition: A Levite town in the land of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, the home of the priest Abiathar and the prophet Jeremiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AN, and the two 'th' sounds are voiceless as in 'thin.' The final vowel is the long o in 'go,' not the 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a place name used in Bible study and sermons.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would say this word only when discussing the Bible, Jeremiah or Old Testament geography. In a sermon or class, you might hear 'Jeremiah from Anathoth' as a standard way to identify the prophet.

distinctions.note: Anath is a personal name in Judges, while Anathoth is a town in Benjamin.
Jerusalem was the capital, and Anathoth was a village a few miles northeast, which explains why its priests were sent there.

examples.everyday: Our pastor said Jeremiah was from a small village called Anathoth, not from Jerusalem.
examples.professional: For the Jeremiah lesson, I added a map showing Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah's identification as one of the priests of Anathoth grounds his prophetic message in a community that rejected him, as Jeremiah 11:21-23 describes.

nuance.analogy: Anathoth is like a small hometown that is famous only because a famous person came from it.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew place name Anatot, of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (uh-NATH-oth) instead of AN.
Mixing it up with Anath, the personal name in Judges.
nuance.biblical_note: Anathoth was a Levitical city in the land of Benjamin (Joshua 21:18). Jeremiah 1:1 identifies Jeremiah as a priest from Anathoth. Jeremiah 11:21-23 reports a threat from the men of Anathoth against the prophet's life, and Jeremiah 32:6-9 describes his purchase of a field there. 1 Kings 2:26 records Solomon sending the priest Abiathar away to Anathoth.

senses.definition: As a coordinating conjunction; expressing two elements to be taken together or in addition to each other.
senses.example: I'd been walking since sunrise, and I was hungry.

senses.definition: Used simply to connect two noun phrases, adjectives or adverbs.
Simply connecting two clauses or sentences.
Introducing a clause or sentence which follows on in time or consequence from the first.
senses.example: I'd been walking since sunrise, and I was hungry.

senses.definition: Used to connect certain numbers: connecting units when they precede tens; connecting shillings to pence in a monetary quantity; connecting tens and units to hundreds, thousands etc. (now often omitted in US); to connect fractions to wholes.
Used to connect more than two elements together in a chain, sometimes to stress the number of elements.
Connecting two identical elements, with implications of continued or infinite repetition.
Introducing a parenthetical or explanatory clause.
Introducing the continuation of narration from a previous understood point; also used alone as a question: 'and so what?'.
Introducing a qualitative difference between things having the same name; "as well as other".
Used to combine numbers in addition; plus (with singular or plural verb).
senses.example: Two and two is/are four.

senses.definition: Expressing a condition.
Connecting two well-formed formulas to create a new well-formed formula that requires it to only be true when both of the two formulas are true.
Sea smoke; steam fog.
In rhythm, the second half of a divided beat.

core.definition: A word used to join two words, phrases or clauses, meaning in addition to or together with.

pronunciation.tip: In normal speech 'and' is usually reduced to 'uhnd' or just 'n', as in 'bread 'n' butter'. Only say the full /æ/ vowel when you are emphasizing it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It has no emotional charge and is used in every register.
nuance.usage_note: Americans reduce 'and' heavily in casual speech, so you will hear 'salt n' pepper' or 'rock 'n' roll'. In writing, keep the full word, especially in formal documents. Starting a sentence with 'And' is common in American fiction and informal writing, but may be considered too casual in some academic or business contexts.

distinctions.note: And combines elements that are both included; or offers a choice between alternatives.
And adds information in the same direction; but signals a contrast or exception.
Plus is informal and usually connects numbers, facts or benefits in speech; and is the standard word in writing.

examples.everyday: Can I get a burger and fries, please?
examples.professional: The model handles missing values and outliers before we train it.
examples.analytical: For Augustine, justice and mercy are not opposites but inseparable expressions of God's love.

nuance.analogy: And is like a bridge between two islands: it lets ideas travel from one to the other without changing either.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'and' or 'ond', meaning also or in addition.
common_mistakes: Writing 'try and' in formal writing; standard usage is 'try to', although 'try and' is common in speech.
Overusing 'and' to link too many clauses in writing, creating run-on sentences.

and.etymology: Middle English *and*, *an*, from Old English *and*, *ond*, *end*, from **andi*, from Proto-Germanic **andi*, **anþi*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₂énti* (“facing opposite, near, in front of, before”).

senses.definition: A robot that is designed to look and act like a human being (not necessarily a male one).
An artificial human.
Possessing human qualities.
Characteristic of men.
senses.example: an android fat distribution

senses.definition: Of the pelvis, having a narrow anterior segment and a heart-shaped brim, typically found in the male.

core.definition: A robot designed to look and act like a human being, not necessarily male.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AN, and the second syllable is a short, reduced uh. The final syllable rhymes with void, and the r is pronounced, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a technology, and in casual speech it may be used as a joke about someone seeming robotic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use android for a human-like robot in science fiction, AI discussions, and robotics news, and in technical contexts they may say humanoid instead. Capital-A Android is also Google's mobile operating system, so Android phone refers to a phone rather than a robot. Calling a person an android is informal and mostly a joke.

distinctions.note: A humanoid is any robot with a human-like body shape, but it need not be designed to pass as human; an android is meant to look and act like a person.
A cyborg is a human body enhanced with machine parts; an android is a fully artificial machine made to resemble a person.

examples.everyday: I watched a movie where an android goes undercover in a hospital, and it was so creepy that I couldn't sleep.
examples.professional: Our robotics group is testing an android prototype for customer service, but the team is still arguing about how human it should look.
examples.analytical: The android in the novel forces us to ask whether a perfect imitation of human behavior would still count as a person.

nuance.analogy: An android is like a lifelike wax figure that moves and speaks, built from circuits and motors instead of muscle and bone.
nuance.etymology: From Greek andro- 'man' and the suffix -oid 'resembling', so 'manlike'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying an-DROID, which is not standard.
Using android for any robot; a robot that does not look human is usually called a robot, not an android.

senses.definition: A physician who specializes in anesthesiology and administers anesthesia.

core.definition: A medical doctor who specializes in anesthesiology and gives anesthesia so that surgery can be done without pain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AH, the syllable in the -ology part, not on the earlier THEE as in anesthesia. The th is voiceless, as in think, and the final -ist is reduced to ist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reassuring; the role is respected and tied to patient safety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use anesthesiologist for the physician who puts patients to sleep or numbs them for surgery. Patients may also meet a nurse anesthetist, which is a different role. In everyday talk people often say the anesthesiologist or the anesthesia doctor, and the American spelling uses a single s, while British English uses anaesthetist.

distinctions.note: Anesthetist is a broader term that may refer to a nurse anesthetist, who is not a physician; an anesthesiologist is always a medical doctor.
Anesthetic is the drug or agent that causes numbness or sleep; anesthesiologist is the person who gives it.

examples.everyday: The anesthesiologist came into my room before the surgery and explained exactly what the medicine would feel like.
examples.professional: The anesthesiologist on our hospital team reviewed the patient's medication history before scheduling the procedure.
examples.analytical: The anesthesiologist's role in surgical safety raises questions about how responsibility should be divided among surgeon, nurse, and physician.

nuance.analogy: An anesthesiologist is like the pilot who manages cabin pressure and oxygen during a flight, keeping the passengers safe while the main work happens elsewhere.
nuance.etymology: From Greek an- 'without', aisthesis 'sensation', plus -logia 'study of' and -ist 'one who practices'.
common_mistakes: Confusing anesthesiologist with anesthetist or nurse anesthetist, who may be a nurse rather than a doctor.
Shifting the stress wrongly: anesthesia is an-ess-THEE-zhuh, but anesthesiologist moves the stress to AH.

senses.definition: (poetic) Again, once more; afresh, in a new way, newly.
senses.example: Each morning, opportunity—like the sun—dawns anew.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: Again, in a new and fresh way, as if starting over.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: uh-NOO. In American English the vowel is 'oo', not 'yoo'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and hopeful, suggesting renewal or a fresh start.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in writing, speeches, sermons and poetry. In casual speech they usually say 'again' or 'from scratch'. It often follows the verb, as in 'start anew' or 'begin anew'.

distinctions.note: Again simply means one more time; anew adds the idea of a fresh approach.
Afresh is nearly identical but sounds more British and rarer in the US.
Newly means recently, as in 'newly built'; it does not mean starting over.

examples.everyday: After the move, we decided to start anew and make some new friends.
examples.professional: Given the data errors, the team will need to rebuild the model anew.
examples.analytical: The prophets call Israel to turn back to God and live anew under the covenant.

nuance.analogy: Like turning to a clean page in a notebook.
nuance.etymology: Middle English, from Old English of niwe, 'from new'.
common_mistakes: Using it for 'recently' (say 'newly').
Pronouncing it 'uh-NYOO'; American speakers say uh-NOO.
Placing it before the verb in casual speech, where it sounds stiff.
nuance.biblical_note: Modern English versions use 'anew' for ideas of renewal. In John 3:3, Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born anew (the RSV also gives 'from above' in the margin), from Greek anothen, meaning both 'again' and 'from above'. This double meaning explains Nicodemus's confusion in 3:4.

anew.etymology: From Middle English *onew*, *of newe*, from Old English *of niowe*.

senses.definition: Arranged so as to form an angle.
senses.example: She set the mirror at an angled position so the sunlight reflected onto the wall.

senses.definition: Forming an angle of a particular type.
senses.example: the right-angled corner

core.definition: Set or formed at an angle, so that it is not straight, flat or level.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and do not add an extra syllable before the d. After the l, the -ed ending is pronounced as a plain d, as in 'angld.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes shape or position and carries no positive or negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'angled' in home improvement, design, photography and sports descriptions, such as 'an angled roof' or 'an angled cut.' It is a practical everyday word, and in casual speech people also use 'slanted' for a tilted surface.

distinctions.note: Slanted means tilted or sloping in one direction, while angled emphasizes a definite corner or angle.
Diagonal describes a line running corner to corner across a shape, whereas angled describes any surface set at an angle.
Angular describes sharp, pointed features, such as a jawline, and is often used for appearance, whereas angled is about position.

examples.everyday: The kitchen has an angled ceiling, so the top shelf is hard to reach without a step stool.
examples.professional: The sensor is mounted on an angled bracket so that it can see the entire loading dock.
examples.analytical: The essay's argument is angled toward skeptical readers, so it anticipates their objections rather than simply stating its thesis.

nuance.analogy: An angled surface is like a ramp rather than a staircase: it is neither flat nor vertical, but tilted at a definite slope.
nuance.etymology: From angle, from Latin angulus, 'corner,' with the past participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, as in ANG-guh-led, instead of one syllable ending in d.
Using 'angled' for a simple tilt when 'slanted' is more natural in everyday speech.

senses.definition: The skeletal joint which connects the foot with the leg; the uppermost portion of the foot and lowermost portion of the leg, which contain this skeletal joint.
senses.example: She twisted her ankle on the icy steps and couldn't put any weight on it.

senses.definition: To walk.
senses.example: We ankled over to the diner after the lecture, too tired to find parking.

senses.definition: To cyclically angle the foot at the ankle while pedaling, to maximize the amount of work applied to the pedal during each revolution.
senses.example: Good cyclists ankle smoothly through each pedal stroke to squeeze out extra power on climbs.

core.definition: The joint that connects the foot with the lower leg, where the shinbone and fibula meet the foot bones.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short a as in cat, then ng, then a reduced syllable kul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain anatomical word used in everyday medical and sports talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ankle in everyday talk about injuries, clothing, shoes and exercise. Sprained ankle is the usual phrase for the injury. The verb sense in the source, to walk, is old-fashioned or dialect, and the cycling sense is technical.

distinctions.note: The heel is the back of the foot below the ankle. The ankle is the joint above the foot.
The foot is the whole part below the leg. The ankle is only the joint between the foot and the leg.

examples.everyday: I twisted my ankle on the stairs, so I'm icing it and skipping the hike.
examples.professional: The warehouse manager said the ankle injury would keep him off the forklift for six weeks.
examples.analytical: The ankle is formed where the tibia, fibula and talus meet, which is why a sprain can affect stability for months.

nuance.analogy: The ankle is like a door hinge between the leg and the foot. It moves up and down so the foot can point and lift.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ancleow, related to Old High German anchal.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as AY-ankle, copying the transcription's diphthong.
Using ankle for the heel or the whole foot.
nuance.biblical_note: Acts 3:7 describes the lame man at the Temple gate whose feet and ankle bones are made strong when Peter heals him. The Greek word is sphyra, meaning ankle or ankle bone.

ankle.etymology: From Middle English *ankel*, *ancle*, *ankyll*, from Old English *ancol* (compare *anclēow* (“ankle”) > Modern, *ancliff*, *ancley*), from **ankul*, from Proto-Germanic **ankulaz* (“ankle”); akin to, *ökli*, *enklaauw*, and perhaps, *ancha* (“thigh,…

senses.definition: Ellipsis of anorexia nervosa.
Any state of being psychologically starved or deprived of something.
senses.example: intimacy anorexia; emotional anorexia

senses.definition: Loss of appetite, especially as a result of disease.
senses.example: The chemotherapy caused anorexia, so she struggled to eat even small meals.

core.definition: A serious eating disorder in which a person refuses to eat enough and becomes dangerously underweight, driven by fear of gaining weight.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on REK, and the 'x' is pronounced 'ks'. The final '-ia' sounds like 'ee-uh', not 'ay-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it names a serious illness, so it should be used respectfully and not as a casual joke.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in health contexts say 'anorexia' or 'an eating disorder' with care. Calling yourself 'so anorexic' after a missed meal is considered insensitive. Full clinical name is 'anorexia nervosa', but 'anorexia' alone is standard in conversation.

distinctions.note: Anorexia nervosa is the full clinical name for the eating disorder; 'anorexia' alone is the common short form.
Loss of appetite is a symptom of many illnesses; anorexia in the eating disorder sense involves restriction and fear of weight gain.

examples.everyday: My sister had anorexia in college, and she is doing much better with therapy now.
examples.professional: The school nurse said we should call a counselor if a student shows signs of anorexia.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether anorexia is primarily a problem of body image, of control, or of both at once.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire starved of fuel, the body slowly burns down while the warning signs are ignored.
nuance.etymology: From Greek an- 'without' plus orexis 'appetite'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in AN-er-EX-ee-uh instead of an-er-REK-see-uh.
Using anorexia casually for someone who is just thin or not very hungry.

senses.definition: In Greek choruses and dances, the returning of the chorus, exactly answering to a previous strophe or movement from right to left.
senses.example: In the Greek tragedy, the chorus performed the strophe, then the antistrophe, moving in the opposite direction.

senses.definition: The lines of this part of the choral song.
senses.example: The second antistrophe echoed the rhythm and imagery of the opening stanza exactly.

senses.definition: The repetition of words in an inverse order.
senses.example: The preacher's line 'Life is for the people, not people for life' is a perfect antistrophe.

senses.definition: The repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses.
senses.example: The sermon relied on antistrophe, ending each clause with the phrase 'by faith alone.'

core.definition: In ancient Greek choral odes, the second stanza, sung while the chorus moved back in the opposite direction after the strophe.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on TIS, the second syllable. The final -phe is pronounced 'fee' in American English, and the middle syllables reduce to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term from classical studies and poetics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet this word in literature, classics, or poetry courses, usually when discussing Greek tragedy or Pindar's odes. It is almost never used in everyday speech. In rhetoric, it is also used for the repetition of words in reverse order, but that sense is rare and less standard.

distinctions.note: The strophe is the first movement of the ode, sung as the chorus moved in one direction. The antistrophe answers it in the same metrical form.
The epode is the third, non-repeating section that follows the strophe and antistrophe pair.

examples.professional: In the seminar we compared the strophe and antistrophe of the chorus to see how the poet kept the meter balanced.
examples.analytical: The antistrophe mirrors the strophe metrically, so the structure of Pindar's odes depends on the paired stanzas and the epode that closes them.

nuance.analogy: It is like a call-and-response in which the second response has exactly the same shape as the first call.
nuance.etymology: From Greek antistrophē, 'a turning back,' from anti- (against) plus strephein, 'to turn.'
common_mistakes: Confusing antistrophe with strophe; the strophe comes first and the antistrophe answers it.
Using antistrophe as a general word for 'opposite' or 'contrary.'

antistrophe.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *antistrophe*, from Ancient Greek *ἀντιστροφή* (“turning about”).

senses.definition: A partial or total loss of language skills due to brain damage. Usually, damage to the left perisylvian region, including Broca's area and Wernicke's area, causes aphasia.
senses.example: After the stroke, my grandfather developed aphasia and struggled to find simple words.

core.definition: A loss or impairment of the ability to speak, understand, read or write, usually caused by damage to the brain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, FAY, and keep the initial ph as an f. Many Americans say the s as a zh sound, as in measure, so you may also hear uh-FAY-zhuh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical, but it can sound frightening to patients and families, so people usually discuss it gently.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, speech-language pathologists and hospital staff use aphasia when describing language problems after a stroke or head injury. Ordinary people often say trouble finding words or word-finding problems, which is softer and more natural in conversation. Aphasia affects language, not intelligence, and a person with aphasia can still think clearly.

distinctions.note: Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder where the muscles are weak or uncoordinated, so the words are hard to say, while aphasia affects the language itself.
Anomia is a specific difficulty recalling words, and it is one symptom of aphasia rather than the whole disorder.
Amnesia is memory loss, while aphasia is a problem with language, though both can follow brain injury.

examples.everyday: My dad had a stroke last year, and he has aphasia now, so he sometimes can't find the word he wants.
examples.professional: The speech therapist said the patient's aphasia is mild, so she can still do most of her work with a few accommodations.
examples.analytical: Studies of aphasia after left hemisphere lesions have shaped our understanding of how language is organized in the brain.

nuance.analogy: It is like having the right thoughts in your head but the wrong wiring between them and your mouth or ears.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aphasia, speechlessness, from a- meaning without and phasis meaning speech.
common_mistakes: Confusing aphasia with amnesia or with being unintelligent.
Pronouncing the initial ph as p.
Using aphasia for every speech problem, when dysarthria is a different condition.

aphasia.etymology: From French *aphasie*, from Ancient Greek *ἀφασία*, from *ἄφατος* (“speechless”), from *ἀ-* (“not”) + *φάσις* (“speech”).

senses.definition: A lens that has been corrected for spherical aberration and coma in order to produce a rectilinear image.

core.definition: A lens corrected for spherical aberration and coma, so it forms a sharp, nearly undistorted image.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, AP. The final syllable has a short a, rhyming with 'cat', not the long 'nate' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Only optics engineers, lens designers, and historians of photography use this term. Americans would more likely say corrected lens or achromatic lens, although aplanat appears in older optical texts.

distinctions.note: An achromat corrects chromatic aberration, the color fringing caused by different wavelengths, while an aplanat corrects spherical aberration and coma.
An apochromat corrects chromatic aberration more completely, often across three colors, while an aplanat focuses on shape-related errors.

examples.everyday: My camera club friend showed me a vintage lens he called an aplanat, and he swears it is sharper than newer ones.
examples.professional: The optics vendor quoted an aplanat objective, so we need to confirm its coma correction before we order.
examples.analytical: The aplanat design eliminates spherical aberration and coma for points near the axis, which is why it was prized in early photographic optics.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror polished to keep every reflected ray meeting at one point.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a-, 'without', and planē, 'wandering', describing rays that do not stray from their focus.
common_mistakes: Confusing aplanat with achromat; they correct different kinds of aberration.
Pronouncing the last syllable as a long 'nate', instead of a short 'nat'.

senses.definition: One who makes an apology.
senses.example: The apologist admitted his mistake and offered a sincere apology to the entire team.

senses.definition: One who speaks or writes in defense of a faith, a cause, or an institution.
Synonym of apologizer.
senses.example: Our office apologist always said sorry first, even when the mistake belonged to someone else.

core.definition: A person who defends a faith, cause or institution in speech or writing, especially a Christian who argues for the faith.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAH, the second syllable. The 'g' is /dʒ/ like 'j', and the middle syllable reduces to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or positive in religious circles (a defender of the faith). In political or media contexts it can be negative, implying someone excuses wrongdoing, as in 'an apologist for the regime'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for Christian thinkers like Justin Martyr or C. S. Lewis, and for defenders of a cause. Said of someone's politics it often sounds like criticism. It does not mean a person who says sorry.

distinctions.note: Defender is the general word; apologist suggests reasoned, public advocacy for a doctrine or cause.
An advocate argues for any cause, while an apologist usually defends something under attack and may seem to excuse it.
