Using it for a literal machine when speaking to Americans; it is mostly figurative for people.

blow-off-steam.etymology: Relief valves released the excess pressure in a steam engine to prevent the boiler from exploding.

conversation.text: After a long week, I like to go to the gym and blow off steam.
The kids need to blow off some steam at the park before dinner.
Sorry I snapped in the meeting. I was just blowing off steam.

senses.definition: A standard piece of program code used routinely and added with a text editor or word processor.
senses.example: Most of the login module is boilerplate, so I copied it from last month's project.

senses.definition: A sheet of metal.
senses.example: The welder cut a boilerplate sheet into strips for the new hull.

senses.definition: A sheet of copper or steel used in the construction of a boiler.
senses.example: The shop ordered steel boilerplate to patch the cracked boiler shell.

senses.definition: Any metal taking the form of sheets used in the construction of a boiler.
senses.example: Workers stacked the boilerplate by the loading dock before riveting the tank together.

senses.definition: A plate attached to industrial machinery, identifying information such as manufacturer, model number, serial number, and power requirements.
senses.example: Check the boilerplate on the compressor for its serial number before ordering parts.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) The rating plate or nameplate required to be affixed to a boiler by the Boiler Explosions Act (1882).
senses.example: The inspector confirmed the boilerplate met the 1882 Act's requirements before issuing the certificate.

senses.definition: A template.
senses.example: They put that boilerplate on all the warning labels.

senses.definition: Syndicated material; repeatable stories, articles or advertisements.
senses.example: The local paper filled its back pages with boilerplate from a national wire service.

senses.definition: A copy for the purpose of making other copies.
senses.example: The printer kept a clean boilerplate of the flyer to run new batches.

senses.definition: Standard text of a legal or official nature added to documents or labels.
senses.example: They put that boilerplate on all the warning labels.

senses.definition: A basic contract that can be modified to make different kinds of contracts.
senses.example: We signed a boilerplate agreement and then negotiated the pricing and delivery terms separately.

senses.definition: Formulaic or hackneyed language.
senses.example: His apology was pure boilerplate, with no mention of what he had actually done.

senses.definition: Tightly packed snow with a hard, icy crust on its surface, which may be dangerous for skiing.
senses.example: Racers found boilerplate on the lower slope, so their edges skidded across the icy surface.

senses.definition: Describing text or other material of a standard or routine nature.
senses.example: The contract contained all the usual boilerplate clauses.

senses.definition: Formulaic, stereotypical.
senses.example: The press release had a boilerplate opening that said nothing new.

senses.definition: Used to refer to a non-functional spacecraft used to test configuration and procedures.
senses.example: A boilerplate spacecraft was used to test the rocket.

senses.definition: To store standard text so that it can easily be retrieved for reuse.
senses.example: Store your signature block so you can boilerplate it into every outgoing email.

core.definition: Standard, pre-written language or text used again and again in documents such as contracts, emails, or code, with little or no change.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, and the second part, 'plate,' has a lighter secondary stress. The middle 'er' is a weak, reduced syllable, so do not pronounce it as 'ay' or 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests generic, unoriginal text, though it is a valued and necessary part of legal and technical work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boilerplate in business, legal, and software settings, as in 'That's just boilerplate language in the contract.' In casual speech, people might say 'that's just standard stuff' when they mean the same thing. It can also be an adjective, as in 'boilerplate disclaimer,' and calling a message boilerplate often implies it was not written for this specific situation.

distinctions.note: A template is a reusable form for creating new documents, while boilerplate is the fixed standard text that appears inside them.
A cliché is an overused phrase that weakens style, while boilerplate is standard legal or technical text that is intentionally repeated.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about that warning on the ticket, it's just boilerplate.
examples.professional: I'll reuse the boilerplate from our last statement of work and only update the pricing section.
examples.analytical: Much of the document is boilerplate, but the indemnity clause quietly shifts the risk onto the smaller party.

nuance.analogy: Boilerplate is like a form letter with blanks to fill in, where most of the words stay the same every time.
nuance.etymology: Originally a steel plate used in boiler construction, later a printing term for stereotyped plates, and then a general term for standard text.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'boiler' as 'bowler,' which changes the vowel sound completely.
Using boilerplate to describe a unique, customized document, where 'tailored' or 'custom' is the accurate word.

senses.definition: In good faith; genuinely, sincerely.
senses.example: The landlord agreed bona fide to return the deposit, which he did within a week.

senses.definition: In good faith; sincere; without deception or ulterior motive.
senses.example: Although he failed, the prime minister made a bona fide attempt to repair the nation's damaged economy.

senses.definition: Genuine; not counterfeit.
senses.example: This is a bona fide Roman coin.

core.definition: Genuine and real, not fake, forged or fraudulent; sincere and made in good faith.

pronunciation.tip: This is a Latin phrase with two stressed words, BOH-nuh and FYDE. Say the first word with a weak second syllable and pronounce the final d clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, since it affirms legitimacy. It can sound stiff or pompous in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bona fide in legal, business, academic and news writing: a bona fide expert, a bona fide offer. In casual talk, people say real, legit or the real deal. Use bona fide when you need to stress authenticity, not as a casual intensifier like really.

distinctions.note: Genuine is everyday and neutral, while bona fide is more formal and often legal or official, stressing good faith.
Authentic stresses true origin or reproduction, while bona fide stresses legitimacy and honest intent.

examples.everyday: Is that dealer bona fide, or should I be careful about the price?
examples.professional: Before we sign the contract, we need proof that the buyer is a bona fide investor.
examples.analytical: A bona fide inquiry seeks the truth in good faith, rather than using debate merely to win a point.

nuance.analogy: Like an official stamp on a document, bona fide confirms that something is what it claims to be.
nuance.etymology: From Latin bona fide, literally in good faith, from bona (good) and fide, the ablative of fides (faith).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as one long word with the stress only on the first syllable; it is two words with two stresses.
Using bona fide as a casual intensifier like really; it means genuine, not very.

senses.definition: The state or characteristic of being a boor or of being boorish; boorish behavior.
senses.example: His boorishness at dinner embarrassed everyone, especially his hosts.

core.definition: Rude, rough, insensitive behavior that shows a lack of good manners toward others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the ending -ness is a reduced vowel sound, like 'nuss'. Keep the r in boor clear, since Americans pronounce it rhotically.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unpleasant, coarse social behavior that makes others uncomfortable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boorishness mostly in writing or formal commentary about someone's manners or about a general social attitude. It is not common in everyday conversation, where people more often say 'rudeness' or 'bad manners'. It sounds literary, so use it carefully in speech.

distinctions.note: Rudeness is the more common everyday word for impolite behavior. Boorishness suggests a coarser, more habitual lack of refinement.
Vulgarity refers to crude or offensive language or taste. Boorishness refers more to rough social conduct, such as interrupting or ignoring others.

examples.everyday: I can handle a little teasing, but his boorishness at parties makes me want to leave early.
examples.professional: Her boorishness in the review meeting made the junior engineers reluctant to speak up.
examples.analytical: Some moralists treated boorishness as a symptom of a deeper failure to take others seriously as persons.

nuance.analogy: Like a sharp edge that cuts without meaning to, boorishness hurts people through rough, careless behavior.
nuance.etymology: From boorish plus the suffix -ness, from boor, a rough, rude person.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, such as 'boor-ish-NESS'; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Confusing boorishness with bashfulness or shyness, which describe quiet discomfort rather than rude behavior.

senses.definition: Something that boosts.
Ellipsis of booster seat.
The first stage of a multistage rocket, providing primary or supplemental thrust for liftoff and early flight.
senses.example: The first stage of the rocket, the booster, fell away two minutes after liftoff.

senses.definition: A motor-generator set used for voltage regulation in direct current electrical power circuits.
senses.example: The engineers replaced the old booster in the substation to keep the DC voltage steady.

senses.definition: Someone who publicly promotes or endorses (something or someone); a fan or supporter.
senses.example: She was a booster of the local bakery, posting photos of its pastries every week.

senses.definition: A member of a booster club.
senses.example: As a booster of the high school band, he volunteers at every home football game.

senses.definition: A booster dose.
senses.example: When did you get your last tetanus booster?

senses.definition: A small quantity of a sensitive explosive that is triggered by a detonator and provides the energy needed to detonate a larger quantity of a less-sensitive explosive.
senses.example: The blasting crew loaded a booster charge into each hole before packing the rest of the explosive.

senses.definition: A term that serves to amplify or strengthen an utterance, such as "really".
senses.example: Linguists say adverbs like really act as a booster, intensifying the adjective that follows.

senses.definition: A power-up item.
senses.example: In the video game, grabbing the red mushroom gives the player a booster that doubles speed.

senses.definition: A package of cards or figurines designed to add to a player's collection.
senses.example: He spent twenty dollars on a booster of trading cards, hoping to finish his set.

senses.definition: A thief.
senses.example: The security guard captured two boosters before they could exit the retail store.

senses.definition: A booster engine fitted to a steam locomotive.
senses.example: The old railway shed kept a booster engine attached to the steam locomotive for climbing the grade.

senses.definition: To give a booster shot to; to boost.
senses.example: Doctors recommend that adults booster their tetanus shots every ten years.

core.definition: Something that boosts or increases energy, strength or amount, such as a booster seat for a child or a repeat vaccine dose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the boost sound rhymes with 'roost.' The final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, not a hard ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually refers to a helpful addition, like a shot or a seat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use booster for a vaccine dose, as in 'I got my COVID booster,' and for a booster seat in a car or at a restaurant. In sports, a booster can also mean a loud, enthusiastic fan, often used informally. Context makes the meaning clear, so listen for the noun it modifies.

distinctions.note: A supporter backs a cause or person; a booster is often more enthusiastic and promotional, sometimes loud in sports or school contexts.
A dose is any measured amount of medicine; a booster is a later shot that renews protection from an earlier vaccine.

examples.everyday: My daughter needs a new booster seat before we drive up to Grandma's.
examples.professional: Sales hopes the new webinar will be a real booster for next quarter's pipeline.
examples.analytical: In the theory of vaccination, a booster renews an immune response that has weakened over time.

nuance.analogy: A booster is like adding fuel to a fire that is burning low, renewing a strength that has faded.
nuance.etymology: From boost, with the agent suffix -er, meaning something or someone that boosts.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -er as ah; it is a reduced, r-colored vowel, as in 'ur.'
Confusing booster shot with a general vaccine; a booster is a repeat dose given later.

senses.definition: That can be enclosed within a ball of finite radius.
senses.example: A compact set must be bounded.

senses.definition: With bounded range.
senses.example: The sensor's bounded range limits how far it can detect nearby objects.

senses.definition: That contains a least element, a, and a greatest element, b, such that for all x ∈ X, a ≤ x ≤ b.
senses.example: Every finite lattice is bounded, since it has both a least and a greatest element.

senses.definition: When restricted to the unit ball.
senses.example: The linear operator is bounded when restricted to the unit ball of the space.

core.definition: Having limits or borders; in mathematics, describing a set or function whose values stay between a fixed upper limit and a fixed lower limit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable, /ɪd/, because the word ends in d. Don't reduce it to a single consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, bounded is rare and usually means 'limited' or 'restricted,' as in 'a bounded budget.' In math and computer science, it is the standard term for a set or sequence that stays within finite limits. Americans say 'bounded above' or 'bounded below' to specify which limit applies. The past tense of the verb bound also uses this spelling.

distinctions.note: Finite means the set has a countable number of elements, while bounded refers to values staying within limits. An interval like (0,1) is bounded but not finite.
Limited is the everyday word for something restricted. Bounded is the precise mathematical term, with a defined upper and lower limit.

examples.everyday: My monthly budget is bounded, so we'll have to choose just one of those two options.
examples.professional: The loss function is bounded below by zero, so gradient descent cannot diverge in that direction.
examples.analytical: A sequence is bounded when every term lies between two fixed numbers, although it need not converge.

nuance.analogy: A bounded set is like a fenced yard: you can walk around a lot, but you can never get past the fence.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of bound, meaning to set limits, from Old French bonde, boundary, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Assuming bounded means finite; a bounded set can contain infinitely many points.
Confusing bounded with boundary, which is a noun for the edge of a region.

senses.definition: The deepest or innermost part.
senses.example: down in the bowels of the Earth

senses.definition: The concept or quality that defines something at its very core.
senses.example: the project’s bowels

senses.definition: The intestines.
senses.example: His bowels were upset after eating the spoiled shellfish at the picnic.

senses.definition: Compassion, sympathy.
senses.example: The judge showed no bowels of compassion toward the men who robbed the elderly widow.

core.definition: The innermost or deepest part of something, such as the bowels of a ship or the bowels of the earth.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is the 'ow' of 'cow', not the 'oh' of 'bowl'. The second syllable is a reduced vowel followed by l and z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the literary sense of depths; in medical or everyday use it can sound clinical or crude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say intestines or bowel in medical contexts, and use bowels mainly in literary phrases like the bowels of the earth. In everyday talk, the singular bowel appears in set phrases like bowel movement. Avoid saying 'my bowels hurt' in polite company; say 'my stomach hurts' or 'my gut hurts'.

distinctions.note: Bowel is the singular medical term for the intestine; bowels is the plural, mainly literary or old-fashioned in its deeper senses.
Guts is an informal word for the stomach or courage; bowels is formal and mainly literary.

collocations: deep in the bowels of the building

examples.everyday: We joked that the basement was the bowels of the old house, dark and full of dusty boxes.
examples.professional: The engineers had to crawl into the bowels of the server room to replace the failed cooling unit.
examples.analytical: The New Testament Greek behind the tender mercy of Luke 1:78 literally refers to the bowels of mercy, the innermost place of feeling.

nuance.analogy: Like the engine room of a ship, the bowels are hidden below the surface, where the real power of something is produced.
nuance.etymology: From Old French boel, from Latin botellus, a sausage, through the sense of intestines.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'bowls' or 'bowl', the dish; the word is BOW-ulz.
Using bowels in everyday talk for stomach pain; say 'stomach' or 'gut' instead.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew rachamim, meaning mercy and related to the word for womb, is often rendered with bowels-language, and Greek splagchna literally means the inward parts, the seat of compassion. Colossians 3:12 in the RSV tells believers to put on compassionate hearts, where the underlying Greek is splagchna. Luke 1:78 speaks of God's tender mercy, using the same bowels-based imagery in Greek.

senses.definition: A motion picture that generates relatively low revenue at the box office, especially less than the budget for producing it.
senses.example: The sci-fi epic was a box office bomb despite its huge marketing budget.

core.definition: A movie that earns much less money in theaters than it cost to make, so it loses money for its studio.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BOX and BOMB, while OF-fice keeps a lighter secondary stress. Americans say the vowel in 'box' and 'bomb' with the same open 'ah' sound, a result of the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals financial failure, though people often use it with humor or sympathy, and it is not an insult to the actors.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in movie news, entertainment talk and casual conversation about films. You can say 'That movie was a box office bomb' or 'It bombed at the box office.' The label depends on the budget and marketing costs, so a film can be a bomb even if it earns a lot overseas but little in North American theaters.

distinctions.note: 'Flop' is a looser, everyday word for any failure, while 'box office bomb' refers specifically to poor ticket sales.
A blockbuster earns very large box office revenue, so it is the opposite of a box office bomb.

collocations: a box office bomb of a film
box office bomb with a huge budget
turned into a box office bomb
despite its stars, a box office bomb

examples.everyday: Did you see that space movie? My friend said it was a box office bomb, but I thought it was fun.
examples.professional: The studio wrote off the film after it became a box office bomb in its opening weekend.
examples.analytical: A film labeled a box office bomb is judged by a financial standard, so its artistic merit can be overlooked in the discussion.

nuance.analogy: Think of a restaurant that spends a fortune on decor but gets almost no customers: the investment is lost before the food is even judged.
nuance.etymology: From 'box office', the ticket window at a theater, and 'bomb', meaning a complete failure, from the 1920s American slang sense.
common_mistakes: Using 'box office bomb' as a verb, for example 'The movie box office bombed' is informal but 'The movie bombed at the box office' is more natural.
Saying 'box office failure' in casual talk, when Americans more often say 'it bombed'.

senses.definition: To stop functioning.
senses.example: I am afraid my computer will break down if I try to run it at too high a speed.

senses.definition: To divide into parts to give more details, to provide a more indepth analysis of.
senses.example: If you don't understand, ask him to break down the numbers for you.

senses.definition: To separate into a number of parts.
senses.example: The chemist let the mixture break down into its component molecules over several hours.

senses.definition: To unexpectedly collapse, physically or in structure.
senses.example: The rotten wooden porch suddenly broke down under the weight of the party guests.

senses.definition: To intentionally demolish; to pull down.
senses.example: The city council voted to break down the abandoned factory to make room for housing.

senses.definition: To fail, especially socially or for political reasons.
senses.example: Talks broke down between Prime Minister John Doe and the opposition party.

senses.definition: To give in or give up: relent, concede, surrender.
senses.example: Is it worth taking it to a repair shop, or should I just break down and buy a new one?

senses.definition: To render or to become unstable due to stress, to collapse physically or mentally.
senses.example: She is back to work now, after she broke down the other day.

senses.definition: To render or to become weak and ineffective.
senses.example: His authority and influence over his coordinates broke down gradually.

senses.definition: To (cause to) decay, to decompose.
senses.example: Leaves and grass will break down into compost faster if you keep them moist.

senses.definition: To digest.
senses.example: His stomach took a while to break down his food.

senses.definition: To bust down or bust a move; to perform energetic, often freestyle or hip-hop moves, frequently during a song’s instrumental break where only drums or bass are playing; see breakdown.
senses.example: At the block party, the teenagers started to break down during the drum solo.

core.definition: To stop working properly, or to lose emotional control and start crying, or to divide something into smaller parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on down, which is the stronger word in this phrasal verb. In speech, break and down often link smoothly, so say brayk-DOWN without a pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually describes a problem, such as a car failing or a person losing composure, but it can also be neutral when analyzing a topic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the car broke down on the highway, or I broke down and cried after the funeral, in everyday conversation. In meetings they often say let's break this down, meaning let's analyze it step by step. When talking about a machine, the noun breakdown is common, as in a breakdown in communications.

distinctions.note: Break alone usually means a sudden physical split, while break down adds the idea of gradual failure or analysis into parts.
Fall apart is more dramatic and suggests complete collapse, while break down can be a temporary failure or a single step in a process.

examples.everyday: My car broke down on the way to work, so I had to call a tow truck.
examples.professional: Can you break down the cost of the project by quarter so the finance team can review it?
examples.analytical: Durkheim sought to break down society into its constituent institutions in order to explain how social order is maintained.

nuance.analogy: Breaking down a problem is like taking apart a clock: you separate each gear so you can see how the whole thing works.
nuance.etymology: From Old English brecan, to break, plus down, referring to something going down or collapsing.
common_mistakes: Using break down without an object when you mean to separate something; say break something down.
Using breakdown as a verb; breakdown is the noun form.

conversation.text: Our car broke down on the highway, so we called a tow truck.
Our car broke down on the way to the beach.
The bus broke down, so we all had to wait for another one.
She broke down in tears when she heard the news.
Can you break it down for me step by step?
Let's break down the sales numbers by region.

senses.definition: The act of breaking up; disintegration or division.
senses.example: The breakup of the old family business forced my grandfather to start over at fifty.

senses.definition: The termination of a friendship or a romantic relationship.
A loss of emotional control; a breakdown.
senses.example: Her emotional breakup at the funeral left everyone in the room silent and uncomfortable.

senses.definition: The season during which winter ice covering bodies of water disintegrates; more generally, spring.
senses.example: Every spring, the river's breakup sends huge sheets of ice grinding downstream past the town.

core.definition: The ending of a romantic relationship, or a relationship that has ended.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BRAYK, because it is a noun; the verb 'break up' stresses the second word, 'break UP'. The t in 'break' is not flapped, and the final 'up' is short and unstressed in the noun.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes a painful event, but the word itself is plain and does not blame anyone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use breakup for the end of a dating relationship or a close friendship, and it is common in everyday talk and social media. A more formal speaker might say 'the end of our relationship' or 'the dissolution of the partnership' in business. A natural reply to news of one is 'I'm so sorry to hear that' or 'Are you doing okay?'

distinctions.note: A divorce is the legal end of a marriage, while a breakup can refer to any romantic relationship, married or not.
Split is more informal and often used for couples or bands, while breakup is the everyday standard term.

examples.everyday: Sorry I've been quiet, I'm still getting over my breakup with Sam.
examples.professional: Our team's breakup with the old vendor went smoothly, and we moved the contract to the new supplier by June.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers of love argue that a breakup reveals what the relationship was actually built on, rather than what the partners believed it was.

nuance.analogy: A breakup is like a bridge that two people built together being taken down: each side can still walk away, but the crossing no longer exists.
nuance.etymology: From the Old English brecan (to break) combined with up; the noun comes from the phrasal verb 'break up'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'breakup with' when the context is clear, or using 'break up' as a noun, which should be 'breakup' with no space.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound like the verb phrase.

senses.definition: To cause.
senses.example: Excessive drinking can bring on depression.

senses.definition: To make something appear, as on a stage or a place of competition.
senses.example: The host will bring on the next contestant after a short commercial break.

senses.definition: To pose a challenge or threat; to attack; to compete aggressively.
senses.example: The underdog team came in ready to bring on the champions in the second half.

senses.definition: To hire or initiate a new employee or participant in a project.
senses.example: I'll bring them on at the end of the month.

core.definition: To cause something to happen, especially something unpleasant such as an illness, a headache, a storm, or a panic attack.

pronunciation.tip: 'On' takes the main stress and has the open 'ah' vowel of most American speakers, not 'oh.' Many Americans with the cot-caught merger pronounce it the same as 'cot,' and the 'ng' in 'bring' stays clean.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, since it most often describes causing something unwelcome. It can be positive when it means producing something good, such as laughter.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bring on' for causes of unpleasant conditions, as in 'Stress can bring on migraines.' The expression 'Bring it on!' is a common American challenge, meaning 'I am ready for whatever you have.' A common polite reply to 'The heat is brutal this week' is 'Tell me about it,' not a use of this phrase.

distinctions.note: 'Bring about' is more formal and neutral and is common in writing about change or results, while 'bring on' is more casual and often for unpleasant effects.
'Set off' emphasizes a sudden trigger that starts something quickly, such as an alarm or an argument.
'Cause' is the general, neutral word for producing an effect, and it is used in both formal and informal speech.

examples.everyday: Too much coffee after lunch can bring on my headaches, so I switch to decaf.
examples.professional: Rapid hiring can bring on quality problems if onboarding does not keep pace with the new staff.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that a sudden credit squeeze can bring on a recession even when the underlying economy is basically healthy.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a trigger that sets off a chain reaction: a small action starts a process that you did not fully control.
nuance.etymology: Bring is from Old English bringan; on is from Old English on.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'bring on' (cause) with 'bring out' (produce, emphasize, or release), which have different meanings.
Pronouncing 'on' as 'own,' which changes the meaning and sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Full of liveliness and activity; characterized by quickness of motion or action.
senses.example: We took a brisk walk yesterday.

senses.definition: Full of spirit of life; effervescing.
senses.example: The brisk young writer filled the room with energy and jokes.

senses.definition: Stimulating or invigorating.
senses.example: This morning was a brisk fall day. It wasn't cold enough for frost, but you wanted to keep moving.

senses.definition: Abrupt, curt in one's manner or in relation to others.
senses.example: The service in that restaurant was brisk and impersonal.

senses.definition: To make or become lively; to enliven; to animate.
senses.example: The sunshine seemed to brisk the crowd as the band began to play.

core.definition: Quick, lively, and energetic; moving or done with a lot of speed and energy.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short 'i' as in 'sit.' Do not add a vowel between 's' and 'k,' so say it as 'brisk,' not 'bri-suk.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests energy, freshness, and efficiency, though it can sound a bit cold when used for a person's manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'brisk walk,' 'brisk pace,' or 'brisk wind' to describe energy or cool weather. It is also used in business to describe strong sales or fast meetings. It is neutral in tone and fits everyday conversation as well as work talk.

distinctions.note: 'Quick' is general and can describe speed of any kind; 'brisk' adds a sense of energy, purpose, and liveliness.
'Prompt' focuses on doing something on time or without delay; 'brisk' describes the energy of the action itself.
'Crisp' describes cool, fresh air or clear, efficient speech; 'brisk' describes motion, pace, or energy.

examples.everyday: Let's take a brisk walk before the sun gets too hot.
examples.professional: The meeting moved at a brisk pace, and we finished all six agenda items in forty minutes.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's brisk dismissals of his rivals often hide a more careful argument beneath the surface.

nuance.analogy: Like a cold splash of water on a sleepy morning: quick, clear, and waking you up.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English brisk, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'brisk' as an adverb ('walk brisk'); the adverb is 'briskly.'
Adding an extra vowel, saying 'bri-suk' instead of one syllable with a clear 'sk' at the end.
Confusing 'brisk' with 'risky' because of their similar spelling and sound.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being broken.
senses.example: Pastors often speak of human brokenness as the starting point for grace.

core.definition: The state of being damaged, fractured or wounded, physically, emotionally or spiritually, in a way that affects the whole person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a schwa, so there is no separate 'in' sound. The word ends with a soft 's' sound, as in 'happiness.'

nuance.connotation: Negative, though in religious and counseling contexts it can be used with hope, because it names a condition that can be healed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'brokenness' most often in church, counseling and personal-growth settings, where it names deep wounds in people or relationships. In everyday conversation it is less common than 'broken,' and it often sounds reflective or serious. Describing objects with it sounds unnatural, so use 'damage' or 'broken' for things.

distinctions.note: Damage is concrete and often describes harm to objects, while brokenness refers to a deep condition of a whole person or relationship.
Fragility is the capacity to break easily, while brokenness is an actual state of having been broken.

examples.everyday: Her honesty about her divorce showed a brokenness I didn't expect from her, and it made me feel closer to her.
examples.professional: The report describes the brokenness of the old data pipeline, with missing keys, duplicate records and no audit trail.
examples.analytical: Christian theology often describes human brokenness as the condition that grace addresses, rather than a defect that human effort alone can repair.

nuance.analogy: Brokenness is like a cracked bowl that still holds water: the damage is real, but it can be mended.
nuance.etymology: From broken, from break (Old English brecan), plus the suffix -ness (Old English -nes).
common_mistakes: Saying 'brokenness' for physical objects, where 'damage' or 'broken' is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle syllable with a clear 'in' sound, which makes the word sound like 'BROH-kin-ness.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the root shavar means to break, and the Psalms and Prophets speak of a broken spirit or heart, the inner state that God meets with mercy. Psalm 34:18 says the LORD is near to the brokenhearted, Psalm 51:17 says God does not despise a broken and contrite heart, and Isaiah 61:1 describes the anointed one sent to bind up the brokenhearted.

traditions.view: Human brokenness is understood as the corruption and mortality inherited from Adam, whose effects are healed through repentance, the sacraments and gradual transformation into God's likeness, rather than through a legal transfer of guilt.

Original sin wounds human nature, leaving a disordered inclination called concupiscence, though baptism removes its guilt. Grace heals and restores human nature through the sacraments and cooperation with God.

Most Protestants, especially in the Reformed tradition, teach that sin corrupts all of human nature and that only God's grace in Christ can heal it. Lutherans stress that the believer is at once righteous and sinful, while Baptists and Pentecostals emphasize personal repentance and new birth.

senses.definition: To add additional elements or components to (a framework, a concept, a device, etc.) in order to extend it.

core.definition: To use something that already exists as a starting point and add to it to develop or improve it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle on, as is typical in phrasal verbs, and link the d of build into on: 'bil-DAHN.' The vowel in on is the same as in hot, because of the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests improving or extending something rather than replacing it.
nuance.usage_note: Build on is common in American meetings and email, where people say 'Let's build on that idea' to add to a colleague's proposal. Informally, Americans also say build off, but build on is the safer choice. In casual conversation it is less common, and people often say 'add to that' instead.

distinctions.note: Expand on means to give more detail about an idea that already exists, while build on means to use it as a base for something new.
Improve on means to do something better than a previous version, while build on does not necessarily judge quality.
Build upon is a less common variant of the same phrasal verb and sounds more formal or literary.

examples.everyday: Your recipe is great, so I'll build on it by adding a little lime.
examples.professional: Let's build on the feedback from last sprint and ship the search filter first.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics builds on the idea of rational autonomy, extending older moral intuitions into a universal principle.

nuance.analogy: Building on an idea is like adding a floor to an existing house: you keep the foundation and extend what is already there.
nuance.etymology: Build from Old English byldan, and on from Old English an, meaning on or upon.
common_mistakes: Saying build up on or build in on; the particle is on.
Using build on for creating something from nothing; it implies something already exists to extend.

conversation.text: I'd like to build on what Sarah just said.
We can build on last year's results.
Let's build on that idea. What if we tested it with one store first?

senses.definition: An object which is sticking out from a surface; a swelling, protuberant part; a bending outward, especially when caused by pressure.
senses.example: a bulge in a wall

senses.definition: The bilge or protuberant part of a cask.
senses.example: The barrel's bulge at the middle held nearly forty gallons of wine.

senses.definition: The outline of a (usually erect) penis visible through one's clothing.
senses.example: The tight pants showed a noticeable bulge at the front, so he changed into looser trousers.

senses.definition: A sudden rise in value or quantity.
senses.example: The company reported a sudden bulge in enrollment after the new scholarship program launched.

senses.definition: The bilge of a vessel.
senses.example: Seawater collected in the bulge of the old fishing boat and had to be pumped out daily.

senses.definition: To stick out from a surface without breaking it.
senses.example: He stood six feet tall, with muscular arms bulging out of his black T-shirt.

senses.definition: (of a container, etc.) To have the surface stretched by something pushing out; to swell; to belly.
senses.example: The submarine bulged because of the enormous air pressure inside.

senses.definition: To bilge, as a ship; to founder.
senses.example: The leaking freighter began to bulge in heavy seas and finally went down off the coast.

core.definition: A part that sticks outward or swells from a surface, like a bulge in a pocket. As a verb, to stick out or swell outward.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the l clearly before the j sound. The ending is a single j sound, as in 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing objects, such as a bulge in a bag. Negative when describing a person's body, since it suggests unwanted fat or swelling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bulge for both objects and bodies, such as 'a bulge in your pocket' or 'a bulge in the tire'. Used about someone's stomach, it can sound rude, so people would say 'your belly is bigger' or simply avoid comments. Be aware that 'bulge' also refers to the outline of male genitals through clothing, a crude sense that you should avoid in polite talk. The phrase 'the Bulge' often refers to the Battle of the Bulge in World War II.

distinctions.note: A bump is usually a small rounded lump that comes from an impact or a surface irregularity, while a bulge is a larger outward swelling of a surface.
Swelling usually refers to an increase in size of a body part from injury or fluid, while bulge describes an outward curve in a surface or object.

examples.everyday: Your wallet is making a bulge in your back pocket, so you might want to move it.
examples.professional: The residuals show a bulge in the upper tail, so we should check for outliers before fitting the model.
examples.analytical: The bulge in the distribution suggests a mixture of two populations rather than a single smooth curve.

nuance.analogy: A bulge is like a balloon that is pushed out from the inside at one spot, while the rest of the surface stays put.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English bulge, from Old French bouge, meaning leather bag or bulge, from Latin bulga, a leather bag.
common_mistakes: Using bulge to describe a person's belly in polite speech, which can sound rude.
Forgetting the l sound and pronouncing the word as 'buj'.

senses.definition: Characteristic of a burden; arduous or demanding.
senses.example: Filling out the paperwork was burdensome, especially for small business owners.

core.definition: Heavy to carry or hard to bear; causing trouble, worry, or hardship, often because it takes much effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is nearly silent, so say BUR-dun-sum with a reduced vowel. The final -some sounds like 'sum,' not 'sewm'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something unpleasant or exhausting, such as a task, a rule, or a financial obligation. It can also be used neutrally about a responsibility that is heavy but worth carrying.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use burdensome for paperwork, regulations, taxes, or duties that feel heavy, and it sounds slightly formal in casual talk. In everyday speech people often say 'a lot of work' or 'a pain' instead. In church settings it can refer to laws or demands placed on people, as in Jesus' criticism of religious leaders.

distinctions.note: Onerous is more formal and suggests a legal or official duty that is heavy and obligatory, as in an onerous contract.
Tiresome describes something that bores or annoys you, while burdensome describes something that is heavy in effort or responsibility.

examples.everyday: Filling out all these forms for the insurance company is really burdensome.
examples.professional: The new reporting requirements are burdensome for our small team, so we should automate part of the process.
examples.analytical: Jesus charges the scribes and Pharisees with binding heavy burdens that are hard to bear, making religious duty burdensome for ordinary people.

nuance.analogy: A burdensome load is like a heavy backpack that slowly wears you down the longer you carry it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English burthen, from Old English byrthen, meaning 'load,' with the suffix -some meaning 'characterized by.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as two full syllables, as in BUR-den-some, when Americans say BUR-dun-sum.
Using burdensome for a person (a burdensome man) when it is normally used for tasks, rules, or costs.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, burdensome often describes laws or demands that are heavy on people. The Greek word behind it is barys, meaning 'heavy.' Matthew 23:4 describes religious leaders who bind heavy burdens, hard to bear, and place them on others' shoulders. Matthew 11:30 contrasts this with Jesus' yoke, which is easy, and his burden, which is light. 1 John 5:3 says that God's commandments are not burdensome.

senses.definition: An inhabitant of a borough with full rights; a citizen.
A member of the House of Burgesses, a legislative body in colonial America, established by the Virginia Company to provide civil rule in the colonies.
senses.example: The burgess rose in the assembly to protest the colony's new tobacco tax.

senses.definition: A person who pays municipal taxes, a ratepayer.
senses.example: As a burgess, she paid municipal taxes that funded the new public library.

senses.definition: (historical) A town magistrate.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A citizen of a borough or town with full civic rights; historically, a member of a colonial legislative assembly such as Virginia's House of Burgesses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending is a weak 'us', not 'ess', and the 'g' is /dʒ/ as in 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical term, and it describes a status rather than a judgment about a person.
nuance.usage_note: In modern American English burgess is rare outside history class, local history, and the name of the Virginia House of Burgesses. Americans would normally say 'citizen' or 'resident' in everyday speech. Use it when discussing colonial governance or old English boroughs.

distinctions.note: Citizen is the everyday word. Burgess is historically specific and carries the idea of full local rights in a chartered town.
A burgher was a middle-class town dweller, mostly in continental Europe. A burgess held political rights, mostly in England and its colonies.
Resident describes where you live now. Burgess describes a legal status tied to the town and to voting or taxpaying rights.

examples.everyday: My history teacher said the Virginia burgesses met in Williamsburg before the Revolution.
examples.professional: The county archive lists each burgess who paid the town rates in the 1720s.
examples.analytical: The burgess's franchise depended on property and residence, not merely on being born in the town.

nuance.analogy: A burgess is like an old-style town council member: someone the community formally recognized as a full member with a voice in local affairs.
nuance.etymology: From Old French burgeis, from burg, 'fortified town', from Late Latin burgus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'burg-ESS' with stress on the second syllable.
Using it as a general word for any citizen in modern American speech, which sounds odd and archaic.

burgess.etymology: From Middle English *burgeis*, from Anglo-Norman *burgeis* (“town-dweller”), of Proto-Germanic origin; either from Late Latin *burgensis* (from Latin *burgus*), or from **burg*, both from Proto-Germanic **burgz* (“stronghold, city”), from…

senses.definition: To become nonfunctional (especially of lightbulbs or similar light-producing devices).
senses.example: The hallway lights burned out again, so the landlord finally replaced the fixture.

senses.definition: To become extinguished due to lack of fuel.
senses.example: The candle finally burned out.

senses.definition: To destroy by fire.
senses.example: The wildfire burned out three cabins before the crews reached the ridge.

senses.definition: To tire due to overwork; to overwork to one's limit.
senses.example: After six months of twelve-hour workdays, most people just burn out and quit.

senses.definition: To cause (someone) to tire due to overwork; to cause (someone) to overwork to one's limit.
senses.example: Constant on-call shifts and endless tickets finally burned me out last spring.

senses.definition: To have one's tires skid against the ground; to peel off, peel out.
senses.example: He floored the truck and burned out the rear tires in the parking lot.

senses.definition: To make (someone) unavailable for work involving exposure to ionizing radiation by employing (the person) in such work until the person's accumulated exposure reaches the maximum permitted for an administrative period, typically a year.
senses.example: The repairs on this nuclear reactor have burned out every welder in the province.

senses.definition: To use up too much energy when first bowled and to therefore not finish strongly.
senses.example: He bowled a strong opening game but burned out badly in the final frames.

senses.definition: To be destroyed by fire.
senses.example: An abandoned tank was burning out at the edge of the battlefield.

senses.definition: (uncommon) To end one's shift at a job.
senses.example: I start my shift at three in the afternoon, and get to burn out at midnight.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: To become exhausted, emotionally drained, and unable to keep working because of long periods of stress or overwork.

pronunciation.tip: In this verb sense, the stress falls on 'out'. As the noun 'burnout', the stress shifts to the first syllable, so 'BURN-out' is a different word form.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a state of exhaustion and a risk to health or performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use burn out in everyday conversation and at work to describe overwork, such as 'I'm burning out at this job.' It is also used literally for machines or lights that stop working. A natural reply is 'Yeah, you need a break before you burn out.'

distinctions.note: Wear out is gradual loss of strength through use. Burn out is caused by intense pressure and emotional exhaustion.
Exhausted describes a state of being very tired. Burn out implies a long-term problem caused by work or stress.

collocations: on the verge of burning out

examples.everyday: I've been working weekends for months, and I'm starting to burn out.
examples.professional: If we keep pushing the sprint schedule, the team is going to burn out before the launch.
examples.analytical: Burning out names a process in which chronic occupational stress gradually depletes a worker's energy and sense of purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle that keeps burning until the wax is gone and only the wick is left.
nuance.etymology: From burn (Old English beornan) and out (Old English ut), from the image of a fire running out of fuel.
common_mistakes: Writing 'burnout' as two words in the verb sense; 'burn out' is the verb and 'burnout' is the noun.
Saying 'I am burn out' instead of 'I'm burned out' or 'I'm burning out'.

conversation.text: If you keep working eighty hours a week, you'll burn out.
She burned out after two years of night shifts.
The bulb in the hallway burned out again.
A lot of teachers burn out in their first few years.

senses.definition: Each of the two large fleshy halves of the posterior part of the body between the base of the back, the perineum, and the top of the legs.
senses.example: She bruised her buttock when she slipped on the icy steps this morning.

senses.definition: The convexity of a ship behind, under the stern.
senses.example: The shipwright carved the buttock of the hull to reduce drag in heavy seas.

core.definition: One of the two fleshy parts of the rear of the body, located between the lower back and the upper legs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel, like 'uk' in 'buck,' but very short. The t is clear, and you should not say 'BUT-tock' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical or clothing contexts. In casual talk Americans often use butt, which can be informal or rude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use buttock in medical, fitness, and formal contexts, and they usually say buttocks in the plural. In casual talk they say butt, which is informal and sometimes considered rude in polite company. In a doctor's office, you might hear the word used for injections or exercise instructions.

distinctions.note: Butt is the informal and more common everyday word, while buttock is a more formal or medical word.
Rear is a general and polite word for the back of the body; buttock refers specifically to the fleshy parts.

examples.everyday: The trainer had us do squats and lunges to work our buttocks and legs.
examples.professional: The medical report notes that the injection was given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, following hospital protocol.
examples.analytical: The anatomy of the buttocks includes the gluteal muscles, which are large and powerful, and they play a major role in walking and standing.

nuance.analogy: The buttocks are like two soft cushions at the base of the spine that help support the body when sitting.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English buttok, a diminutive of butt, 'end, thick part,' related to buttock as the rounded end of the body.
common_mistakes: Using buttock in the singular when speaking about both sides; Americans usually say buttocks in the plural.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a long vowel, like BUT-ock.

buttock.etymology: Middle English *buttok*, probably from Old English *buttuc* (“end; end piece”; also, “short piece of land”).

senses.definition: At a pay rate for each item produced, according to the amount completed.
senses.example: The seamstresses were paid by the piece, so faster sewing meant bigger paychecks.

core.definition: Paid or priced according to how many finished items a worker makes or a product represents, not by time worked.

pronunciation.tip: 'Piece' rhymes with 'peace,' with a long e, not two syllables. Stress falls on PEECE, and 'the' reduces to thuh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business settings, but sometimes suggests low pay or uneven quality when applied to workers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'by the piece' in business, manufacturing and craft work to describe piece-rate pay or pricing. It sounds neutral in contracts and job descriptions. In casual talk, a listener might ask 'So how much per item?' A natural reply is 'Depends on the batch,' or 'It's a flat rate per unit.'

distinctions.note: 'Piecework' is the noun for paid work measured by output, while 'by the piece' is the phrase describing how something is paid or priced.
'By the hour' pays for time worked, while 'by the piece' pays for completed items.

examples.everyday: My cousin gets paid by the piece for sewing wedding dresses, so her income changes every month.
examples.professional: The contractors are paid by the piece, so their earnings depend on finished units rather than hours on site.
examples.analytical: Piece-rate systems, which pay by the piece, align incentives with output but can erode quality if inspection is weak.

nuance.analogy: Like a tailor paid per shirt: each finished piece adds to the pay.
nuance.etymology: Piece from Old French piece, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'the' and saying 'by piece'; the phrase is 'by the piece.'
Pronouncing 'piece' with two syllables, like 'pee-ess.'

senses.definition: To obtain something by wit or guile; to convince people to do something they might not normally do.
senses.example: Are ye gannin te cadge a lift of yoer fatha?

senses.definition: To carry hawks and other birds of prey.
senses.example: The falconer taught his apprentice how to cadge the hawks across the moor.

senses.definition: A circular frame on which cadgers carry hawks for sale.
senses.example: The cadge rested on the cart, ready to hold a dozen hooded falcons for market.

core.definition: To get something, especially a small favor, food, or money, by asking for it informally or persistently.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word. The vowel is the short 'a' of 'cat,' and the ending is the 'j' sound of 'judge.' Do not add a second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests asking for things you could pay for yourself, and it sounds a little embarrassing for the person asking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cadge in casual speech, often about a cigarette, a ride, a free drink, or a bit of food. It is friendly and light, but if you say you cadged something from someone, it implies you did not really need to ask. A natural reply is 'Sure, go ahead' or 'Ask Dave, he has extra.'

distinctions.note: Beg implies desperate need and is more serious; cadge is informal and usually about small, convenient favors.
Borrow implies an agreement to return the item; cadge implies you probably will not pay it back.

examples.everyday: Can I cadge a ride home from you? My car is still in the shop.
examples.professional: Don't cadge free software licenses from the vendor; let's put the purchase request through procurement.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that a culture of cadging favors erodes the trust that makes reciprocity possible.

nuance.analogy: Like picking up a stray french fry from a friend's plate, small, quick, and a little cheeky.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly related to cadger, a peddler or beggar.
common_mistakes: Using cadge with a neutral meaning of borrowing, when it implies you will not repay.
Adding a second syllable (KAY-dge); the word is one syllable.

cadge.etymology: From Middle English *caggen* (“to tie, fasten, bind”), probably from Old Norse.

senses.definition: A base or despicable person; a wretch.
Especially despicable; cowardly.
senses.example: The caitiff knight fled the battle, abandoning his men to die alone in the mud.

core.definition: A cowardly, despicable person; a wretch. This is an archaic or literary term.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAY, and make the ending 'tif,' with a short 'i' like 'if.' The 'ai' is a long 'a' as in 'day.'

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It insults someone as cowardly and contemptible, and it sounds old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use caitiff in ordinary speech. You will see it in older literature, such as medieval romances or Shakespeare, or in deliberately old-fashioned writing. If you need a modern word, say 'coward' or 'scoundrel.' It is best understood as a recognition word rather than one to use actively.

distinctions.note: Coward is everyday and common; caitiff is archaic and carries a stronger sense of base or despicable behavior.
Scoundrel means a dishonest, rascally person; caitiff focuses more on cowardice and baseness.

examples.professional: The old memo calls the vendor a caitiff for abandoning the contract, but in a current report we should say breach of contract.
examples.analytical: In medieval romance, the caitiff knight is the foil to the hero, whose cowardice reveals the ideal of courage the story upholds.

nuance.analogy: Like a faded coat of arms in a museum, meaningful to scholars but no longer worn in daily life.
nuance.etymology: From Old French caitif 'captive,' from Latin captivus 'captive.'
common_mistakes: Using caitiff in casual speech, where it sounds archaic or theatrical.
Confusing it with caddy or cadet because of the similar sound.

senses.definition: A versioning scheme where each release number is based on the build date, usually in the ISO 8601 format, allowing for easy sorting.

core.definition: A software versioning scheme in which each release number is based on the release date, often in a year-and-month format.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on VUR in versioning, while the first word keeps a weaker secondary stress. The -ing ending is light, so avoid saying 'ver-SHUN-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a technical convention and carries no evaluative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the United States use calendar versioning, often called CalVer, for projects that release on a regular schedule. Ubuntu uses a year-and-month form for its releases. In a code review or planning meeting, people usually contrast it with semantic versioning.

distinctions.note: Semantic versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbers to signal the kind of change, while calendar versioning uses dates to show when a release was made.

examples.everyday: Our app updates are numbered by date, so the June release is version 24.06.
examples.professional: Let's switch the release process to calendar versioning so the team can tell at a glance when a build shipped.
examples.analytical: Calendar versioning ties each release identifier to a date, which makes chronology explicit but says nothing about compatibility.

nuance.analogy: Calendar versioning is like labeling food containers with the date they were packed: you know how fresh they are, but not what is inside.
nuance.etymology: Combines calendar, from Latin kalendae 'first day of the month', with versioning, from version.
common_mistakes: Stressing versioning on the final syllable instead of VUR.
Assuming calendar versioning means a release is tied to the year of purchase rather than the build or release date.

senses.definition: A heat stroke or fever, often suffered in the tropics.
senses.example: Sailors in the tropics sometimes suffered calenture, a fever that made them see green meadows in the sea.

senses.definition: A delirium occurring from such symptoms, in which a stricken sailor pictures the sea as grassy meadows and wishes to dive overboard into them.
senses.example: Delirious with calenture, the sailor begged to dive overboard into the grassy meadows he saw.

core.definition: A historical tropical fever, once thought to make sailors see green meadows in the sea and want to jump overboard.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending '-ture' is pronounced like 'cher', not 'tyoor', and the middle 'en' is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a historical condition in a descriptive way, though the image it names is eerie.
nuance.usage_note: Almost no one uses this word in modern American speech. You may meet it in maritime history, old medical writing, or literature about the sea. For modern conversation, say 'heatstroke' or 'delirium' instead.

distinctions.note: Heatstroke is the modern medical term for dangerous overheating, while calenture is a historical name that included hallucinations.
Delirium is a general term for confusion and hallucination, while calenture specifically refers to a tropical fever with visions of the sea as meadows.

examples.everyday: I read a sailor's story about calenture, and it sounded like severe heatstroke with hallucinations.
examples.professional: The ship's surgeon logged several cases of calenture among the crew during the Caribbean crossing.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century accounts of calenture describe sailors who see green meadows in the sea and long to dive into them.

nuance.analogy: Like an old map label for a danger that modern doctors have renamed.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish calentura, fever, from Latin calere, to be warm.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'caliber' or 'calendar' because of the similar spelling.
Using it as a modern medical term; it is historical and rarely used in current medicine.

senses.definition: To become less excited, intense, or angry.
senses.example: Calm down before you hurt somebody.

senses.definition: To cause to become less excited, intense, or angry.

core.definition: To become less upset, excited, or angry, or to make someone become less upset or angry.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on down, while calm has a lighter secondary stress. The word down is a diphthong, so say 'down' with a clear 'ow' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It is useful and common, but telling someone to calm down can sound dismissive when they are upset.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calm down in casual conversation, at work, and with family, such as 'Calm down, we'll figure it out.' It is a phrasal verb and can be separable when used with an object: 'calm him down.' A natural response from the upset person is 'I am calm,' or 'Sorry, I'm just frustrated.'

distinctions.note: Relax means to rest or become less tense, often without any prior upset, while calm down implies someone was agitated first.
Cool down can refer to temperature or to anger, while calm down focuses on emotional agitation or excitement.

examples.everyday: Calm down, the flight's delayed, but we'll still make the wedding.
examples.professional: Let's calm down and walk through the outage timeline before we start blaming the vendor.
examples.analytical: The debate only became productive once both sides agreed to calm down and separate emotion from evidence.

nuance.analogy: To calm down is like letting a pot cool off after it has been boiling, until it can be handled safely.
nuance.etymology: Calm comes from Old French and Medieval Latin, and down meaning to lower or reduce, used here as an adverb.
common_mistakes: Placing the object after the particle incorrectly, as in 'calm down him' instead of 'calm him down.'
Using calm down for calm up or calm off, which are not natural.

conversation.text: Calm down, it's just a scratch on the car.
It took me twenty minutes to calm the baby down.
Things should calm down at work after the holidays.
Calm down. We'll find your phone.
I sang to the baby to calm her down.

senses.definition: (historical) An artillery soldier who maintains and operates a cannon, or some other piece of heavy artillery.
senses.example: Luckily, the cannoneer was only mildly injured when his cannon malfunctioned.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A soldier who loads, aims, and fires a cannon or other heavy artillery piece.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last strong syllable, NEER, and the r is pronounced clearly as in 'ear.' Do not stress the first syllable as you would in cannon.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a military role and is mostly used in history or military description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cannoneer mainly for historical armies, reenactments, and museum displays. In modern American military language, people usually say 'artillery soldier,' 'artilleryman,' or 'gunner.' You will hear it in Civil War histories and living-history presentations.

distinctions.note: Gunner is a broader, more modern term that can refer to any crewman on a gun, including tanks and ships.
Artilleryman is a more general older term for any soldier in an artillery unit, not specifically the cannon operator.

examples.everyday: My great-grandfather served as a cannoneer in the Civil War, and we still have a few of his letters.
examples.professional: The museum is recruiting a volunteer to portray a cannoneer for its living-history demonstrations next season.
examples.analytical: The cannoneers' precise drill gave their batteries a discipline that infantry commanders came to rely on during the battle.

nuance.analogy: A cannoneer is like the pitcher in a bullpen who must know the exact arc, weight, and timing needed to hit a target far away.
nuance.etymology: From cannon plus the suffix -eer, denoting a person who works with or operates something.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as canoneer, which is missing an n and is closer to canoeist.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the final syllable, as in KAN-uh-neer.
Confusing it with canoeist, a person who travels by canoe.

senses.definition: In a capable manner.

core.definition: In a skillful, competent way, showing that a task was done well enough by someone who knows what they are doing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, KAY, and the first vowel is the long a of cape. Many learners wrongly say KAP, with the short a of cat, which is incorrect here.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's skill and reliability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use capably in reviews, reports, and formal praise more than in casual talk. In everyday conversation, people often say 'well' or 'did a good job' instead. It is a natural word in workplace and academic writing.

distinctions.note: Well is the everyday word, while capably is more formal and stresses competence in handling a responsibility.
Skillfully focuses on technique or craft, while capably focuses on reliable competence in getting the job done.
Efficiently emphasizes speed or low waste, while capably emphasizes competence and good judgment.

examples.everyday: My brother handled the car repair pretty capably, even though he's never done a brake job before.
examples.professional: She capably managed the database migration with almost no downtime for customers.
examples.analytical: The essay capably defends a difficult thesis, although its final section does not fully answer the strongest objection.

nuance.analogy: Working capably is like a good chef who makes a complicated dish look easy.
nuance.etymology: From capable, from Late Latin capabilis, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as the short a of cat, as in KAP-uh-blee.
Using capably in casual speech where well would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Describing a ring, all of whose atoms are carbon.

core.definition: Describing a ring of atoms in which every atom in the ring is carbon, with no nitrogen, oxygen, or other elements.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the SY syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on kahr. Pronounce the r clearly and say the ending as klik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise chemical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Carbocyclic is used mainly in chemistry, biochemistry, and medicinal chemistry papers and lab conversations. Americans usually use it to contrast with heterocyclic, meaning a ring that includes other elements. Outside science, the word almost never comes up.

distinctions.note: Heterocyclic describes rings containing at least one atom other than carbon, such as nitrogen or oxygen, while carbocyclic rings contain only carbon atoms.
Aromatic describes a special stability and electron pattern in a ring, while carbocyclic only describes what atoms make up the ring.

examples.everyday: Our chemist friend said the ring in this drug is carbocyclic, so it has no nitrogen or oxygen inside it.
examples.professional: The medicinal chemistry team replaced the sugar with a carbocyclic analog to improve the molecule's stability in the bloodstream.
examples.analytical: Whether a carbocyclic framework preserves the biological activity of the original molecule depends on its three-dimensional geometry.

nuance.analogy: A carbocyclic ring is like a necklace made only of identical carbon beads, with no beads of any other kind mixed in.
nuance.etymology: From carbo-, combining form of carbon, and cyclic, from Greek kyklos, circle.
common_mistakes: Shifting the main stress to the first syllable, as KAR-boh-sy-klik.
Confusing carbocyclic with heterocyclic, which reverses the meaning.

senses.definition: The natural removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere by the soil and plants.
Any of several processes for the removal of excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in an effort to mitigate global warming.

core.definition: The process of capturing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it long-term in plants, soils, oceans, or underground rock.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on STRAY, the fourth syllable of the phrase. Carbon has a secondary stress on its first syllable, and the second 'qu' in sequestration is pronounced like 'kw', not like 'kes'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scientific, but often carries a positive tone in climate discussions because it describes a solution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use carbon sequestration mainly in environmental policy, energy news, agriculture, and climate debates. In casual talk people say 'carbon capture' or 'storing carbon'. The term can refer to natural processes such as forest growth, or to engineered systems such as underground injection. When discussing it with non-experts, add a short explanation, since it is a technical term.

distinctions.note: Carbon capture refers to trapping CO2 at its source or from the air, while sequestration is the long-term storage after capture.
A carbon offset is a financial credit for reducing or removing emissions elsewhere, while sequestration is the physical storage process itself.

examples.everyday: My uncle works on a farm that's trying carbon sequestration by planting cover crops.
examples.professional: Our sustainability team wants to report the carbon sequestration rate for the new forest project by the end of the quarter.
examples.analytical: Debates about carbon sequestration reveal a tension between technological optimism and the slow, uncertain nature of natural carbon cycles.

nuance.analogy: Like putting money into a savings account that you cannot easily withdraw: the carbon is stored away from the air for a long time.
nuance.etymology: Carbon comes from French carbone, from Latin carbo, charcoal; sequestration comes from Latin sequestrare, to put in safekeeping.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable of sequestration, as in 'se-KWES-tration'.
Using sequestration in its legal sense of 'government spending cuts' when talking about climate; the context matters in American news.

senses.definition: One of the four foundational virtues identified by Greek and Christian philosophers, on which other virtues depend: justice, temperance, prudence, or fortitude.

core.definition: The four foundational moral virtues in classical and Christian thought: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress on VUR in 'virtues', with a rhotic r; 'cardinal' has secondary stress on KAR. The 'tu' becomes 'ch'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, a classic moral framework.
nuance.usage_note: Used in philosophy, ethics and Catholic moral theology. 'Cardinal' here means 'pivotal' (Latin cardo, 'hinge'), not the bird or church officer.

distinctions.note: The theological virtues are faith, hope, and love, given by grace, whereas cardinal virtues are acquired moral virtues.
The deadly sins are vices, while cardinal virtues are excellences of character.
Values are personal or cultural preferences, while the virtues are stable habits of character.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor said courage is one of the cardinal virtues.
examples.professional: Our leadership workshop is built on the cardinal virtues of prudence and justice.
examples.analytical: Aquinas integrates Aristotle's moral virtues with Christian faith by treating prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance as cardinal.

nuance.analogy: Like four hinges on which the door of good character swings.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cardinalis, 'pertaining to a hinge' (cardo); virtues were hinges for other virtues.
common_mistakes: Confusing them with the seven deadly sins.
Mispronouncing virtues as 'vir-TOO-es'.
Listing faith, hope, and love as cardinal virtues.
nuance.biblical_note: The four virtues are named together in Wisdom of Solomon 8:7 (in the Apocrypha/deuterocanon): wisdom's labors yield self-control, prudence, justice, and courage. The New Testament treats faith, hope, and love as central (1 Corinthians 13:13).

senses.definition: Someone who carves; an artist who produces carvings.
senses.example: The village carver spent winters shaping cedar into totem poles.

senses.definition: An armchair as part of a set of dining chairs (originally for the person who is to carve the meat).
senses.example: Grandpa always insisted on sitting in the carver at the head of the table.

senses.definition: A ski with curved edges, allowing smooth turns.
senses.example: The new carver skis made turning on icy slopes much easier for me.

senses.definition: (dated) A carving knife.
senses.example: Hand me the carver so I can slice the roast before it cools.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A butcher.
senses.example: The old carver down on Main Street sold the best short ribs in town.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who cuts shapes or designs into wood, stone, or other material to make decorative or artistic objects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the r in both syllables. The final -er is a reduced, rhotic schwa, not a clear 'ver' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It refers to a skilled craftsperson, and it is usually used with respect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use carver mostly in compounds such as woodcarver or stone carver, or for the person who slices meat at a buffet or holiday table. A carving knife is the tool used for that job. The ski sense of carver, a ski with curved edges, is a specialized term used mainly by skiers.

distinctions.note: A sculptor makes three-dimensional art by carving, modeling, or casting, while a carver specifically removes material to shape it.
A woodworker builds functional objects such as furniture, while a carver focuses on decorative or figurative shapes.

examples.everyday: The ice carver at the wedding made a swan in about twenty minutes.
examples.professional: We hired a stone carver to restore the carved columns at the building's entrance.
examples.analytical: The medieval carver signed his name on the choir stall, a rare acknowledgment of individual craft in a communal project.

nuance.analogy: A carver is like an editor who removes everything that is not the figure, leaving only the shape they meant to show.
nuance.etymology: From carve, from Old English ceorfan, meaning to cut, with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing carver, the person, with carving, the object or the art form.
Pronouncing the first vowel like the a in 'cat' instead of the ah in 'car'.

senses.definition: Toward the tail end (hind end) of the body; in bipeds such as humans, this direction corresponds to inferior.
Pertaining to the tail or posterior or hind part of a body.
A caudal vertebra.
senses.example: The radiologist noted a fracture in the third caudal vertebra of the injured dog.

core.definition: Relating to the tail or the hind end of the body; in humans, toward the lower end of the spine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'au' is the open 'ah' vowel of General American, not the 'aw' of 'caught'. The final 'al' is a syllabic l, so the word ends with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise anatomical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Mainly used by doctors, veterinarians, biologists and anatomists. Ordinary speakers say 'tail end' or 'lower back' instead. In a conversation with a vet or doctor, you might hear it when the location of a lump or injury is described, and a natural reply is simply to ask where that is.

distinctions.note: Cranial means toward the head, the opposite direction of caudal in most animals.
Posterior means toward the back in general, while caudal specifically means toward the tail or lower end of the spine.

examples.everyday: The vet pointed to a small bump near the dog's caudal end, right where the tail meets the body.
examples.professional: The imaging protocol records the caudal margin of each lesion so the readings can be compared across scans.
examples.analytical: Describing a structure as caudal to the diaphragm requires a fixed orientation convention, or the description means nothing across species.

nuance.analogy: Caudal is to the tail what 'toward the feet' is to a person lying down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cauda, 'tail'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'au' like 'caught' (/ɔ/) instead of the General American /ɑ/.
Using 'caudal' for everyday body parts, where 'lower back' or 'tail end' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: An early human or closely related species, popularly held to reside in caves.
senses.example: The political cartoon showed the politician as a caveman, clubbing the budget depicted as a mammoth.

senses.definition: A person with backward, primitive behavior, opinions, or interests.
senses.example: The football squad was made up of cavemen who were responsible for trashing many a locker room.
