examples.everyday: I can't believe they killed off my favorite character on that show last night.
examples.professional: We need to kill off the old reporting tool once the new dashboard is stable, so people stop using both.
examples.analytical: Some novelists kill off their protagonists to show that meaning does not depend on a hero's survival.

nuance.analogy: Like pruning a garden so that weak branches are removed and the rest of the plant can grow.
nuance.etymology: Combines kill with the adverb off, meaning away or completely, from Old English of.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on kill instead of off; the particle is usually stressed.
Using 'kill off' for a single quick death in a neutral sense, when 'kill' alone is more natural.

senses.definition: So as to kill; fatally.
senses.example: The dose was killingly strong, so the nurse double-checked the chart before administering it.

senses.definition: So as to incapacitate with laughter.
senses.example: Her impression of our boss was killingly funny, and we were on the floor laughing.

core.definition: In a way that causes death or is extremely funny, used mostly with adjectives such as funny, boring, or hot.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a clear, light ee sound, so it ends with 'lee' and not 'ly' as in 'lie.'

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive or playful when used for humor, and negative when used for death. Americans rarely use it in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use killingly mainly in writing, especially fiction or criticism, and in a few fixed expressions such as 'killingly funny.' It is seldom heard in casual conversation, where people say 'really funny' or 'so funny I died.' Using it in speech can sound affected unless you are describing something with real dramatic flair.

distinctions.note: Fatally is precise and clinical, meaning in a way that causes death, whereas killingly can also mean extremely funny or hot.
Hilariously is the everyday word for something very funny, while killingly is a more dramatic, literary way to say the same thing.

examples.everyday: Your brother's impression of the principal was killingly funny, and I laughed until I cried.
examples.professional: The vendor's demo was killingly slow, so we decided to test a different platform before signing.
examples.analytical: The poison acted killingly fast, leaving the physicians no time to administer the antidote.

nuance.analogy: Killingly is like a fireworks show that is so bright it nearly stops you breathing: the intensity is the point.
nuance.etymology: From killing (adjective) plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using killingly as a common everyday adverb, when most speakers would say 'really' or 'so'.
Confusing it with 'killing,' the adjective, which takes different grammatical contexts.
Stressing the last syllable, which makes it sound like 'kil-ing-LEE.'

core.definition: A walled town of Moab, named in prophecies and in an Assyrian deportation of Syrians.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one short syllable with a rolled or tapped r, as in the American word kirk. Americans say the r clearly, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical place name with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Kir appears only in Bible study, sermons and commentaries, so Americans rarely meet it outside church settings. Readers often confuse it with Kiriath or Kiriathaim, which are different places. Kir-hareseth, a related name, is sometimes used for the same fortified city in Moab.

examples.everyday: My friend asked me where Kir is, and I told him it was a city in Moab.
examples.professional: In the seminar on the minor prophets, we mapped Kir alongside the other cities named in Amos.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether Kir in Amos 1:5 and 2 Kings 16:9 refers to the same region or to two distinct locations.

nuance.etymology: Hebrew qir, meaning wall or walled place; the exact sense is debated.
common_mistakes: Confusing Kir with Kiriath, which is a different name and a different place.
Pronouncing it with a long i as in kite instead of a short i as in kit.
nuance.biblical_note: Kir is a walled town or region associated with Moab in some passages and with Aram or the Syrians in others. The Hebrew word qir means wall or walled place. Amos 1:5 says Syrians will go into exile to Kir, Amos 9:7 recalls God bringing Syrians from Kir, and 2 Kings 16:9 says the king of Assyria captured Damascus and carried the people to Kir. Isaiah 22:6 names Kir with Elam as a nation bearing arms, which shows its role as a military or political power.

kir.etymology: French *kir*, named after Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon.

senses.definition: How facts and rules about the world are stored in a form a computer can reason with.

core.definition: The way facts, rules, and relationships about the world are encoded in a form that a computer can store and reason with.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on "knowledge" and on "tay" in representation, so the middle syllables are reduced. Say the r clearly and avoid adding an extra syllable to "representation".

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is a formal term in AI and logic.
nuance.usage_note: In American computer science and AI programs, knowledge representation is a standard course and research area. People use it when discussing ontologies, logic, rules, and semantic networks. It is rarely used in casual speech, but it is common in academic and engineering meetings.

distinctions.note: A knowledge base is a store of information, while knowledge representation is the choice of formal structure used to encode that information.
Machine learning often learns representations from data automatically, while classical knowledge representation encodes explicit symbolic facts and rules.

examples.everyday: My cousin's graduate class is about knowledge representation, and she says it's about teaching computers to store facts.
examples.professional: In the design review, we agreed on a knowledge representation that keeps product rules separate from the pricing data.
examples.analytical: Any knowledge representation embodies a theory of what the world is made of, and its limits shape what a system can conclude.

nuance.analogy: Knowledge representation is like choosing a filing system: the same documents are useful or useless depending on how they are labeled and organized.
nuance.etymology: Knowledge from Middle English knowleche; representation from Latin repraesentare, to present again.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in representation, as in "rep-re-SEN-ta-tion".
Using knowledge representation for the general idea of showing knowledge; in AI it is a technical term for encoding.

conversation.text: Knowledge representation studies how to encode facts about the world so a program can reason with them.
Choosing a knowledge representation early saves a lot of rework when the rules start piling up.

senses.definition: Fastened with lace or laces (light cordage).
senses.example: She pulled on her laced leather boots and headed out into the cold morning.

senses.definition: Adorned with lace (delicate fabric).
senses.example: The bride wore a laced gown with long sleeves and a high collar.

senses.definition: Intentionally tainted with something, especially a drug.
senses.example: I don't know what it was laced with, but he passed out a minute after drinking that first beer.

core.definition: Fastened or closed with laces, as in laced-up boots; also, secretly mixed with alcohol or a drug.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that ends in a -st cluster, so the final t is clearly pronounced. Do not add a vowel and say 'lay-sed,' which is not correct.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for shoes, clothing, and food descriptions. Negative when it describes a drink or food secretly spiked with a drug.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use laced most often for laced boots, laced shoes, or food laced with an ingredient like cream or spice. The drug sense is informal and implies a crime or danger, so use it carefully. The phrase laced with usually follows a noun about a food or drink.

distinctions.note: Tied is a general word for knotted fastening, while laced specifically refers to threaded cords or laces through eyelets.
Spiked is informal and usually means adding alcohol to a drink. Laced more often suggests a drug or a deliberate additive.

examples.everyday: She wore leather boots laced tight for the trail, and they never came loose.
examples.professional: The proposal was laced with jargon that confused the client and slowed the decision.
examples.analytical: His prose is laced with irony, which makes the author's sincerity hard for readers to judge.

nuance.analogy: Like a shoe that stays snug only when every eyelet is threaded.
nuance.etymology: From lace, from Old French laz, noose or snare, from Latin laqueus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two syllables, like 'lay-sed.'
Using laced for a drink without implying a secret or unwanted addition in a casual context.
Confusing laced with lacy; lacy describes lace-like fabric or patterns, while laced means fastened or mixed.

senses.definition: An arbitrary (non-specific) point in time, too close to a deadline to reasonably begin a critical task.
senses.example: I like to do everything at the last minute. It does tend to make me late for things, though.

senses.definition: Very close to a deadline.
senses.example: That last minute revision really paid off in the exam!

core.definition: The final moment before a deadline or event; or done at that moment, with little time left.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'MIN' in 'minute', meaning the unit of time, which sounds like 'MIN-it'. Do not say 'my-NOOT', which means tiny. In speech, the 'st' of 'last' links to the 'm' of 'minute'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in plans and logistics, but often stressful when it suggests rushing or procrastination.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'at the last minute' as an adverbial phrase and 'last-minute' with a hyphen before a noun: 'last-minute changes.' People use it for plans, travel, shopping and deadlines. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, sorry I left it so late.'

distinctions.note: Eleventh hour is an idiom for a crisis moment, often formal or dramatic; last minute is everyday and neutral.
Last-ditch describes a desperate final effort; last minute only describes timing.
Short notice refers to how little warning someone gets; last minute refers to the time just before a deadline.

examples.everyday: Can you pick up milk? We're having people over, and I decided at the last minute.
examples.professional: Please send the slides today; I don't want last-minute changes before the review.
examples.analytical: Procrastination produces decisions made at the last minute, which often rely on quick heuristics rather than full analysis.

nuance.analogy: Like sprinting for the bus just as the doors begin to close.
nuance.etymology: 'Last' from Old English latost, and 'minute' from Medieval Latin minuta, a small part of an hour.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in the last minute'; the usual phrase is 'at the last minute'.
Pronouncing 'minute' as 'my-NOOT', which means very small.
Writing 'last minute' without a hyphen before a noun, such as 'last minute changes'.

conversation.text: We booked the trip at the last minute.
Sorry for the last-minute change to the agenda.
He always does his homework at the last minute.

senses.definition: An introduction; something that leads into the beginning of something.
senses.example: After the long lead-in, the climax of the story was a disappointment.

senses.definition: A region of data at the beginning of a compact disc, holding the table of contents.
senses.example: The disc's lead-in contains the table of contents, so the player reads it first.

senses.definition: A short phrase that begins the caption of a photograph.
senses.example: The photo editor wrote a short lead-in before the caption for the flood image.

core.definition: An introductory part that leads into something larger, such as a speech, story, song, or TV segment; a warm-up or preliminary remark.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and 'lead' here is pronounced like the verb 'lead' (LEED), not like the metal. The second syllable is a short, reduced 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes a function, not a judgment, though a clumsy lead-in can make a presentation feel awkward.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lead-in for the opening of a TV show, a radio segment, a presentation, or a conversation, as in 'Give me a good lead-in to the topic.' In broadcasting, the lead-in can also be the program that airs just before a show to attract viewers. Writing it hyphenated as a noun is standard American style, while the verb is two words: 'lead in.'

distinctions.note: Intro is a casual, shortened word that usually means the opening of a song, video, or presentation; lead-in is slightly more technical and can refer to a remark that sets up a larger point.
Preamble is formal and usually refers to the introductory statement of a law, treaty, or document, not to a casual opening.
Prelude is more literary and can mean an event or piece of music that comes before a larger one; a lead-in is more practical and tied to transitions.

examples.everyday: The host gave a nice lead-in before the band came on stage.
examples.professional: Let's shorten the lead-in to the slide deck so we can get to the metrics faster.
examples.analytical: The opening paragraph serves as a lead-in that frames the argument before the thesis appears.

nuance.analogy: A lead-in is like the wind-up before a pitch: it sets the motion before the real action begins.
nuance.etymology: From the verb lead (Old English lǣdan, to cause to go) plus in, describing something that leads in.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing lead as the metal (LED) instead of LEED.
Writing the noun as two words, lead in, when a hyphenated noun is standard.

senses.definition: Of the Leguminosae family of peas, beans etc.
Resembling a legume.

core.definition: Belonging to the legume family, or relating to plants such as peas, beans, and clovers that grow seeds in pods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GYOO, the third syllable from the start, and the ending is a weak 'nuss.' Do not confuse it with 'luminous,' which begins with a different sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise scientific term and does not carry emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'leguminous' in botany, agriculture, and nutrition writing, often in phrases like 'leguminous crops.' In everyday conversation people usually say 'bean' or 'pea plants' instead. It is a formal word that signals scientific precision.

distinctions.note: 'Legume' is a noun for the plant or its pod; 'leguminous' is the adjective describing plants or traits that belong to that family.

examples.everyday: My neighbor grows a leguminous vine on his fence, and it keeps the soil healthy.
examples.professional: The farm plan includes leguminous crops to reduce the amount of fertilizer we buy each year.
examples.analytical: The leguminous plants in the study formed symbiotic relationships with soil bacteria that fix nitrogen.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name that marks everyone who shares the same traits: 'leguminous' tells you a plant belongs to the bean and pea family.
nuance.etymology: From Latin leguminosus, from legumen 'pulse, pod.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'luminous,' which means glowing or bright
Using 'leguminous' as a noun instead of 'legume'

leguminous.etymology: From Middle English *leguminous*, from Medieval Latin *legūminōsus*, ultimately from oblique stem of Latin *legūmen* (“bean, pulse”) *-ous*.

senses.definition: Suggests meeting to talk about what's new.

core.definition: A friendly suggestion to meet or talk so you can hear what is new in each other's lives since you last spoke.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on UP. In 'let's,' the 's' links to 'catch', so it sounds like 'lets-katch'. The 'tch' sound in 'catch' is one consonant sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It signals interest in reconnecting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to friends, former coworkers, or relatives they have not seen for a while. It is casual and often does not lead to an exact plan, so the reply may need a time or place, such as 'Sure, how about coffee next week?' You can also say 'Let's catch up soon,' which is very common in both casual and professional settings.

distinctions.note: Let's get together suggests a social meeting in general; let's catch up focuses on sharing news since the last conversation.
Catch up on means to finish or learn what you missed, such as work or a TV show; let's catch up is about talking with a person.

collocations: it's been too long, let's catch up

examples.everyday: It's been years since college, so let's catch up over coffee sometime.
examples.professional: Let's catch up after the meeting to talk about your project timeline.
examples.analytical: In the essay, the reunion is framed as a moment when old friends let's catch up, revealing how distance changes relationships.

nuance.analogy: Like running to catch a bus that has already left, you are trying to reach the current news of someone's life.
nuance.etymology: 'Catch up' comes from the 16th-century sense of catching or overtaking someone who is ahead.
common_mistakes: Saying 'catch up each other', which is wrong; use 'catch up with each other' or simply 'catch up'.
Using 'let's catch up' for work that is behind, where 'catch up on' is needed.

conversation.text: I've been so busy lately. Let's catch up over lunch next week.
"Let's catch up soon!" "Yes, I'll text you this weekend."
Let's catch up after the meeting; I want to hear about your trip.

senses.definition: Concerning the vocabulary, words, sentences or morphemes of a language.
Concerning lexicography or a lexicon or dictionary.
senses.example: The lexical database includes over fifty thousand entries, each tagged with part of speech.

senses.definition: Denoting a content word as opposed to a function word.
senses.example: a lexical verb

senses.definition: Relating to alphabetical order or a generalization thereof.
senses.example: Our script sorts the file in lexical order, so "10" appears before "2" in the output.

core.definition: Relating to the words or vocabulary of a language, rather than to its grammar.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the final '-ical' to a light 'kul'. The middle vowel is a short 'ih', not 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise academic term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lexical' in linguistics, language teaching, lexicography and programming, rarely in everyday speech. In casual talk, people say 'vocabulary' or 'word choice' instead. In linguistics, 'lexical' often contrasts with 'grammatical' or 'functional' words.

distinctions.note: Vocabulary is the noun for the set of words a person or language knows; lexical is the adjective describing things related to those words.
Lexical items carry meaning, such as nouns and verbs; grammatical items show structure, such as articles and prepositions.

examples.everyday: That book has a lot of lexical variety, so I keep learning new words while I read it.
examples.professional: The language model's lexical coverage is strong, but its grammar still breaks on long sentences.
examples.analytical: The poem's power lies in its lexical choices, since each word carries a theological weight that the syntax alone would not convey.

nuance.analogy: If grammar is the skeleton of a sentence, the lexical words are the flesh and color that give it meaning.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'lexikos' (of words), from 'lexis' (word, speech).
common_mistakes: Using 'lexical' as a noun; the noun is 'lexicon' or 'vocabulary'.
Mixing up 'lexical' and 'lexicographic'; lexicography is the practice of making dictionaries.

senses.definition: The conduct or activities of a libertine; licentiousness.

core.definition: Behavior that is morally unrestrained, especially sexual licentiousness, typical of a libertine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LIB. Some speakers imitate the French pronunciation, lee-ber-tee-NAHZH, but Americans in ordinary speech say LIB-er-tin-ij.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests moral disorder and excess, although it can be used neutrally in historical or literary study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use libertinage in everyday speech. It appears mainly in literature, history and academic writing about the eighteenth century and French culture. In casual talk, people would say licentiousness, debauchery or wild living.

distinctions.note: Libertinism is the more common English word for the general lifestyle. Libertinage is more literary and often linked to French or historical contexts.
Licentiousness is the more widely understood English word for unrestrained sexual or moral behavior. Libertinage is more formal and bookish.

examples.professional: The seminar paper examines libertinage in eighteenth-century French fiction and its link to political critique.
examples.analytical: Critics read the characters' libertinage as a critique of aristocratic privilege rather than as mere personal pleasure.

nuance.analogy: Libertinage is like a house with every door left open: nothing is locked, but the structure is no longer protected.
nuance.etymology: From French libertinage, from libertin, from Latin libertinus, 'freedman.'
common_mistakes: Confusing libertinage with libertarian, which refers to political views about freedom.
Using libertinage in casual conversation, where licentiousness or wild living sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The English word libertinage is not in Scripture, but the Greek aselgeia (licentiousness, debauchery) names the same kind of unrestrained conduct. Romans 13:13 lists debauchery and licentiousness among works of darkness, and Galatians 5:19 includes licentiousness among the works of the flesh. Both passages present such conduct as the opposite of life in the Spirit.

senses.definition: That which binds or acts as a ligament.
senses.example: The surgeon repaired the torn ligament in my knee during a three-hour operation.

senses.definition: A band of strong tissue that connects bones to other bones.

core.definition: A strong band of tough connective tissue that joins one bone to another and holds a joint in place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, so the word has three syllables, not four. Do not insert a vowel between the g and the m.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ligament in medical settings, sports injury talk, and physical therapy. Athletes often say they tore an ACL or sprained a knee ligament. Ligament is not used for tissue that attaches muscle to bone, which is a tendon.

distinctions.note: A tendon connects muscle to bone, while a ligament connects bone to bone.
Cartilage is a flexible tissue that cushions joints; a ligament is a tough band that holds them together.

examples.everyday: My son tore a ligament in his knee playing soccer, so he's on crutches for six weeks.
examples.professional: The physical therapist said the ligament should heal in about three months if he keeps weight off the joint.
examples.analytical: The author uses ligament as a metaphor for the bond that holds a community together, arguing that love is the connective tissue keeping distinct members in one body.

nuance.analogy: A ligament is like a strong strap buckled between two beams: it keeps them from sliding apart.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ligamentum 'band, bond', from ligare 'to bind'.
common_mistakes: Confusing ligament with tendon, which connects muscle to bone.
Calling a muscle injury a ligament injury in everyday talk.

ligament.etymology: From Middle English *ligament*, from Latin *ligāmentum*, from *ligō* (“tie, bind”).

senses.definition: In terms of lines; linewise.
senses.example: The data was stored lineally, one record per row, so the file loaded quickly.

senses.definition: By direct descent.

core.definition: In a direct line of descent from one generation to the next, without passing through side relatives.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LIN. The ending -ally is light, like uh-lee, not a strong al sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes inheritance or descent in a technical, objective way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use lineally in everyday speech. You will mainly see it in legal documents, genealogy, or history books, where phrases like lineally descended from are common. In casual talk, say directly descended from or passed down from parent to child.

distinctions.note: Linearly means in a straight line or in a sequential way, as in linearly increasing. Lineally means by direct family descent.
Directly is the everyday word for something without a middle step. Lineally is narrower and refers only to family line.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's name passed down lineally, from mother to daughter, for five generations.
examples.professional: The family business passed lineally to the eldest son, so the board had no role in the succession.
examples.analytical: The crown descended lineally in that dynasty, but the succession laws were ambiguous about cousins and collateral heirs.

nuance.analogy: Like water flowing straight down a single river channel, without branching into side streams.
nuance.etymology: From lineal plus the adverb suffix -ly; lineal from Latin linea, meaning line.
common_mistakes: Using lineally to mean in a straight line; that sense belongs to linearly.
Using lineally in everyday speech where directly sounds natural.

senses.definition: Relating to literature.
senses.example: literary fame

senses.definition: Relating to writers, or the profession of literature.
senses.example: a literary man

senses.definition: Knowledgeable of literature or writing.
Appropriate to literature rather than everyday writing.
senses.example: Her essay used literary language that felt more suited to a novel than a newspaper.

senses.definition: Bookish.
senses.example: My uncle is a literary man who reads Latin poetry and quotes Dickens at every dinner.

core.definition: Relating to literature, writers, or serious written works such as novels, poetry and plays; also knowledgeable about books.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIT. Pronounce the second r clearly, and end on a clear ee sound. Do not add an extra syllable or turn it into 'lit-RAIR-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests artistic quality and sophistication, though it can sound snobbish when used about people's tastes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use literary in book talk, publishing, school and academic contexts, such as 'literary magazine' or 'literary agent.' Describing someone as 'literary' means they love reading and know books well, which is a compliment. In casual talk, 'books' or 'reading' is more natural than 'literary' unless you are discussing serious writing.

distinctions.note: Literate means able to read and write, or educated; literary concerns writing and literature as an art.
Literal means word-for-word or exact; literary means relating to literature. The words look alike but are unrelated in meaning.

examples.everyday: She reads literary novels, not thrillers, so she'd probably love this one.
examples.professional: We need a literary agent who represents debut novelists, so could you send me a short list?
examples.analytical: Her literary analysis reads the sonnet's shifts in tone as a response to the political anxieties of its period.

nuance.analogy: Like a bookshelf of novels and poems rather than a shelf of manuals: the same medium, but aimed at art.
nuance.etymology: From Latin litterarius, 'of letters', from littera 'letter'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the second r or adding syllables; say LIT-uh-rer-ee.
Confusing literary with literal or literate, which mean very different things.

senses.definition: Logical.
senses.example: Her proof was logic from start to finish, so the reviewers had nothing to dispute.

senses.definition: A method of human thought that involves thinking in a linear, step-by-step manner about how a problem can be solved. Logic is the basis of many principles including the scientific method.
senses.example: apply logic

senses.definition: The study of the principles and criteria of valid inference and demonstration.
The mathematical study of relationships between rigorously defined concepts and of mathematical proof of statements.
senses.example: Students in the discrete mathematics course spent weeks studying formal logic and proof techniques.

senses.definition: A formal or informal language together with a deductive system or a model-theoretic semantics.
senses.example: Our compiler team chose a temporal logic to specify the behavior of concurrent programs.

senses.definition: Any system of thought, whether rigorous and productive or not, especially one associated with a particular person.
senses.example: It's hard to work out his system of logic.

senses.definition: The part of a system (usually electronic) that performs the boolean logic operations, short for logic gates or logic circuit.
senses.example: Fred is designing the logic for the new controller.

senses.definition: A system of thought or collection of rhetoric, especially one associated with a social practice.
senses.example: The seminary professor critiqued the logic of the colonial theology that justified the mission.

senses.definition: To engage in excessive or inappropriate application of logic.
senses.example: Don't logic the decision to death; we need to pick something and ship it.

senses.definition: To apply logical reasoning to.
senses.example: I tried to logic through the bug, testing each assumption until the cause appeared.

senses.definition: To overcome by logical argument.
senses.example: I finally logicked my skeptical brother into agreeing to the new budget plan.

core.definition: The systematic study of valid reasoning, and the step-by-step principles used to decide whether a conclusion follows from its premises.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'g' is soft, like the 'j' in 'judge', and the final '-ic' is a short 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. 'That's just logic' sounds reasonable, while 'cold logic' implies a lack of feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'the logic behind it' or 'that's the logic' in everyday talk to explain a decision. In philosophy, mathematics and computing, 'logic' names a formal field, as in 'formal logic' or 'predicate logic'. The adjective is 'logical'.

distinctions.note: Reason is the general human capacity to think, while logic is a structured method for checking whether reasoning is valid.
Reasoning is the process of working through a problem, while logic is the set of rules that makes that reasoning valid.
Common sense relies on practical experience and intuition, while logic relies on explicit rules and steps.

examples.everyday: I get the logic behind the new schedule, even if I don't like it.
examples.professional: The logic of the proposal is sound, but the cost estimates need to be checked before we present it.
examples.analytical: Gödel's results show that any consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic cannot prove all its own truths.

nuance.analogy: Logic is like the grammar of thought: it sets the rules, even though people speak without thinking about grammar.
nuance.etymology: From Greek logikē (technē), 'the art of reasoning', from logos ('word, reason').
common_mistakes: Using 'logic' as a verb, as in 'to logic it out', which sounds unnatural; say 'reason it out' or 'figure it out'.
Writing 'The plan is logic' instead of 'The plan is logical'; the noun and the adjective are different words.

logic.etymology: From Middle English *logike*, from Old French and Latin *logicus*, from Ancient Greek *λογῐκός*.

senses.definition: To relax; to spend time lazily; to stand, sit, or recline, in an indolent manner.
senses.example: We like to spend our Sundays lounging about at home in our pyjamas.

senses.definition: To walk or go in a leisurely manner.
senses.example: After dinner we lounged down the boardwalk, stopping to watch the boats.

senses.definition: The act of someone who lounges; idle reclining.
senses.example: After a long week, he wanted nothing more than a long lounge with a good novel.

senses.definition: A large comfortable seat for two or three people or more, a sofa or couch; also called lounge chair.
senses.example: The living room has a leather lounge that seats three comfortably.

senses.definition: A waiting room in an office, airport etc.
senses.example: We waited in the airport lounge until our gate was announced.

senses.definition: An establishment, similar to a bar, that serves alcohol and often plays background music or shows television.
senses.example: After work, the team gathered at a lounge downtown for drinks and karaoke.

senses.definition: (rare) A place where one can lounge; an area, establishment, house etc. where loungers gather and where one can relax and be at ease. A couch.
senses.example: The old cafe had a faded velvet lounge where regulars gathered every afternoon.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To relax in a casual, comfortable way by sitting, leaning, or lying down with no particular purpose.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the single syllable, and the final 'nge' is the sound 'dzh' as in 'judge.' Don't pronounce the g separately or say 'lown-guh.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests comfort and rest, though it can imply laziness in a critical context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'lounge around' or 'lounge on the couch' for relaxing at home on a weekend, which is friendly and casual. The verb is not used for hard work, so calling someone a 'lounger' in a critical way means they are idle. In hotels and airports, 'lounge' as a noun is the more common everyday usage.

distinctions.note: 'Relax' is a general word for rest, while 'lounge' emphasizes sitting or lying in a comfortable, lazy posture.
'Loaf' means to idle without doing anything useful and is more informal and mildly negative than 'lounge.'

examples.everyday: On Sunday afternoons I like to lounge on the couch and read the paper.
examples.professional: After the sprint review, the team did not lounge; they went straight to fixing the outage.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that modern leisure often becomes a form of lounging that dulls rather than restores the mind.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat stretched out in a sunny spot, fully at ease and not hurrying anywhere.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly related to a Middle English or dialect word for lazy or lean.
common_mistakes: Using 'lounge' for an active or energetic movement; the verb means relaxing, not walking briskly.
Saying 'lounge in' with a room, as in 'lounge in the house'; 'lounge around the house' is the natural phrase.

senses.definition: Synonym of low point:.

core.definition: The lowest point in a situation, a time when things are at their worst; the American term is low point.

pronunciation.tip: Say the first word with a diphthong, then stress dot with the short o of cot, which is the same vowel as in father in most American accents. The word low point is the common form, so practice the stress on the first element of that phrase too.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a bad moment or a low level of performance or mood.
nuance.usage_note: Low dot is not a standard American term, and you will not hear it in ordinary speech, so use low point instead. Americans say 'That was a low point in my career' or 'hit rock bottom' for emotional lows. Low point is informal and neutral enough for work, school and everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Low point is the standard American term, and dot is not an established word in this sense.
Rock bottom is more emotional and suggests the worst possible moment, while low point is more neutral.

collocations: a low point in her career

examples.everyday: Getting laid off right before the holidays was a low point for me.
examples.professional: Q3 sales hit a low point, so we need a recovery plan by Friday.
examples.analytical: Historians often treat the early 1930s as the low point of the Depression in American economic history.

nuance.analogy: It is like the bottom of a valley before the road climbs again, the place where the only way is up.
nuance.etymology: Not an established English term; low comes from Old English lāh, and dot, meaning a spot or point, has its own separate history.
common_mistakes: Using low dot in American conversation; say low point instead.
Saying in low point instead of at a low point.

senses.definition: Of inferior quality.
Not steep; nearly level (having a low grade).
senses.example: The low-grade road climbs so gently that cyclists barely notice the incline.

senses.definition: Minor.

core.definition: Of poor or inferior quality; also, mild or minor, as in a low-grade fever.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, GRADE, as in most compound adjectives placed before a noun. Say low with a clear OH vowel and keep the r in grade, since American speech is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing goods or work, meaning cheap or poor; neutral when doctors describe a mild, persistent symptom like a low-grade fever.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use low-grade for products, materials, or work that is poor but not terrible, such as low-grade paper. In health talk, a low-grade fever is a temperature only slightly above normal, usually under about 100.4°F, and parents and doctors use the phrase often. Calling a person low-grade is unusual and sounds insulting.

distinctions.note: Poor is the general word for bad quality; low-grade is more specific and suggests something cheap or second-rate rather than broken.
Mild describes intensity; low-grade describes level or quality, though both can describe a fever.

examples.everyday: I think I'm getting a low-grade cold, so I'm skipping the gym tonight.
examples.professional: We can't ship this batch because the raw materials are low-grade and would fail the spec.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on low-grade evidence, mostly anecdotes dressed up as data, so it cannot bear its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like coffee that tastes faintly burnt: not undrinkable, but clearly below the standard you expect.
nuance.etymology: Low (Old English lāg) plus grade, from Latin gradus, step.
common_mistakes: Using low-grade to describe a person's character in a neutral way; it sounds insulting.
Leaving out the hyphen when the phrase comes before a noun.

senses.definition: A room designated as a place to eat lunch.
senses.example: Company policy was to eat snacks only in the lunchroom.

senses.definition: A diner or small restaurant that serves lunch.
senses.example: I don't know how they stay in business serving only lunch, but the lunchroom on the corner is cheap and fast so I like it.

core.definition: A room where people, especially students or workers, eat their lunch.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'LUNCH,' with a lighter secondary stress on 'room.' The 'r' in 'room' is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a practical, everyday space and carries no special emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'lunchroom' for a school dining area, although 'cafeteria' is more common in that setting. In offices, people say 'break room' or 'kitchen' for a place to eat and relax. A small restaurant that serves lunch is also called a lunchroom in some regions, but this use is less common now.

distinctions.note: A cafeteria is a self-service dining hall; a lunchroom is a room used for eating lunch, which may or may not have a cafeteria line.
A break room is a workplace room for short breaks, coffee and snacks; a lunchroom is mostly for eating a full lunch.
A luncheonette is a small restaurant; a lunchroom is usually an institutional or workplace room.

examples.everyday: I'll meet you in the lunchroom after second period.
examples.professional: Please take your leftovers out of the lunchroom fridge by Friday afternoon.
examples.analytical: Sociologists have long studied the school lunchroom, where seating patterns quietly reveal social hierarchies.

nuance.analogy: A lunchroom is the kitchen table of a building: a shared space where people eat, talk and recharge.
nuance.etymology: From 'lunch' and 'room.'
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words ('lunch room') in formal writing; standard American spelling is usually one word.
Using 'lunchroom' for a quick coffee space, which is usually called a 'break room.'
Assuming it is a formal word; it is plain and everyday.

senses.definition: Involving or relating to lustration.

core.definition: Relating to lustration, a ritual cleansing of a person, place, or group using water, fire, or sacrifice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LUS, and the middle syllables are reduced to a schwa. The final -tive has a short i, so it sounds like 'tiv', not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word in daily life; it appears in academic writing about religion, anthropology, and classics. It usually modifies ritual nouns like 'rite' or 'water'. If you want a common word, say 'purifying' or 'cleansing'.

distinctions.note: The two adjectives are close synonyms with the same root; lustral also has a separate meaning about five-year periods.
Cleansing is an everyday word for any washing; lustrative names a formal ritual with a religious or civic purpose.

examples.everyday: The temple guide explained the lustrative bath that visitors took before going inside.
examples.professional: The seminar slides compare the lustrative rites of three ancient cities.
examples.analytical: The author reads the washing scene as lustrative, showing purity as a condition for entering the community.

nuance.analogy: Like scrubbing a kitchen before a holiday dinner: the ritual clears the space so something new can begin.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lustrare, to purify, related to lustrum.
common_mistakes: Using lustrative to mean any kind of cleaning; it refers specifically to ritual purification.
Putting the stress on the wrong syllable, as in luh-STRAY-tiv; the stress falls on the first syllable.

senses.definition: A person who acts in a capricious, impulsive, or reckless manner.
senses.example: The madcap rode his bicycle through the crowded market at full speed.

senses.definition: A very foolish or irresponsible person; a fool, an idiot.
senses.example: Don't listen to that madcap, he'll get us all lost on this mountain.

senses.definition: Capricious, impulsive, or reckless; also, bizarre, crazy, zany; or foolish, idiotic.
senses.example: a madcap activity a madcap idea a madcap plan

core.definition: Impulsive, reckless, or wildly playful in a way that is zany and unpredictable, such as a madcap plan or comedy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAD, and keep the vowel in both syllables short, like the a in cat. Do not stretch the second syllable into kayp.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to playful. It can criticize reckless behavior, but it is often used affectionately for a fun, chaotic adventure in movies or stories.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use madcap most often with plans, adventures, comedies, or schemes, as in a madcap road trip or a madcap caper film. Calling a person madcap is a friendly way to say they act impulsively. In a serious workplace, it sounds too playful, so use reckless or impulsive instead.

distinctions.note: Reckless implies real danger or disregard for consequences. Madcap suggests a fun, chaotic energy that is less dangerous.
Zany stresses comical oddness and silliness. Madcap stresses rushing, impulsive action.

examples.everyday: We took a madcap road trip to Vegas with no hotel reservations.
examples.professional: Let's drop the madcap plan to launch on Friday and stick with the tested schedule.
examples.analytical: The novel's madcap plot hides a serious argument about how institutions reward chaos.

nuance.analogy: A madcap plan is like a car with the brakes removed: exciting, fast, and hard to control.
nuance.etymology: From mad plus cap, a dialect or informal word for head, so literally a crazy head.
common_mistakes: Writing mad cap as two words when it is used as an adjective before a noun.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound like a different compound.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, operating by, or caused by magnetism.
senses.example: a magnetic recorder

senses.definition: Having the properties of a magnet, especially the ability to draw or pull.
senses.example: The magnetic field from the old speaker wiped the data off the hard drive.

senses.definition: Determined by earth's magnetic fields.
senses.example: magnetic north

senses.definition: Having an extraordinary ability to attract: attractive, alluring, persuasive.
senses.example: He has a magnetic personality.

core.definition: Relating to magnetism or to a magnet; also, having a strong personal appeal that draws people to you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NET, not the first. The final '-ic' is a short 'ik' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive in personal use ('a magnetic smile'), neutral in physics and navigation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'magnetic' in science and everyday talk. In physics, it describes fields and materials. In navigation, 'magnetic north' differs slightly from true north. In casual speech, a person with a 'magnetic personality' is charming and easy to be around. Avoid 'magnetic' for something merely attractive to look at; 'attractive' or 'appealing' is more natural there.

distinctions.note: 'Charismatic' suggests inspiring leadership or a special gift to motivate others. 'Magnetic' suggests a pull that draws people toward you, often socially.
'Magnetized' describes an object that has been made into a magnet. 'Magnetic' describes the property or relationship, such as a magnetic field.

examples.everyday: Her smile is so magnetic that everyone at the party wanted to talk to her.
examples.professional: We stored the old backups on magnetic tape, which is slow but cheap for long-term archiving.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes the will as drawn by a kind of magnetic desire, though he is careful to distinguish attraction from compulsion.

nuance.analogy: Magnetic people are like the moon in the night sky: you feel drawn toward them without being forced.
nuance.etymology: From Latin magneticus, from magnes (magnet), from Greek magnēs.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'MAG-net-ik', which sounds unnatural.
Using 'magnetic' for physical beauty instead of 'attractive' or 'appealing'.

senses.definition: The main serving or dish of a meal, usually cooked.
senses.example: For the main course, we ordered roasted salmon with lemon butter and asparagus.

core.definition: The biggest and most substantial dish of a meal, served after the appetizer or soup and before dessert.

pronunciation.tip: Both words carry stress, with 'KORS' a bit stronger. The 'r' in 'course' is strongly pronounced, and 'main' sounds like 'mane'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday, used in restaurants and at home.
nuance.usage_note: In American restaurants, the menu usually lists appetizers, salads, soups, main courses or entrees, and desserts. 'Entree' is also common in the US and sometimes means the main dish, but in some places it means a starter. When ordering, you can say 'I'll have the main course' or 'What comes with the main?' In casual speech, people often just say 'main'.

distinctions.note: In American English, 'entree' usually means the main dish; in British English it often refers to the first course.
An appetizer comes before the main course and is smaller.

examples.everyday: I'll have the salmon as my main course, and the mushroom soup to start.
examples.professional: At the company dinner, the caterer will serve a salad first and then a choice of two main courses.
examples.analytical: In the structure of a formal meal, the main course is the organizing center around which the other courses are arranged.

nuance.analogy: The main course is like the headline of a meal, the part everything else is arranged around.
nuance.etymology: 'Main' from Old English 'mæġen', strength, and 'course' from Latin 'cursus', a running or sequence, referring to the order of dishes.
common_mistakes: Saying 'main plate' or 'principal dish' in ordinary conversation, which sounds unnatural.
Using 'main course' to mean 'main meal', as in lunch or dinner as a whole.

conversation.text: Let's save room for dessert and not go crazy on the main course.
For the main course, I'm thinking the roast chicken.
The appetizers were great, but the main course took forever to come out.

senses.definition: A host telling a guest to relax and feel comfortable.

core.definition: A host's polite phrase telling a guest to relax and act comfortably, as if in their own house.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on HOME, and 'yourself' is weakened, with 'your' reducing to 'yer'. Link the words smoothly, and don't stress 'at'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm. It signals hospitality and friendliness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a guest arrives at a house, apartment, or office. The usual reply is a simple thank you, such as 'Thanks, I will,' or 'Thanks, this is nice.' It is friendly but casual, so it suits friends, neighbors, and relaxed gatherings rather than formal dinners, where a host might say 'Please, have a seat.'

distinctions.note: Nearly the same meaning, but 'comfortable' focuses on physical ease, while 'at home' stresses acting freely, like family.
'Help yourself' is said about food or drinks, and 'make yourself at home' covers the whole visit.

examples.everyday: Come on in, make yourself at home. The snacks are on the counter.
examples.professional: When the visiting client arrived at our office, I told her to make herself at home in the conference room while we set up.
examples.analytical: The phrase suggests that hospitality is a temporary transfer of ownership, in which the host gives the guest a provisional share in the house.

nuance.analogy: It works like opening a door and offering someone a seat at your kitchen table.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Make yourself to home' or 'Make yourself at house'; the phrase uses 'at home.'
Answering with 'Yes, I make myself home' instead of a simple thanks.

conversation.text: Come on in and make yourself at home.
Make yourself at home. The bathroom's down the hall on the left.
"Can I sit anywhere?" "Of course, make yourself at home."

senses.definition: The state of being malignant or diseased.
A malignant cancer; specifically, any neoplasm that is invasive or otherwise not benign.
senses.example: The biopsy confirmed a malignancy in the lower lobe of her left lung.

senses.definition: That which is malign; evil, depravity, malevolence.
senses.example: Her novel explores the malignancy at the heart of a family that hides its secrets.

core.definition: A cancerous growth that is invasive and can spread, or a state of being harmful, evil, or diseased.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIG, the second syllable. The middle syllables are reduced to 'nun,' and the final 'cy' is a clear 'see.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious disease or harmful quality, usually in medical or moral discussion.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, malignancy is used mainly by doctors and in medical reports, such as 'a malignancy was found.' In everyday talk people say 'cancer' or 'a tumor.' The word can also describe evil in a literary way, but it is less common.

distinctions.note: Cancer is the everyday word for the disease. Malignancy is the more technical term for a growth that can invade and spread.
A tumor is any abnormal growth, while a malignancy is specifically a cancerous or invasive one.
Benignity describes a harmless growth or a kind nature. Malignancy describes the dangerous opposite.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the lump was not a malignancy, so I can stop worrying about it.
examples.professional: The clinical trial measured the rate of new malignancy among patients over five years.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes evil not as a substance but as a privation, which means malignancy is a corruption of a good nature.

nuance.analogy: A malignancy is like a weed that spreads through the garden roots and crowds out healthy plants before anyone sees the damage.
nuance.etymology: From malignant, from Latin malignare, 'to act maliciously,' from malignus 'ill-disposed.'
common_mistakes: Using it for any tumor; a malignancy must be cancerous or invasive, so use 'tumor' for a generic growth.
Saying 'malignity' in medical speech; malignancy is the usual American term.

senses.definition: A man who doesn't speak much; a habitually terse or taciturn man.
senses.example: My father is a man of few words, but when he speaks, everyone listens.

core.definition: A man who speaks little and says only what is necessary; someone habitually quiet or brief in speech.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on WORDS, with secondary stress on FEW. In American speech the 'r' in 'words' is strong and the final 'z' is voiced, while 'of' reduces to 'uhv'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or neutral. It suggests thoughtfulness and dignity, though it can sound critical if the person is evasive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this about a quiet, reliable person, often a coworker, relative or older man who speaks only when he has something important to say. It is a familiar idiom and works well in both casual and professional talk. A natural reply is 'Yeah, but when he talks, it's worth hearing.'

distinctions.note: Quiet describes temperament or volume; this phrase emphasizes deliberate economy in speech, often with an admiring tone.
Taciturn is more formal and can sound disapproving, while this idiom is usually warm or respectful.

collocations: known as a man of few words
a man of few words but great ideas
a man of few words in meetings
true to his reputation as a man of few words

examples.everyday: Dan's a man of few words, but when he does talk, everybody listens.
examples.professional: In the sprint review, Tom was a man of few words, but his two-sentence summary answered every question the team had.
examples.analytical: Wisdom literature often prizes the man of few words, though silence can also conceal evasion rather than prudence.

nuance.analogy: Like a short, well-aimed arrow rather than a shotgun spray.
nuance.etymology: English idiom from man, Old English mann, and word, Old English word; few from Old English feawa.
common_mistakes: Applying the idiom to a woman; say 'a person of few words' instead.
Mispronouncing 'words' with a final 'd' sound; in American speech it is simply WURDZ.

senses.definition: The increase in cost that accompanies a unit increase in output; the unit cost of that additional output; the partial derivative of the cost function with respect to output.
senses.example: The company's marginal cost of producing one more unit rose sharply once the factory ran at full capacity.

senses.definition: Synonym of break-even point.
senses.example: Our analysts argued that marginal cost was the true threshold where the startup would finally stop losing money.

core.definition: In economics, the added cost of producing one more unit of a good or service, after production has already begun.

pronunciation.tip: In the phrase, the strongest stress usually falls on 'cost', and 'marginal' reduces to 'mar-juh-nul'. The cot-caught merger makes 'cost' sound like 'kawst' in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise economic term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'marginal cost' in economics, business planning, and pricing discussions. It refers to the extra cost of one more unit, not the average. Some dictionaries list it as a synonym of break-even point, but that is incorrect: break-even is the level where total revenue equals total cost. In everyday talk, people say 'the extra cost' instead.

distinctions.note: Average cost is total cost divided by total output; marginal cost is the change in total cost from one extra unit.
Fixed costs do not change with output; marginal cost is the cost that does change when you produce one more unit.
Break-even is the output where revenue equals cost; marginal cost is a per-unit concept and does not define that point.

examples.everyday: Once the oven is hot, the marginal cost of baking one more batch of cookies is pretty small.
examples.professional: In the pricing meeting, we need to set the discount based on marginal cost, not on the average cost per user.
examples.analytical: A firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, a result that follows from the first-order conditions of the profit function.

nuance.analogy: Like the price of one extra slice after you have already bought the whole pizza.
nuance.etymology: 'Marginal' from Latin margo, 'edge'; 'cost' from Old French coster, from Latin constare, 'to stand at a price'.
common_mistakes: Treating marginal cost as the same as average cost.
Saying 'the marginal cost is the break-even point', which is wrong.

senses.definition: A male surname from Russian, feminine equivalent Markova.
senses.example: Our new analyst, Dmitri Markov, joined the team from Boston last spring.

core.definition: Andrey Markov, the Russian mathematician whose name is attached to Markov chains and related probability models.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final v is voiced, like the v in 'very,' though many Americans say it closer to 'MAHR-kawf.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name used in technical and academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In American statistics and computer science classes, people say Markov to refer to the mathematician or to the adjective Markovian. You will hear it in phrases like Markov model, and the name is almost always said as a technical term rather than as a family name in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Markov is the name of the person, while Markov chain is the term for the probability process named after him.
Markovian is the adjective meaning having the Markov property, so a Markovian process is one whose future depends only on the present.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in statistics keeps mentioning Markov, a Russian mathematician from about a century ago.
examples.professional: The team's Markov model predicts customer churn from each user's most recent behavior.
examples.analytical: Markov's 1906 work on dependent sequences of events laid the groundwork for the modern theory of stochastic processes.

nuance.analogy: Markov is like a name on a recipe: it tells you who invented the method, not the method itself.
nuance.etymology: Named for the Russian mathematician Andrey Andreyevich Markov (1856-1922).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final v as 'f' in technical talk, which may confuse a listener.
Using Markov alone to mean the process; say Markov chain or Markov model.

senses.definition: Independent and unconventional behavior.

core.definition: Independent, unconventional behavior that deliberately refuses to follow the views, rules, or habits of a group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAV. The middle syllables are weak, so 'uh' and 'ih' are very short, and the final '-ism' is 'izm' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can praise independent thinking or criticize someone as stubbornly contrary, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use maverickism in everyday talk. They usually say maverick, as a noun or adjective, for someone who goes their own way, such as 'a maverick senator' or 'a maverick chef'. Maverickism is mainly found in literary, political, or academic writing that discusses a pattern of behavior.

distinctions.note: Eccentricity refers to odd personal quirks. Maverickism is a deliberate rejection of group norms, usually in a public or professional setting.
Nonconformity is the general state of not following norms. Maverickism stresses a bold, self-assured independence and often carries a sense of rebellion.

examples.professional: Her maverickism in code review pushed the team to drop the old framework and try a leaner design.
examples.analytical: Scholars often read the poet's maverickism as a deliberate rejection of the literary establishment of her day.

nuance.analogy: Maverickism is like a horse that refuses to join the herd and runs its own path across the field.
nuance.etymology: From Samuel A. Maverick, a Texas rancher whose unbranded cattle gave the word maverick its sense of an independent person.
common_mistakes: Using maverickism in casual speech where maverick is more natural.
Misspelling it as 'mavrickism' by dropping the 'e' from maverick.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or containing meat.
Resembling meat in flavor, smell, etc.
senses.example: This tastes rather meaty. Are you sure it's vegetarian?

senses.definition: Of a person or a body part, large and solid.
senses.example: The linebacker had a meaty build, with thick shoulders and arms like tree trunks.

senses.definition: Substantial.
senses.example: I got a nice, meaty bonus.

core.definition: Containing a lot of meat or tasting like meat; also describes a thing that is substantial, dense or full of real content.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a long ee sound in both syllables. The word ends in a clear ee, not a short 'uh' or 'eh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, suggesting richness and substance. Calling a person 'meaty' sounds rude or odd, so use 'beefy' or 'stocky' for people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meaty' for sauces, sandwiches, fish and vegetables that taste hearty, and in a more figurative way for an issue or chapter that has substance. Describing a person as 'meaty' is unusual and can sound insulting, so Americans prefer 'beefy' for a muscular person. In a meeting, saying a topic is 'meaty' means there is a lot to discuss.

distinctions.note: Beefy describes a person who is large and muscular, and it is more natural for people; meaty is mostly used for food or substance.
Substantial is a general word for large or important; meaty suggests a rich, dense or content-heavy quality.

examples.everyday: This chili is so meaty that I didn't even miss the beans.
examples.professional: The Q3 report has some meaty content on customer churn, so let's schedule a longer review.
examples.analytical: The argument is meaty, but it rests on an unexamined assumption about intention that deserves scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: A meaty idea is like a sturdy loaf of bread: it fills you up and takes some work to chew through.
nuance.etymology: From meat with the suffix -y, meaning 'having the qualities of' or 'full of'.
common_mistakes: Calling a person 'meaty' in English, which can sound insulting; use 'muscular' or 'beefy' instead.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a short vowel; it should be a long ee sound.

senses.definition: A person of strength, integrity, and honor or compassion; a gentleman.

core.definition: A decent, honorable person who does the right thing and treats others with kindness and integrity.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short e, like the vowel in 'bet'. The final ch is a single sound as in 'church', and the word rhymes with 'bench'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and warm; it praises someone's character more than their achievements.
nuance.usage_note: Americans, especially in New York and in Jewish communities, use mensch as a high compliment for someone who is kind, reliable and does the right thing when it counts. You can say 'He's a real mensch' about a friend who helped you move. It is informal and is nearly always used of a person. A natural reply is a simple thanks or 'He really is.'

distinctions.note: Gentleman suggests manners and social class; mensch emphasizes integrity and kindness regardless of background.
Good person is general; mensch is a warmer, more specific compliment about someone who acts decently under pressure.

examples.everyday: When my car broke down on the highway, Dan drove forty minutes to pick me up. He's a real mensch.
examples.professional: Maria stayed late to cover the release for the whole team without asking for credit. She's a real mensch.
examples.analytical: In Jewish ethical discourse the mensch is a figure of practical moral character, a person whose decency shows in concrete acts rather than doctrine.

nuance.analogy: A mensch is like a reliable anchor: you can count on them when the weather turns.
nuance.etymology: From Yiddish mentsh, from German Mensch 'human being', ultimately from Old High German mennisco.
common_mistakes: Saying it with a 'sh' sound as in 'mensh', or stretching the vowel into 'men-sh'; the final sound is ch.
Using it for a gentle, pleasant person with no moral strength; it implies integrity under pressure.

mensch.etymology: From Yiddish *מענטש* (“an honorable person”), from Middle High German *mensch*, *mensche*, *mennische*, from Old High German *mennisko* (“man, human being”), from Proto-Germanic **manniskaz* (“human”).

core.definition: A priest in the Bible, son of Uriah, who helped weigh temple treasures and repair Jerusalem's walls after the exile.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the final 'th' is unvoiced, like the th in 'think.' Americans pronounce the middle syllable with a light, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical proper name used in Bible study, historical discussion, or religious writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Meremoth almost only in Bible study, church teaching, or academic discussion of the Old Testament. It is not a common name for people today, though it could appear in a historical or scriptural context. In everyday talk, you would not use it, but a Bible study leader might mention it in discussing Nehemiah.

distinctions.note: Uriah is Meremoth's father and a separate biblical figure, so Meremoth is not Uriah himself.
Ezra 8:33 and Nehemiah 3:4 both mention Meremoth son of Uriah, and they describe him in different roles within the same restoration story.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we read about Meremoth, who helped repair the walls of Jerusalem with the other families.
examples.professional: The commentary notes that Meremoth appears in several lists of workers, which helps date the restoration accounts.
examples.analytical: Ezra 8:33 places Meremoth son of Uriah among those entrusted with weighing the silver and gold, which suggests priestly responsibility for temple property.

nuance.analogy: Meremoth is like a name on a restoration crew list: small in the story, but present in the work that rebuilt the city.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in mer-e-MOTH; the stress falls on the first syllable.
Confusing Meremoth with Uriah, his father.
Pronouncing the final th as a /t/ instead of an unvoiced th sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Meremoth was a priest, son of Uriah, who lived in the post-exilic period when Ezra and Nehemiah led the return and restoration of Jerusalem. Ezra 8:33 says that the silver and gold and the vessels were weighed in the house of God into the hands of Meremoth, showing his role in handling temple treasures. Nehemiah 3:4 and 3:21 name Meremoth son of Uriah among those who repaired sections of the walls of Jerusalem. These passages show him as a priest who took part in both the sacred and practical work of rebuilding.

senses.definition: Synonym of Event-Driven Architecture.
senses.example: Our data pipeline uses message-driven architecture so services react to events without waiting on each other.

core.definition: A software design in which components communicate by sending asynchronous messages through a broker or queue instead of calling each other directly.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AR in architecture, and the -ture ending sounds like chur. The word driven reduces to driv-un, so do not say it as a full drive plus en.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in software engineering often prefer event-driven architecture, so message-driven architecture may sound less standard. The two terms overlap a lot, so people often treat them as synonyms. Use message-driven when you want to stress explicit messages sent to specific receivers. It appears in design documents, conference talks and architecture reviews.

distinctions.note: Event-driven architecture emphasizes notifications that something happened, while message-driven architecture emphasizes messages sent to particular receivers.
Request-response waits for a reply in a direct call, while message-driven systems often send messages asynchronously.

examples.everyday: My cousin's team is moving to a message-driven architecture, so they talk about queues all day at dinner.
examples.professional: We chose a message-driven architecture so the fraud service can scale apart from the checkout service.
examples.analytical: A message-driven architecture makes each interaction explicit, because every exchange is recorded as a message with a sender and a receiver.

nuance.analogy: A message-driven architecture is like an office with memos in labeled trays: people work independently and pick up what is addressed to them.
nuance.etymology: Message comes from Old French message; driven is the past participle of drive, from Old English drifan; architecture comes from Latin architectura.
common_mistakes: Using message-driven as a synonym for any messaging app, when it describes a design pattern.
Forgetting the hyphen when using the phrase as a compound adjective before a noun.

senses.definition: A very small thing; especially one which is conspicuously smaller than expected or by comparison.
senses.example: the midget pony

senses.definition: A short person, particularly one with dwarfism.
senses.example: Growing up as a midget, he learned early to ignore the stares of strangers.

senses.definition: Something for use by a small person; especially something designed or made for one.
senses.example: The hardware store sold a midget workbench made for my daughter's small hands.

core.definition: Something much smaller than the usual size of its kind, such as a midget tomato or a midget submarine.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the ending is a short, reduced 'it', not 'eet'. The 'dg' sounds like the 'j' in 'judge'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when used of people, since the term for a person with dwarfism is now considered offensive; neutral for objects, though still informal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans consider midget offensive when used for a person with dwarfism, and most people now say 'person with dwarfism' or 'little person'. For objects, midget remains common in phrases like midget car, midget submarine and midget tomato, but small or miniature is often safer. Avoid using it about people, even as a joke.

distinctions.note: Miniature is neutral and polite for small objects; midget is informal and can be offensive when used of people.
Tiny is a general everyday word for very small size; midget often suggests a smaller version of a standard type.
Dwarfism is a medical term for a condition; midget is a dated and offensive label for the person.

collocations: a midget version of the original

examples.everyday: We grew midget tomatoes on the balcony, and they fit in a salad bowl.
examples.professional: The vendor offered a midget router for small offices, with the same ports in half the size.
examples.analytical: Disability advocates have rightly rejected midget as a label for people, because it reduces a person to a size.

nuance.analogy: A midget car is like a dollhouse version of a real house: the same design, shrunk down.
common_mistakes: Using midget for a person; say 'person with dwarfism' or 'little person' instead.
Mispronouncing the ending as 'mid-JEET'; the final syllable is short, like 'it'.

senses.definition: By supernatural or uncommon causes, e.g. by a god; that cannot be explained in terms of normal events.
Very surprising; amazing.
senses.example: Her recovery after the accident was miraculous, and the doctors were stunned.

core.definition: So surprising, lucky or wonderful that it seems beyond normal explanation; also, caused by God or supernatural power.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, RAK, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. The middle syllable, spelled cu, is usually pronounced 'yuh' or 'juh', and many learners wrongly add an extra syllable, such as 'mi-ra-ku-lous'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it expresses admiration or relief. It can be used ironically for something that is not actually remarkable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use miraculous for very good luck or for a surprising recovery, such as 'a miraculous recovery' after surgery. In everyday speech it is often exaggerated for effect, so it is common to hear it about a good parking spot. In religious contexts, it means caused by divine action.

distinctions.note: Lucky means fortunate by chance, while miraculous suggests something so unlikely that it seems to defy normal explanation.
Wonderful is a general word for something delightful, while miraculous implies a surprising event that seems beyond ordinary causes.

examples.everyday: The car was totaled, but she walked away with only a scratch, which is nothing short of miraculous.
examples.professional: The server failed during the demo, but the team restored it, and the miraculous recovery saved the presentation.
examples.analytical: Hume argued that a report of a miraculous event should be weighed against the uniform experience of how nature normally behaves.

nuance.analogy: A miraculous result is like a bridge built across a river that everyone thought was impossible to cross.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin miraculosus, from miraculum, 'object of wonder.'
common_mistakes: Using miraculous as a noun, as in 'a miraculous of God'; use 'a miracle' instead.
Adding an extra syllable in the middle, such as 'mi-ra-ku-lous,' instead of 'MIR-uh-kyuh-lus' in standard US speech.

senses.definition: To read wrongly; misconstrue; misinterpret; mistake the sense or significance of.
An instance of reading wrongly.

core.definition: To read or interpret something incorrectly, so that you get its meaning or significance wrong.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'read'. The past tense and past participle are spelled the same but pronounced /mɪsˈɹɛd/ ('mis-RED'), so say 'I misread' and 'I had misread' with a short e sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes an honest mistake, but it can sound critical when someone is blamed for misreading a situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this verb for written text, signs, maps, data, and social cues, as in 'I misread the room.' It is neutral in everyday talk and common in meetings and casual conversation. A natural reply to a correction is 'Oh, my mistake' or 'Sorry, I totally misread that.'

distinctions.note: 'Misinterpret' focuses on the meaning you assign to words, actions, or data; 'misread' often applies to text, signs, or social cues you literally or figuratively scan.
'Misunderstand' is broader and everyday, covering any failure to grasp what someone means; 'misread' implies a specific error in reading a text, signal, or situation.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I misread your text and thought you were coming tonight instead of tomorrow.
examples.professional: We misread the churn data because the dashboard grouped customers by the wrong signup date.
examples.analytical: Many readers misread the parable as a moral rule when it is really a challenge to the listener's assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like reading a road sign backward, you see the words clearly but get the direction wrong.
nuance.etymology: From Old English rǣdan, meaning to advise or interpret, with the prefix mis- (wrongly).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the past tense 'misread' as 'mis-REED' instead of 'mis-RED'.
Using 'misread' for a spoken misunderstanding where 'misunderstand' is more natural.

misread.etymology: From Middle English *misreden*, from Old English *misrǣdan* (“to advise wrongly; read wrongly”), equivalent to *mis-* + *read*.

senses.definition: To miss an experience or lose an opportunity, etc. that should not be missed.
senses.example: Anybody who does not try the homemade ice cream is really missing out.

core.definition: To fail to get or enjoy something good, such as an opportunity or experience, because you were not present or did not act.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on OUT, and miss is lightly stressed. Keep the 'miss' short and do not stretch the vowel, and make the final t clear before a pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests missing something enjoyable or valuable, sometimes with mild regret.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use miss out very often in casual speech with friends, family, and coworkers, especially about parties, trips, deals, or events. It is often used with 'on': 'You missed out on the best pizza.' A natural reply is 'Oh no, next time!' or 'Yeah, I know, I was stuck at work.'

distinctions.note: Miss can mean to fail to catch, see, or attend something, while miss out specifically stresses losing a benefit or pleasure that others got.
Skip means to choose not to do something on purpose, while miss out often happens by accident or circumstance.

examples.everyday: You really missed out last night, because the band at the bar was amazing.
examples.professional: If you don't submit your request by Friday, you'll miss out on the training budget for this quarter.
examples.analytical: Students who skip the optional seminar may miss out on the discussion that shapes the final exam, which is why attendance matters more than it seems.

nuance.analogy: Missing out is like arriving at a train station just after the train has left: the train was real, and you were close, but the chance is gone.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the preposition 'on' after miss out when naming the thing lost: say miss out on, not miss out the thing.
Using miss out for simply missing a bus or appointment without any sense of losing a benefit.

conversation.text: You missed out on a great party last night.
Sign up now so you don't miss out.

senses.definition: Anything of mixed kind.
senses.example: That dog is a mongrel; who knows what breed it could be!

senses.definition: A dog with a lineage of two or more breeds.
senses.example: That dog is a mongrel; who knows what breed it could be!

senses.definition: A person of mixed race.
Of mixed breed, nature, or origin; of or like a mongrel.
senses.example: English spelling is often regarded as confusing and unpredictable due to the mongrel nature of that language.

core.definition: A dog of mixed breed, or anything made of mixed kinds that lacks a pure origin. The word can also be an insult for a person.
