Stressing the first syllable, as in PRE-mature-ly; the stress belongs on -TUR-.

senses.definition: In AI: Already trained on a large general dataset, ready to be fine-tuned or used directly.
Having been trained before.
senses.example: The pretrained nurses at the clinic adapted quickly to the new electronic records system.

senses.definition: Having undergone initial training to acquire a base of general-purpose knowledge, representations, or capabilities.
senses.example: We fine-tuned a pretrained language model on our hospital's anonymized clinical notes.

core.definition: In AI, already trained on a large general dataset so it can be fine-tuned for a specific task or used directly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PREE, the first syllable. The 'pre' is a long 'ee' sound, and the final 'ed' is pronounced as a 'd', not as 'ed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a positive description of a model that saves time and data.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pretrained mostly in data science, machine learning, and AI conversations. It usually comes before the noun, as in 'a pretrained model,' or after a verb, as in 'the model was pretrained on web text.' When explaining to a client, you can say 'a model that already learned from a huge general dataset.' Many writers also use the spelling 'pre-trained'.

distinctions.note: A pretrained model is trained first on general data; fine-tuning is the further training that adapts it to a specific task.
A model trained from scratch starts with random weights; a pretrained model starts with knowledge learned from a broad dataset.
Untrained means no learning has happened yet; pretrained means general learning has already been done.

examples.everyday: My kid's new drawing app uses a pretrained model, so it recognizes cats without any setup.
examples.professional: We can start with a pretrained model and fine-tune it on our claims data instead of training from scratch.
examples.analytical: A pretrained representation transfers statistical structure from a broad corpus to narrower tasks, which is why it generalizes with fewer labels.

nuance.analogy: Like a new employee who already knows the basics of the industry, so training focuses only on the company's specific work.
nuance.etymology: From pre- ('before') and trained, from Old French trainer, 'to drag or draw along'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'pre-TRAYND' instead of 'PREE-traynd'.
Pronouncing the final 'ed' as an extra syllable, 'PREE-tray-ned'.

conversation.text: We started from pretrained weights rather than random initialization, which cut training time dramatically.
The model was pretrained on a mix of web text, books, and code before any fine-tuning.
Pretrained means the model already learned general language patterns before we taught it your specific task.

senses.definition: The chief member of the cabinet and head of the government, especially in a parliamentary democracy; often the leader of the majority party.
senses.example: This is a list of all prime ministers since Churchill.

core.definition: The head of government in a parliamentary country, usually the leader of the largest party in the national parliament.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MIN in minister, and prime has a lighter secondary stress. Many Americans drop the m in prime, so it sounds like 'PRY-mih-nis-ter'. The final -er is a reduced r-sound, not a full 'tear'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard political title with no negative associations.
nuance.usage_note: The United States has a president, not a prime minister, so Americans use this term when talking about other countries such as the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, or Israel. Americans capitalize it before a name, as in 'Prime Minister Trudeau', but use lowercase when it stands alone, as in 'the prime minister'. A casual reply to a news mention is usually just 'Oh, really?' or 'What did they decide?'

distinctions.note: A president is the head of state in a presidential system such as the United States, while a prime minister usually leads the government in a parliamentary system.
Premier is used for the head of government in some Canadian provinces and Australian states, and for the leader of China's State Council; it is less common than prime minister for national leaders.

examples.everyday: My neighbor, who grew up in Ireland, always watches the prime minister's speeches on television.
examples.professional: Our London team says the prime minister will announce new trade rules next week, so we should update the forecast.
examples.analytical: In a parliamentary system, the prime minister depends on the confidence of the legislature rather than on a separate popular mandate.

nuance.analogy: Like the captain who runs the ship day to day, while the head of state is more like the flag that represents the nation.
nuance.etymology: Prime comes from Latin primus, 'first'; minister comes from Latin minister, 'servant, attendant'.
common_mistakes: Saying primer minister, which confuses the word with the book primer.
Capitalizing the title when it stands alone, as in 'the Prime Minister said', instead of writing 'the prime minister said'.

senses.definition: To print (a computer document).

core.definition: To print a computer file or document onto paper.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves to OUT, the particle, so print gets only secondary stress. In fast speech, 'print it out' links as 'prin-tih-DOWT,' with the t of it becoming a soft flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is an everyday office and home action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say print out all the time in offices and at home, as in 'I'll print it out for the meeting.' It is separable, so you can say 'print it out' or 'print out the file,' but never 'print out it.' The noun printout is one word and stresses PRINT.

distinctions.note: Print out means the same as print in most offices, but it emphasizes that you are getting paper you can hold.
Printout is the noun for the paper copy; print out is the verb for making it.

examples.everyday: Could you print out my boarding pass before we get to the airport?
examples.professional: I'll print out the budget summary so we can review the numbers together.
examples.analytical: Printing out the full code lets reviewers mark each assumption by hand instead of trusting the summary.

nuance.analogy: Like pressing a photo onto paper, print out turns a file on the screen into something you can hold.
nuance.etymology: From print, from Middle English, plus out, from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Putting a pronoun after out, as in 'print out it'; say 'print it out.'
Using print out as a noun; the noun is printout, written as one word.

senses.definition: One who makes prints.
A device, usually attached to a computer, used to print text or images onto paper; an analogous device capable of producing three-dimensional objects.
senses.example: ; see also the derived terms below

senses.definition: The operator of a printing press or the owner of a printing business; any printing business.
senses.example: The small printer on Fifth Street rushed our wedding invitations in just two days.

core.definition: A machine connected to a computer that prints text or images onto paper.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PRINT. The second syllable is a weak, r-colored vowel, so keep the rhotic r rather than saying 'PRINT-uh.' Keep the t crisp, since after n it does not become a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is an ordinary tool, though a jammed printer at work can be frustrating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use printer for the office or home device and usually say the printer with the definite article, as in 'the printer is out of toner.' For 3D printing, add the word: a 3D printer. A printing business is called a print shop, not a printer, which in everyday American English means the machine.

distinctions.note: A copier makes copies by scanning an original page, while a printer produces pages from digital files sent by a computer.
A printing press is a large machine for mass-producing printed material; a printer is the everyday desktop device or the person who runs a press.

examples.everyday: The printer at home is out of ink again, so I'm going to the library.
examples.professional: Please send the report to the shared printer on the third floor.
examples.analytical: The printer's throughput depends as much on the driver as on the hardware, which complicates benchmark comparisons.

nuance.analogy: A printer is like a scribe who copies whatever the computer dictates, one page at a time.
nuance.etymology: From print, with the agent suffix -er meaning one that performs the action.
common_mistakes: Calling a copy machine a printer; Americans usually say copier or copy machine for a device that copies original pages.
Dropping the r in the final syllable, or stressing -er instead of PRINT.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to procrastination.
senses.example: procrastinatory cognition

core.definition: Of or relating to procrastination; describing behavior, habits or systems that cause delay.

pronunciation.tip: Stress KRAS, and give the -tor- syllable a lighter secondary stress so it is clearly pronounced with the r. The final -ee is short and light.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes delay as a fault in habits, writing or systems.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word found mainly in academic writing or sharp commentary about habits, systems or prose that delays. Americans would more often say 'procrastinating' or 'a habit of procrastination.' In casual talk, using it can sound like a joke about your own habits.

distinctions.note: Procrastinating is the everyday participle used for actions; procrastinatory is a rare adjective describing behavior or systems that cause delay.
Dilatory means slow or intended to delay, often in legal or formal settings; procrastinatory describes the habit of postponing.

examples.everyday: I catch myself falling into procrastinatory habits whenever the weather is nice.
examples.professional: The sprint retrospective pointed to a procrastinatory pattern in how we handle code reviews.
examples.analytical: The essay examines the procrastinatory tendencies that shape modern academic writing and its endless revisions.

nuance.analogy: A procrastinatory habit is like a clock that always runs five minutes slow, so everything slips a little each day.
nuance.etymology: From procrastinate, from Latin procrastinare, 'to put off until tomorrow', with the adjective suffix -ory, meaning relating to.
common_mistakes: Using procrastinatory to describe a person; say 'a procrastinator' for the person.
Stressing the -NAT- syllable instead of KRAS.

senses.definition: Anything that is produced; a result.
senses.example: The product of last month's quality standards committee is quite good, even though the process was flawed.

senses.definition: The amount of an artifact that has been created by someone or some process.
senses.example: They improve their product every year; they export most of their agricultural production.

senses.definition: A consequence of someone's efforts or of a particular set of circumstances.
senses.example: Skill is the product of hours of practice. His reaction was the product of hunger and fatigue.

senses.definition: A quantity obtained by multiplication of two or more numbers.
senses.example: The product of 2 and 3 is 6. The product of 2, 3, and 4 is 24.

senses.definition: Any operation or a result thereof which generalises multiplication of numbers, like the multiplicative operation in a ring, product of types or a categorical product.
senses.example: In the ring, the product of two elements remains associative and distributive over addition.

senses.definition: Any tangible or intangible good or service that is a result of a process and that is intended for delivery to a customer or end user.
senses.example: The company's new product, a budgeting app, launched to customers last week.

senses.definition: A commodity offered for sale.
senses.example: That store offers a variety of products. We've got to sell a lot of product by the end of the month.

senses.definition: Illegal drugs, especially cocaine, when viewed as a commodity.
senses.example: I got some product here — you buying?

senses.definition: Ellipsis of beauty product: any preparation to be applied to the hair, skin, nails, etc. Often specifically a preparation used to hold one's hair in a desired arrangement.
senses.example: Wash excess product out of your hair.

senses.definition: A chemical substance formed as a result of a chemical reaction.
senses.example: This is a product of lime and nitric acid.

core.definition: Something that is made or grown, especially an item for sale, or the result of a process or effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PRAH. The second syllable is a weak, reduced 'uh' sound, and the final 't' is released quietly. Do not stress the second syllable or add a vowel before the 'kt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts. It can be positive when describing quality results, or negative when used of an unwanted outcome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say product constantly for things sold in stores and for the outcome of work or effort, such as 'a new product' or 'the product of years of effort'. In math it means the result of multiplication. In business, 'product' often refers to a software or service offering, so a product manager is a person who guides what a company sells.

distinctions.note: Produce as a noun means fresh fruits and vegetables in American stores; product means something manufactured or created.
Result is neutral and general; product often implies something made or manufactured by a process.

examples.everyday: I bought a new laundry detergent, and it's the best product I've used in years.
examples.professional: Our team is preparing the product launch for next quarter, so every feature needs to be tested first.
examples.analytical: A theory of meaning is often judged by the product it yields: the explanations and predictions that follow from it.

nuance.analogy: A product is like the bread that comes out of the oven: it is the finished thing that the ingredients and the baking were meant to create.
nuance.etymology: From Latin productum, the neuter past participle of producere, to lead forth.
common_mistakes: Using product for fresh fruits and vegetables; Americans say 'produce' for those.
Putting the stress on the second syllable, as in 'pruh-DUKT'.

product.etymology: From Middle English *product*, from Latin *prōductus*, perfect participle of *prōdūcō*, first attested in English in the mathematics sense.

senses.definition: Showing promise, and likely to develop in a desirable fashion.
senses.example: a promising young apprentice

senses.definition: Encouraging and inspiring confidence.
senses.example: Her first experiment produced promising results, so the team asked for more funding.

senses.definition: The act of making a promise.
senses.example: Her promising to fix the bug by Friday kept the release on schedule.

core.definition: Showing signs that it will turn out well or succeed in the future; encouraging and full of potential.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, PRAH. The middle syllable has a short i, as in sit, and the -ing ending is a single nasal sound, not -eeng.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests potential and encouragement without guaranteeing success.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use promising for people, projects and results that show potential, as in a promising young writer or promising results. It is strongly positive but not a guarantee, so a promising start can still fail. In casual speech, people often say looks good or good sign.

distinctions.note: Promising describes a thing or person with signs of success; hopeful describes someone's feeling of expectation.
Potential is a noun for ability not yet used; promising is an adjective describing signs of success already visible.

examples.everyday: The new taco place down the street looks promising, so let's try it Friday.
examples.professional: The pilot results are promising, but we need more data before we scale the model.
examples.analytical: The early results of this interpretation are promising, though the textual evidence remains limited.

nuance.analogy: Promising is like a seedling in spring: it shows real signs of growth, but the harvest is still ahead.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of the verb promise, from Latin promittere, to send forth or pledge.
common_mistakes: Using promising as a verb; the verb is promise, and promising is the adjective that describes potential.
Saying promising results when you mean guaranteed results; promising means encouraging, not certain.

senses.definition: A person who is guided and supported by an older and more experienced person (a protector or mentor).
senses.example: His status as a protégé of the great artist had many benefits, but was ultimately a burden.

core.definition: A person, usually younger or less experienced, who is guided, trained and supported by a more senior mentor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the final syllable like the French-derived zh sound followed by ay. Drop the French accent in speech and do not pronounce a final t.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests respect, growth and a good mentoring relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use protégé in workplaces, universities and professional circles, often when someone says a colleague is their protégé. For a woman, protégée is the traditional feminine form, though many people now use protégé for everyone. In casual talk people often say mentee, which is more common in corporate settings.

distinctions.note: Mentee is the common modern workplace term, while protégé sounds more classic and suggests a close relationship of support and influence.
An apprentice learns a trade formally, often through a set training period, while a protégé is supported more broadly by a patron.

examples.everyday: My aunt is a famous chef, and she's been like a mentor to her protégé, a young cook from her restaurant.
examples.professional: Our VP of engineering has been championing her protégé for the lead role on the data platform team.
examples.analytical: The relationship between a master and protégé shapes not only skill but also the moral style that a student inherits.

nuance.analogy: A protégé is like a plant grown in a greenhouse: carefully supported until it is strong enough to stand on its own.
nuance.etymology: From French protégé, past participle of protéger, to protect, from Latin protegere.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word as PRO-tee-gay, with a long e in the middle.
Forgetting the accent mark on the final e in written English, which is usually kept in formal writing.

senses.definition: (archaic) Pride.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Pride, especially an excessive sense of one's own importance or worth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PROWD. Say the d and n together without a vowel between them, then end with a soft 's' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it refers to arrogance or vanity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use this word today; they say pride or arrogance instead. You may meet it in older literature or in historical writing. Using it in conversation would sound old-fashioned and could puzzle listeners.

distinctions.note: Pride is the normal modern word and can be positive (self-respect) or negative (arrogance), while proudness is archaic and almost always negative.
Arrogance is a modern, clearly negative word for acting superior to others; proudness is an older term for the inner attitude behind it.

examples.professional: In the retrospective, the team's proudness about the first release blinded them to the warning signs in the logs.
examples.analytical: The essayist treats proudness not as a single vice but as the root attitude from which many other failures of character grow.

nuance.analogy: Like a sail filled too full of wind, carrying a boat past where it should stop.
nuance.etymology: From proud (Old English prūd) with the suffix -ness, meaning the state of being proud.
common_mistakes: Using proudness as a positive word for self-respect; in modern English it is negative.
Using it in everyday conversation instead of pride.

senses.definition: In AI: Removing weights or neurons that contribute little, to make a model smaller and faster.
A removal of excess material from a tree or shrub.
senses.example: Spring pruning keeps the apple trees healthy and encourages better fruit production.

senses.definition: A method of enumeration that allows the cutting out of parts of a decision tree.
senses.example: Cost-complexity pruning reduces overfitting by cutting branches that add little predictive accuracy.

senses.definition: Something obtained by pruning, as a twig.
senses.example: I tossed the pruning into the wheelbarrow beside the hedge.

core.definition: In AI, removing weights or neurons that contribute little, so a trained neural network becomes smaller and faster.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PROO. The second syllable is short and unstressed, so do not stretch it into 'PROO-neeng'. The -ing ending is a short ih sound plus ng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In gardening it is a positive, healthy activity; in AI it is a neutral engineering step with no negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American machine learning and data science teams, pruning is a standard term in papers, code, and meetings about model compression. Engineers often say they pruned the model to mean they cut its size. Outside tech, Americans use it about gardening, so the meaning depends on context.

distinctions.note: Pruning removes weights or neurons, while quantization lowers the numerical precision of the weights; teams often use both.
Distillation trains a smaller model to copy a larger one, while pruning shrinks the existing model by removing parts.

examples.everyday: My gardener is pruning the roses this weekend, so the bushes should look better in spring.
examples.professional: After pruning the network, we cut the model size by forty percent and the inference latency dropped noticeably.
examples.analytical: Pruning raises a question about which parameters carry the model's function, since removing low-magnitude weights can preserve accuracy while revealing redundancy in the learned representation.

nuance.analogy: Pruning a neural network is like trimming a hedge: you cut the branches that add little, so the plant stays healthy and easier to manage.
nuance.etymology: Derived from the verb prune, meaning to trim branches.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stressed vowel as a long i, as in 'PRY-ning'.
Using pruning to mean deleting data; in AI it refers to removing parts of a model.

conversation.text: Pruning removes weights or whole neurons that contribute little, making the model smaller.
Unstructured pruning often saves less in practice than expected, because sparse matrices are hard to accelerate.
Spring pruning keeps the rose bushes healthy.

senses.definition: Performed by or pertaining to the psyche (the mind, spirit, or both): mental, psychic.
senses.example: The therapist studied the psychical roots of his patient's recurring anxiety.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the animal nature of man, as opposed to the spirit.
senses.example: Some ancient theologians contrasted the psychical life of animals with the spiritual life of humans.

senses.definition: Outside the realm of the physical; supernatural, psychic.
senses.example: The detective dismissed the séance as a fraud, though the psychical claims were hard to test.

core.definition: Relating to the mind or soul rather than the physical body, or to supernatural phenomena studied as mental events.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'kul'. Keep the p silent and avoid stressing the middle syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, somewhat old-fashioned term for mental or spiritual matters, often in academic or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use psychical in everyday talk. It appears in older psychology and philosophy writing, and in discussions of psychical research on paranormal topics. In modern speech people would normally say psychological or mental instead.

distinctions.note: Psychical is more old-fashioned and often refers to the soul or spiritual side of the mind, while psychological is the standard modern term for mental processes.
Psychic is the everyday word for paranormal powers, while psychical is more academic and refers to mental or spiritual matters in general.

examples.everyday: She says her headaches are as psychical as they are physical, and I think she is probably right.
examples.professional: The team's report separates physical fatigue from psychical strain, which helps us design better shift schedules.
examples.analytical: Early psychologists often treated psychical phenomena as a domain separate from the physical body, a distinction now largely abandoned.

nuance.analogy: A psychical event is like the weather inside a house: it is real and affects everything, even though you cannot see it directly.
nuance.etymology: From Greek psychikos, meaning of the soul or mind, from psychē, with the English suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using psychical where psychological is expected in everyday speech.
Confusing psychical with psychic when describing paranormal abilities.

senses.definition: Having a tendency to argue or fight; aggressive, combative.

core.definition: Quick to argue or fight; aggressive, combative and eager to start a conflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the NAY syllable, the second syllable of the word. The first vowel is the short uh of cup, and the ending is shus, not shee-us.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes someone who is too eager to fight or argue.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pugnacious in news, sports coverage and descriptions of people who are combative, often in politics or online debate. It is more formal than mad or angry and can sound slightly literary. It describes a personality trait rather than a single outburst.

distinctions.note: Aggressive can describe behavior in general, including business or sports, while pugnacious focuses on a fighting or quarrelsome temperament.
Belligerent is stronger and often implies open hostility or a readiness to make war, while pugnacious suggests a tendency to argue or fight over small things.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor gets pretty pugnacious whenever someone parks in his spot.
examples.professional: Keep the feedback constructive, because the pugnacious tone in that thread will discourage people from speaking up.
examples.analytical: The pugnacious style of the polemicist may win applause, but it rarely persuades the undecided reader.

nuance.analogy: A pugnacious person is like a dog that barks at every passing car, always ready to start a fight.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pugnax, combative, from pugnare, to fight.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable, as in PUG-nay-shus.
Confusing pugnacious with pugilistic, which is more often used for boxing.

senses.definition: An instance of the action of a pump; one stroke of a pump; any action similar to pumping.
senses.example: It takes thirty pumps to get 10 liters; he did 50 pumps of the weights.

senses.definition: A device for dispensing liquid or gas to be sold, particularly fuel; a gas pump.
senses.example: This pump is out of order, but you can gas up at the next one.

senses.definition: A device for moving or compressing a liquid or gas.
senses.example: This pump can deliver 100 gallons of water per minute.

senses.definition: A swelling of the muscles caused by increased blood flow following high intensity weightlifting.
senses.example: After his leg workout, the pump in his biceps lasted for hours.

senses.definition: A ride on a bicycle given to a passenger, usually on the handlebars or fender.
senses.example: She gave the other girl a pump on her new bike.

senses.definition: The heart.
senses.example: The doctor said his pump was working well after the stress test.

senses.definition: A type of women's shoe which leaves the instep uncovered and has a relatively high heel, especially a stiletto (with a very high and thin heel)
senses.example: She was wearing a lovely new pair of pumps.

senses.definition: A dancing shoe.
senses.example: She laced up her pumps before walking onstage for the ballet recital.

senses.definition: A type of shoe without a heel.(Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: She wore flat black pumps with no heel to the office.

senses.definition: To use a pump; to move (water or other liquid) by means of a pump.
senses.example: I've been pumping for over a minute but the water isn't coming through.

senses.definition: To inject or pour (something) into someone or something in a manner similar to a pump.
senses.example: The nurse pumped fluid into the IV bag to keep the patient hydrated.

senses.definition: To express milk from (a breast) by means of a breast pump.
senses.example: She pumps milk at work three times a day so the baby can have it.

senses.definition: To fill with air by means of a pump; to inflate.
senses.example: He pumped up the air-bed by hand, but used the service station air to pump up the tires.

senses.definition: To move rhythmically, as the motion of a pump.
senses.example: I pumped my fist with joy when I won the race.

senses.definition: To load a shell into the chamber of a pump-action shotgun by pumping the mechanism.
senses.example: He ran on, pumping another round up into his scattergun.

senses.definition: To gain something, especially information, from (a person) by persistent questioning.
senses.example: Reporters kept pumping the senator for details about the secret budget.

senses.definition: To enlarge the body by means of weightlifting or steroid use.
senses.example: He started pumping himself up with steroids before his bodybuilding competition.

senses.definition: To shake (a person's hand) vigorously.
senses.example: He pumped my hand enthusiastically and congratulated me on the promotion.

senses.definition: Of music: to be loud, to have strong bass and rhythms; to be full of energy.
senses.example: The waves were really pumping this morning.

senses.definition: To pass (messages) into a program so that it can obey them.
senses.example: The engineer pumped the test commands into the server so it could execute them.

senses.definition: To inject silicone into the body in order to try to achieve a fuller or curvier look.
senses.example: She regretted letting an unlicensed clinic pump silicone into her hips.

senses.definition: To fire a bullet from a firearm.
senses.example: The gunman pumped three rounds into the wall before police arrived.

senses.definition: To kick, throw, or hit the ball far and high.
senses.example: The slugger pumped a towering fly ball over the left-field fence.

core.definition: The machine at a gas station from which you pump fuel into your car; the dispenser you use to fill your tank.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short u sound of cup, not the oo of pool. End with a clean mp cluster without adding a vowel after the p.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical, used in everyday driving life.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, people say pump for the fuel dispenser and gas station for the place. Phrases such as 'pump number four' or 'I'll pay at the pump' are very common, and pump gas or pumping gas is a casual way to say fill up the tank. Britons would say petrol station and forecourt, so American usage differs here.

distinctions.note: A pump is the machine that dispenses fuel, while a gas station is the entire business with its store and lot.
Gas is the fuel itself in everyday American speech, while pump is the machine; pump gas is an informal way to refer to fueling.
Pumps in the plural can mean women's shoes, which is an unrelated sense of the same word.

examples.everyday: I'll grab a coffee while you fill up at the next pump.
examples.professional: The fleet card works at any pump, so drivers do not need to pay inside at the register.
examples.analytical: Economists studying fuel prices often track the posted price at the pump, since it shapes consumer expectations.

nuance.analogy: Like a straw that draws the drink from the glass into your mouth.
common_mistakes: Using gas station to mean the pump itself
Saying pumping the gas in formal writing when pump gas or fill the tank is more natural

pump.etymology: From Middle English *pumpe*, possibly from Middle Dutch *pompe* (“pipe, water conduit”) or *pumpe* (“pump”), probably ultimately.

conversation.text: Pump number four isn't working, so pull up to the next one.
In New Jersey, you aren't allowed to pump your own gas.
I need to pump up my tires; the warning light came on.

senses.definition: In a punctilious manner.

core.definition: In a very careful and exact way, following rules, manners, or details precisely.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, TIL, and the next vowels are reduced. Do not stress the first syllable, and do not say tish for the ti; it is a plain /tɪ/.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying respect for standards and courtesy, though it can suggest stiffness if the carefulness is excessive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use punctiliously mainly in formal writing, business policies, etiquette discussions, or literary description. In everyday speech they say carefully, precisely, or by the book. You might hear it in a formal toast or a letter of thanks, but not usually in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Meticulously stresses thoroughness and fine detail in the work itself, while punctiliously stresses following rules, customs, or manners exactly.
Punctually means on time, whereas punctiliously means with exact care about rules and details, so the two are not interchangeable.
Scrupulously implies moral conscientiousness about what is right, while punctiliously focuses on the formal correctness of procedure or manners.

examples.everyday: At the wedding, she punctiliously thanked every host and wrote each of them a handwritten note afterward.
examples.professional: The auditor punctiliously checked each invoice against the purchase order before approving the payment.
examples.analytical: Medieval monks punctiliously observed the Rule of Benedict, treating each hour of prayer as a matter of obedience.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls every foul exactly by the rulebook, it insists on correctness in every detail.
nuance.etymology: From punctilious, from punctilio (a fine point of conduct), from Italian puntiglio, from punto (point).
common_mistakes: Confusing punctiliously (with exact care about rules) with punctually (on time).
Misplacing the stress on the first syllable, which makes it sound unfamiliar to Americans.

senses.definition: To make someone retire, especially due to advancing age.
senses.example: They've put John out to pasture and replaced him with someone who's got half his experience.

senses.definition: To discontinue something.
senses.example: That version of the program has been put out to pasture.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see put out,‎ to,‎ pasture.

core.definition: To make someone retire, especially because of age, or to stop using something that is no longer useful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAS, and pasture is pronounced 'PASS-cher', not 'PASS-tyoor'. The to reduces to 'tuh' in normal speech.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or mildly demeaning when used about a person, since it suggests they are no longer valued; neutral when used about a product or a system.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom about employees, athletes, politicians, or old equipment, often with a hint of humor or criticism. Saying it directly to an older colleague can sound insulting, so use it carefully. A natural reply is 'Well, he had a good run.' For a more neutral choice, say 'retire' or 'phase out' for systems.

distinctions.note: 'Retire' is neutral and polite, while 'put out to pasture' sounds humorous, dismissive, or critical.
'Phase out' is used for gradually stopping a product or policy, while 'put out to pasture' can describe people or things and has a more colorful tone.
'Sideline' means to remove someone from an active role, often without a formal end, while 'put out to pasture' suggests final retirement.

collocations: put out to pasture after thirty years
was put out to pasture by the board
put the old software out to pasture
put him out to pasture at sixty-five
put the veteran coach out to pasture

examples.everyday: My dad still jokes that his company put him out to pasture, but he loves having time for his garden.
examples.professional: The team agreed to put the legacy reporting tool out to pasture once the new dashboard was stable.
examples.analytical: Scholars sometimes argue that a theory is put out to pasture not because it is refuted but because a more fashionable paradigm has replaced it.

nuance.analogy: Like retiring an old working horse to a grassy field, where it still lives but no longer pulls the plow.
nuance.etymology: From the farm image of turning an old working animal out to graze, later used figuratively for retirement.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing pasture as 'PASS-tyoor'; the American form is 'PASS-cher'.
Omitting 'out' and saying 'put to pasture', which is less standard in American speech.

put-out-to-pasture.etymology: Derived from the historical practice of retiring aged draft animals from labor by allowing them to graze in pasture.

senses.definition: A polygon with four sides.
An area defended by four fortresses supporting each other.
senses.example: The Venetian quadrilateral comprised Mantua, Peschiera, Verona, and Legnano.

senses.definition: Having four sides.
senses.example: They spoke at a quadrilateral meeting of the trade ministers of the United States, the European Union, Canada, and Japan.

core.definition: A flat shape or polygon with exactly four straight sides, such as a square, rectangle, or trapezoid.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on LAT, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, and the t in 'lateral' is a flap, so it sounds close to a d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: In American schools, quadrilateral is the standard word for any four-sided polygon, and students learn it in geometry. Everyday speakers usually say 'four-sided shape' or name the specific shape, such as square or rectangle. The word is used in the military sense of a fortified area only in historical writing.

distinctions.note: A square is one specific quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles; quadrilateral covers all four-sided polygons.
A polygon is any closed shape with straight sides; quadrilateral is the subset with exactly four sides.

collocations: sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral

examples.everyday: The tile pattern in the kitchen is a quadrilateral shape, so the pieces fit together easily.
examples.professional: The design team needs the plot to be a quadrilateral, so the survey points define four boundary corners.
examples.analytical: Any simple quadrilateral has interior angles that sum to 360 degrees, which follows from splitting it into two triangles.

nuance.analogy: A quadrilateral is a four-cornered fence around a yard, no matter how crooked the sides are.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quadrilaterus, from quadri- 'four' and latus 'side'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying kwah-drih-LAT-er-al with a full vowel in the last syllable.
Using quadrilateral for a shape with more than four sides.

senses.definition: A believer of the Quaker faith and a member of the Society of Friends, known for their pacifist views.
A player of any game in the Quake series of first-person shooters.
senses.example: Nobody beats Marcus in the arena, because he's the best Quaker on our server.

core.definition: A member of the Religious Society of Friends, a Christian group known for pacifism, plain living and silent worship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced vowel followed by an r, so it sounds like 'KWAY-kur', not 'KWAY-kwer'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and factual; Quakers themselves use the term without offense, though many prefer the name Friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Quaker for members of a Christian movement that began in 17th-century England. Capitalize it. Many Quakers call themselves Friends. Americans also know the word from the Quaker Oats brand, and there are Quaker schools and meetinghouses across the country. Calling someone a Quaker is polite and factual.

distinctions.note: Friend is the name Quakers use for themselves; Quaker is the common outside name.
Both are historic peace churches with pacifist views, but Mennonites come from Anabaptist roots and have different beliefs and church structures.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a Quaker, and she hosts a silent meeting at her house every Sunday morning.
examples.professional: The nonprofit was founded by Quakers, and it still follows their commitment to nonviolent conflict resolution.
examples.analytical: Quaker theology emphasizes the Inner Light, the belief that God speaks directly to every person, which shaped their rejection of a paid clergy.

nuance.etymology: First a mocking nickname from about 1650, from quake, after George Fox told a judge to tremble at the word of the Lord.
common_mistakes: Writing it in lowercase; capitalize Quaker because it names a religious group.
Assuming every pacifist is a Quaker; Quakerism is a specific Christian tradition.

quaker.etymology: From *quake* + *er*; a name given to members of the Religious Society of Friends, supposedly by the magistrates Gervase Bennet and Nathaniel Barton, when George Fox "bade them tremble at the word of the Lord"; the term was previously applied to certain…

senses.definition: To satisfy, especially a literal or figurative thirst.
senses.example: The library quenched her thirst for knowledge.

senses.definition: To extinguish or put out (as a fire or light).
senses.example: Firefighters used foam to quench the blaze before it reached the neighboring warehouse.

senses.definition: To cool rapidly by direct contact with liquid coolant, as a blacksmith quenching hot iron.
senses.example: The swordsmith quenched the sword in an oil bath so that it wouldn't shatter.

senses.definition: To terminate or greatly diminish (a chemical reaction) by destroying or deforming the remaining reagents.
senses.example: Adding excess sodium thiosulfate will quench the reaction after exactly five minutes.

senses.definition: To rapidly change the parameters of a physical system.
senses.example: The engineers quench the magnet's field by rapidly changing its current in the test loop.

senses.definition: To rapidly terminate the operation of a superconducting electromagnet by causing part or all of the magnet's windings to enter the normal, resistive state.
senses.example: If someone is pinned against the MRI magnet by a ferromagnetic object, you may need to quench the magnet in order to free them.

senses.definition: The act of quenching something; the fact of being quenched.
senses.example: The quench of the hot steel in brine gave the blade its hardness.

senses.definition: The abnormal termination of operation of a superconducting magnet, occurring when part of the superconducting coil enters the normal (resistive) state.
senses.example: A quench in the cryogenic coil forced engineers to shut down the magnet immediately.

senses.definition: A rapid change of the parameters of a physical system.
senses.example: The simulation paused after a quench in the temperature parameters of the system.

core.definition: To satisfy a thirst, or to put out a fire or flame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the only syllable, with a short 'e' like 'bench'. End with a clear 'ch' sound, not a 'sh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing thirst relieved; neutral or negative when describing fires or hopes being ended.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'quench' most naturally with thirst, as in 'a cold drink to quench your thirst,' a phrase used in ads and everyday talk. For fires, Americans more often say 'put out' or 'extinguish'. In figurative use, 'quench' appears in writing about hope, enthusiasm or curiosity.

distinctions.note: 'Satisfy' is general for fulfilling any need; 'quench' is specific to thirst or a burning feeling.
'Extinguish' is formal and used for fires or lights; 'quench' is more literary or idiomatic.
'Douse' means to drench or soak something with water; 'quench' focuses on stopping heat or thirst.

examples.everyday: After the hike, a big glass of lemonade really quenched my thirst.
examples.professional: The new budget will quench the team's need for better tools, so we can finally fix the old pipeline.
examples.analytical: The sermon argues that spiritual hunger is not quenched by material success alone.

nuance.analogy: Quench is like pouring water on a campfire: the heat and flame stop when the water reaches them.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'cwencan' (to extinguish, quench), related to 'cwincan' (to vanish).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'qu' as 'k' alone; it is 'kw' with a clear 'w' sound.
Saying 'quench the fire' in casual speech where 'put out the fire' is more common.

quench.etymology: From Middle English *quenchen*, from Old English *cwenċan*, from Proto-Germanic **kwankijaną*.

senses.definition: A proportional part or share; the share or proportion assigned to each in a division.
senses.example: Each partner received an equal quota of the profits after expenses.

senses.definition: A prescribed number or percentage that may serve as, for example, a maximum, a minimum, or a goal.
senses.example: Our sales team has a quota of twenty new accounts every quarter.

senses.definition: A restriction on the import of something to a specific quantity.
senses.example: The government set a quota on imported steel to protect domestic mills.

core.definition: A fixed share or limited number assigned to a person or group, such as a sales target, a minimum requirement, or a maximum limit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a weak 'uh' sound. In fast American speech the middle t is a flap that sounds almost like a d, so it sounds close to 'KWOH-duh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most business contexts, but often negative when a quota is imposed unfairly or seems to force bad behavior, as in debates about police or immigration quotas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quota constantly at work for sales targets ('I hit my quota this month') and in policy debates about immigration, imports or hiring. Saying you have a quota in casual talk usually means you have a required amount to finish, not a gentle goal. The word is politically charged when used about hiring or admissions, so choose your context carefully.

distinctions.note: A target is a goal you aim for, while a quota is a required minimum that may come with consequences if you miss it.
A limit is usually a maximum, but a quota can be a minimum, a maximum or a fixed share.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to finish my reading quota for the week before the book club meets on Thursday.
examples.professional: Everyone on the team has a quota of twelve new client accounts this quarter.
examples.analytical: A quota fixes a numerical share in advance, so it can distort the very behavior it was meant to measure.

nuance.analogy: A quota is like a punch card at a coffee shop: you need a set number of visits before the reward counts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quota, 'how great' or 'how many,' from quotus, 'which in number.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'KWO-tah' with a hard, open final vowel; the ending is a weak 'uh.'
Using quota as a vague word for 'amount' in casual speech, when it means a required or assigned share.

senses.definition: A female storyteller.
senses.example: The raconteuse held the dinner guests spellbound with tales from her years in Lisbon.

core.definition: A woman who tells stories skillfully and entertainingly, usually at social gatherings.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, TOOZ, which rhymes with booze. The final -euse is a single z sound, not an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests charm, wit, and skill as a storyteller.
nuance.usage_note: Raconteuse is a French-derived word used mostly in writing, reviews, or formal descriptions of an entertaining host. Most Americans say raconteur for both men and women, or simply storyteller. In casual speech the word can sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Raconteur is the standard term for both sexes in American English, while raconteuse is the explicitly feminine form and is less common today.
Storyteller is the everyday, neutral term, while raconteuse implies a polished, witty social performer.

examples.everyday: Aunt Marge is the real raconteuse at every family reunion, and she always has the whole table laughing.
examples.professional: The keynote speaker was a gifted raconteuse who made our budget numbers memorable.
examples.analytical: The memoir reads like the work of a born raconteuse, shaping private memory into public story.

nuance.analogy: A raconteuse is like a skilled cook: the ingredients are ordinary, but the way she prepares them makes them irresistible.
nuance.etymology: From French raconteuse, the feminine of raconteur, from raconter, to relate.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable at the end, such as oo-ZEE
Using it for any storyteller, when it suggests skill and charm

senses.definition: Condensed water falling from a cloud.
senses.example: We've been having a lot of rain lately.

senses.definition: Any matter moving or falling, usually through air, and especially if liquid or otherwise figuratively identifiable with raindrops.
An instance of particles or larger pieces of matter moving or falling through air.
senses.example: A rain of mortar fire fell on our trenches.

senses.definition: To have rain fall from the sky.
senses.example: Judging by the black cloud, it will rain later today.

senses.definition: To fall as or like rain.
senses.example: Tears rained from her eyes.

senses.definition: To issue (something) in large quantities.
senses.example: The boxer rained punches on his opponent's head.

core.definition: Water that falls from clouds in drops, or the period of time when it falls.

pronunciation.tip: Rain is one syllable with the diphthong ay. Keep the r rhotic, and do not confuse it with the homophones rein and reign, which share the same sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive for gardens and farms or negative when it ruins plans.
nuance.usage_note: Americans talk about rain constantly, especially in weather small talk, and a common greeting is 'Looks like rain.' Rain is an uncountable noun in general, so say 'the rain' or 'heavy rain,' while 'a rain' is used rarely for a single shower. The idiom 'rain check' is a common everyday phrase for postponing an invitation.

distinctions.note: A shower is a brief fall of rain, while rain can continue for hours or days.
Drizzle is very light rain with small drops, while rain is heavier and more substantial.

examples.everyday: Take an umbrella with you, because the rain is supposed to start this afternoon.
examples.professional: The rain delay pushed our site inspection back until Thursday, so the schedule needs updating.
examples.analytical: Rain forms when water vapor condenses into droplets heavy enough to fall against the updrafts inside a cloud.

nuance.analogy: Rain is the sky's way of returning water to the ground, like a sponge wrung out over a field.
nuance.etymology: From Old English regn, a Germanic root for falling water.
common_mistakes: Confusing rain with rein (a horse's strap) and reign (to rule); they sound the same but mean different things.
Saying 'it is rainy falling' instead of 'it is raining'; use the verb rain for the action.

rain.etymology: Middle English *reyn*, *rein*, from Old English *reġn*, from **regn*, from Proto-Germanic **regną*, of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: A thing or person that is genuine, authentic, or worthy of serious regard.
senses.example: Her handmade quilts are the real deal, not mass-produced knockoffs from a discount store.

senses.definition: An authentic bargain.
A beneficial result or a favorable state of affairs.
senses.example: Honestly, the real deal for our team is a shorter commute and a bigger budget.

core.definition: Something or someone genuine and authentic, not a fake, imitation, or copy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'deal'. Link the words so it sounds like 'reel-DEEL', and keep the 'r' strongly pronounced at the start.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises authenticity and quality, often with enthusiasm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the real deal' casually about people, food, music, or products they admire, such as 'This pizza is the real deal.' It is informal, so avoid it in formal writing. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it really is' or 'No kidding!'

distinctions.note: 'The genuine article' is similar but slightly more formal and emphasizes true origin rather than general quality.
'The real thing' is very common and can be casual or neutral, while 'the real deal' often carries stronger praise.

examples.everyday: That taco truck on Fifth Street is the real deal, so get the carnitas.
examples.professional: The new engineer is the real deal; she caught the data pipeline bug in under an hour.
examples.analytical: Critics debated whether the memoir was the real deal or a carefully staged performance of honesty.

nuance.analogy: Like a diamond among cubic zirconia, 'the real deal' separates what is authentic from what only looks similar.
nuance.etymology: From 'real' (genuine) and 'deal' in the sense of a transaction or matter, now used idiomatically.
common_mistakes: Using 'real deal' for a bargain in ordinary speech; in American English it usually means authentic.
Writing 'the real deal' without 'the' in the idiomatic sense.

conversation.text: This taco truck is the real deal; it tastes just like Mexico City.
The new hire is the real deal. She knows her stuff.
After one bite, I knew this barbecue was the real deal.

senses.definition: To change the order or arrangement of (one or more items).

core.definition: To change the order, position, or arrangement of one or more items so they are organized differently.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, REYNJ, and make the 'ge' sound like 'j'. The first 'ea' is two sounds, 'ee-uh', so avoid pronouncing it as 'rare'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday word for changing arrangements.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'rearrange' constantly for furniture, schedules, seating charts, and documents. It is neutral in tone and suitable for both home and office. For changing a time or date, Americans usually say 'reschedule' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Reorganize' changes the structure or system of an organization, while 'rearrange' changes the positions or order of items.
'Reschedule' changes the time of an event, while 'rearrange' changes the order or placement of things, which can include a schedule.

examples.everyday: Let's rearrange the living room so the couch faces the window.
examples.professional: Can we rearrange the sprint agenda so the data pipeline review comes first?
examples.analytical: The proof rearranges the terms so that the inequality becomes visible without changing its meaning.

nuance.analogy: Rearranging is like shuffling a deck of cards: the same cards are present, but their order is different.
nuance.etymology: From 're-' (again) plus 'arrange', from Old French 'arangier', to put in a row or order.
common_mistakes: Using 'rearrange' when you mean 'reschedule' a meeting or appointment.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'REE-uh-range', which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: To summarize or repeat in concise form.
senses.example: The entire symphony was recapitulated in the last four bars.

senses.definition: To reproduce or closely resemble (as in structure or function).
senses.example: The software's new interface recapitulates the layout of the old system almost exactly.

senses.definition: To mirror or repeat in analogous form, especially in reference to an individual's development passing through stages corresponding to the species' stages of evolutionary development.
senses.example: Early embryos appear to recapitulate their ancestors' evolutionary stages, a belief once popular in biology.

core.definition: To summarize the main points of something in short form, or to repeat them in order.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on PICH, with a secondary stress on the first syllable, REE. The middle -uh- syllables are reduced, and the final -ate is a clear 'ayt'. The 'tch' is one sound, like in 'pitch'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a careful, orderly summary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use recapitulate in academic, legal, and formal writing or speech, for example 'Let me recapitulate the main findings.' In everyday talk they say 'recap' or 'sum up' instead. It can sound stiff at casual gatherings, so reserve it for presentations, papers, or formal settings.

distinctions.note: Recap is the casual, everyday form; recapitulate is more formal and literary.
Summarize is the general word for condensing any content; recapitulate implies repeating the sequence of main points.
Reiterate means saying something again for emphasis; recapitulate means restating the whole structure briefly.

examples.everyday: My uncle likes to recapitulate the whole trip before we leave, just to make sure nothing was forgotten.
examples.professional: Before we open questions, I'll recapitulate the three findings from the pilot and the risks we identified.
examples.analytical: The conclusion recapitulates the argument of the first chapter, showing how each premise leads to the final claim.

nuance.analogy: To recapitulate is like replaying the highlight reel of a game: the key plays come back quickly in the same order.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin recapitulare, 'to sum up', from re- plus capitulum, 'chapter, heading'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the wrong syllable, such as ree-kuh-PIT-yoo-layt; the stress is on PICH.
Using recapitulate for simply repeating a point; it implies summarizing the whole sequence.

recapitulate.etymology: From Late Latin *recapitulātus*, past participle of *recapitulāre* (“to go over the main points of a thing again”), from *re-* + *capitulum*, from *caput* + *ulus*; see *capitulate*.

senses.definition: Careless or heedless; headstrong or rash.
senses.example: Her reckless decision to quit her job without a backup plan worried her family.

senses.definition: Indifferent or oblivious to danger or the consequences thereof.
senses.example: Reckless about the thin ice, the children kept jumping onto the frozen pond.

core.definition: Doing dangerous or foolish things without thinking about the consequences or the risk to yourself or others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, REK, and the final syllable is a reduced 'lus'. Americans often reduce the middle vowel, so it sounds like 'REK-lus' with no strong vowel in the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes someone for taking unnecessary risks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reckless about drivers, spending, or decisions that risk harm, such as 'reckless driving' or 'reckless behavior'. It is a strong word, so it can sound harsh about a friend. A softer alternative is 'careless' or 'impulsive'.

distinctions.note: Careless means not paying enough attention, while reckless means ignoring obvious danger on purpose.
Bold is often positive and courageous, while reckless suggests a harmful lack of caution.

examples.everyday: Pulling out in front of that truck was reckless, so please slow down next time.
examples.professional: Deploying the model without testing it would be reckless, given the risk to our customers.
examples.analytical: A reckless ethic treats consequences as irrelevant, which makes it difficult to justify any action taken in their name.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds through a red light without looking: the danger is obvious, but the driver ignores it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English reccelēas, 'careless', from reck, 'to heed', plus -less.
common_mistakes: Using reckless for a mild mistake; it is stronger than careless and implies real danger.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'lees' instead of a reduced 'lus'.

reckless.etymology: From Middle English *rekles*, *reckeles*, *rekkeles*, (also *recheles*), from Old English *rēcelēas* (“reckless, careless, negligent”), equivalent to *reck* + *less*.

senses.definition: Happening or occurring frequently, with repetition.
senses.example: He has recurring asthma attacks.

senses.definition: Of a decimal: having a set of digits that is repeated indefinitely.
senses.example: Every rational number can be written as either a terminating decimal or a recurring decimal.

senses.definition: A recurrence; a coming round again.

core.definition: Happening again and again, often at regular intervals or in a repeated pattern.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KUR, and the ending is a light 'ing'. Keep the r clear and do not turn the first syllable into 're'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound negative when used for problems, and positive for pleasant traditions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use recurring in everyday talk for regular events or charges, such as 'a recurring meeting' or 'a recurring charge' on a bill. In math, it describes repeating decimals, though American schools often say 'repeating decimal.' Both expressions are understood, and recurring decimal sounds more formal.

distinctions.note: Recurrent is more formal and often medical or technical, while recurring is the everyday choice for things that come back.
Periodic means happening at regular intervals, often on a fixed schedule, while recurring can be irregular.

examples.everyday: We have a recurring dinner with friends every second Friday, so put it on your calendar.
examples.professional: The product team has a recurring standup every Monday, so we can review the open tickets together.
examples.analytical: The recurring tension between faith and reason is central to the argument of the whole book.

nuance.analogy: Like a weekly alarm that rings again each week: the same event returns on its own schedule.
nuance.etymology: From recur, from Latin recurrere 'to run back,' with the participial suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'reccuring' with two c's; the correct spelling is recurring with double r.
Using recurring for something that happens only once.

senses.definition: The act of defining an object (usually a function) in terms of that object itself.
senses.example: n! = n × (n − 1)! (for n > 0) or 1 (for n = 0) defines the factorial function using recursion.

senses.definition: The act of recurring.
senses.example: Doctors tracked each recursion of the infection, noting how often the symptoms returned after treatment.

senses.definition: The invocation of a procedure from within itself.
senses.example: This function uses recursion to compute factorials.

core.definition: A method of defining something, or solving a problem, by referring to smaller versions of the same thing, often through a function that calls itself.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the 'sion' ending is pronounced like 'zhun' as in 'vision.' Many learners say 'ree-KUR-shun,' which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, recursion is mostly used by programmers, mathematicians, and logicians. Non-specialists rarely use it, though people sometimes joke about recursion in a loose way. In technical settings, the term is used without hesitation.

distinctions.note: Iteration repeats steps with a loop; recursion solves a problem by calling the same procedure on smaller inputs.
Repetition is a general word for doing something again; recursion specifically refers to self-reference in definition or calling.
Recurrence means the act of happening again over time; recursion refers to self-referential definition or code.

examples.everyday: My kid thinks it's funny that a joke about a joke about a joke is a kind of recursion.
examples.professional: We fixed the bug by adding a base case to stop the recursion in the directory-traversal function.
examples.analytical: Gödel's proof relies on the recursion of self-reference, in which a statement is encoded so that it refers to itself.

nuance.analogy: Recursion is like a set of Russian nesting dolls: each doll contains a smaller version of itself until you reach the smallest one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin recursio, 'a running back,' from recurrere, 'to run back.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'shun' instead of 'zhun.'
Confusing recursion with recurrence, which means something happening again over time.
Using recursion as a synonym for iteration; they are related but distinct approaches.

recursion.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *recursiō* (“the act of running back or again, return”), from *recurrō* (“run back; return”), from *re-* (“back, again”) + *currō* (“run”).

senses.definition: The puma.

core.definition: An old or regional name for the puma, the large wild cat of the Americas also called cougar or mountain lion.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TY, the first syllable of tiger. The g is hard, as in 'get', and the final -er is a light American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds old-fashioned and can confuse listeners.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans call the puma a cougar or mountain lion, so 'red tiger' will sound unusual in everyday talk. You will meet it mainly in older nature writing or in regional stories. Use cougar or mountain lion when speaking to ordinary listeners.

distinctions.note: Cougar is the standard American name for the puma, while red tiger is rare and mostly literary.
A tiger is a large Asian cat, while a red tiger is a puma that is not related to tigers.

examples.everyday: Grandpa swore he saw a red tiger on the ridge, but I think it was a cougar.
examples.professional: In the wildlife report we list the puma as cougar, since red tiger is outdated.
examples.analytical: Older naturalists' writings sometimes call the puma a red tiger, a regional name that the scientific community has largely dropped.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a soda 'pop' in one part of the country and 'soda' in another, a nickname that stays local.
common_mistakes: Thinking a red tiger is a tiger species, when the puma is a different animal.
Using it in modern American conversation without context, which can sound confusing.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see red,‎ face.
With a red face; flushed, due to emotional or physical causes. embarrassed.
senses.example: A red-faced John edged his way quietly out of the room.

senses.definition: Embarrassed.
senses.example: A red-faced John edged his way quietly out of the room.

senses.definition: Inebriate.
senses.example: Coming home late and red-faced every night from the pub is not what I expected of you.

senses.definition: Angry.
senses.example: The customer gave a red-faced account of the argument with the waiter.

senses.definition: Flustered.
senses.example: "I can't for the life of me think where I left the tickets!", she cried out, red-faced.

senses.definition: Exhausted.
senses.example: He collapsed, red-faced from the effort, against the door jamb.

core.definition: Having a flushed, reddened face from embarrassment, anger, heat, or exertion; also, feeling embarrassed.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on RED, the first part of this compound adjective. The -faced ending is lighter, and the t is a plain final sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It usually describes someone who looks embarrassed or upset.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for visible flushing, such as 'He came in red-faced after raking leaves' or 'a red-faced apology.' It describes appearance, while embarrassed describes the feeling. Use it for a person's face or skin, not for a sunburned arm.

distinctions.note: Flushed is a more neutral term for a reddened face from heat, exercise, or emotion, while red-faced often suggests embarrassment or anger.
Ruddy describes a healthy, reddish complexion and is usually positive, while red-faced often describes a temporary flush.

examples.everyday: He came in from the yard red-faced and sweaty after raking leaves.
examples.professional: The manager gave a red-faced apology after the report had the wrong numbers.
examples.analytical: Shame often makes people red-faced, a visible sign of an emotion that the self cannot easily hide.

nuance.analogy: Like a tomato left in the sun, the face turns red from heat or pressure.
nuance.etymology: From red plus face, both from Old English.
common_mistakes: Writing it without a hyphen before a noun, as in 'red faced man'.
Confusing it with the noun phrase 'red face', which is less common in speech.

senses.definition: (rare) Redundancy.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The state of being redundant, meaning extra or unnecessary; a rarer form of redundancy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DUN, and the final -ance is a weak, reduced syllable that sounds like 'duns', not 'dance'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, implying waste or surplus.
nuance.usage_note: Redundance is rare in American English; nearly every speaker, writer and editor says redundancy. Use redundancy in conversation, email and technical writing, and recognize redundance mainly from older or literary texts.

distinctions.note: Redundancy is the standard American form, used in everything from job cuts to engineering backups, so it is the one to learn.
Repetition is the act of saying or doing something again; redundancy is extra content or parts that add nothing new.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the second page of that form is pure redundance.
examples.professional: We removed the duplicate checks to cut redundance in the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the repeated refrain creates a literary redundance that deepens the poem's mood.

nuance.analogy: Packing two chargers for one phone, when one would do, is redundance.
nuance.etymology: From Latin redundare, to overflow.
common_mistakes: Using redundance in everyday conversation; Americans say redundancy.
Stressing the last syllable; say rih-DUN-duns.

senses.definition: Of a word or phrase applied to a particular person, place, or thing and not to any other.
Of or relating to a referent.
senses.example: In semantics, a referential term points to a specific object in the world.

senses.definition: Of or relating to reference or allusion.
senses.example: The poem's referential style rewards readers who recognize the biblical echoes in every stanza.

senses.definition: Serving as a reference.
senses.example: The lab kept a referential copy of the dataset for auditing future model changes.

core.definition: Of a word or phrase, designating a particular person, place, or thing in the world rather than a general class.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REN, the second syllable of the -ential stem, and the ending -ial sounds like 'shul', not 'ee-al'. The first syllable has a short 'eh', and the middle 'er' is a weak 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in linguistics, philosophy, logic, and software or data work, not in everyday talk. Outside those fields, people usually say specific or the one I mean. In a design meeting, saying that field is referential means it points to one defined record. The adverb referentially follows the same pattern.

distinctions.note: A referent is the actual person, place, or thing a word points to, while referential is the adjective describing that pointing relationship.
Allusive means indirectly suggesting something, such as a book or event, while referential means directly designating a specific thing.

examples.everyday: When I said the guy in the red truck, I meant one specific guy, so the phrase was referential.
examples.professional: In the API docs, make sure the customer field is referential so it points to exactly one customer record.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that proper names are purely referential, contributing an object to a sentence rather than a description.

nuance.analogy: A referential word is like a pointing finger: it directs attention to one thing in the room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin referre, 'to bring back, relate', plus the suffix -ial.
common_mistakes: Confusing referential, the adjective, with referent, the noun for the thing being pointed to
Stressing the first syllable, as in REF-ur-en-shul

senses.definition: Any of various elongate fish from the family Echeneidae, the dorsal fin of which is in the form of a suction disc that can take a firm hold against the skin of larger marine animals.
senses.example: A remora attached itself to the shark's belly, riding along and feeding on its scraps.

senses.definition: A serpent.
senses.example: In the old sermon, the remora slithered through the garden, whispering lies to Eve.

core.definition: A small fish that attaches to large sea animals such as sharks by a suction disc on its head.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, REM. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, and the final a is an uh sound, not a long ah. The r in American English is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biology term, though it can be used metaphorically for a parasite-like person.
nuance.usage_note: Remora is used mainly in marine biology, aquariums, and nature documentaries in the United States. In casual speech Americans would say suckerfish, which is a common name for it. Metaphorical uses exist but are rare.

distinctions.note: A shark is a large predator. A remora is a small fish that often rides on sharks, eating scraps and parasites.
A parasite lives on or in a host and harms it. A remora usually benefits from the attachment and does little harm.

collocations: a remora attached to a shark
hitching a ride like a remora

examples.everyday: At the aquarium, the guide pointed out a remora clinging to the side of the shark tank.
examples.professional: Our marine biology report describes the remora's suction disc as a key adaptation for feeding.
examples.analytical: The remora's attachment to larger animals raises questions about symbiosis, since the relationship is commensal rather than parasitic.

nuance.analogy: Like a passenger who hitches a free ride on a larger vehicle, staying close and getting carried along.
nuance.etymology: From Latin remora, meaning delay or hindrance, from re- and mora, delay.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final a as a long ah sound; it is uh.
Confusing remora with Remoras as a plural; the plural is remoras.

senses.definition: At a distance, far away.
Not much; scarcely; hardly.
senses.example: I'm not remotely in love with you.

core.definition: From a distance, without being physically present, usually by means of a computer or other device.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MOHT, the second syllable. The final '-ly' is a short 'lee' sound, not 'lee-ly'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an action done at a distance, and it has a positive or practical feel in technology contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'remotely' for controlling or accessing something from a distance, such as 'log in remotely' or 'unlock the door remotely'. With 'not', as in 'not remotely close', it is an informal emphasis meaning 'not at all'. In that use, it sounds casual and is common in conversation.

distinctions.note: Distantly describes a far-off or cool relationship or memory, while remotely describes physical or technical distance or being absent.
Far is a broad everyday word for distance, while remotely specifically suggests doing something from a distance through a device or system.

examples.everyday: I can check the thermostat remotely from my phone when we're on vacation.
examples.professional: Can you join the review remotely, or do you need the conference room link?
examples.analytical: The phenomenon can be observed only remotely, through instruments that detect light from distant stars.

nuance.analogy: Like steering a remote-controlled car from across the yard, where your hands never touch the car.
nuance.etymology: From remote (from Latin remotus 'moved away') plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'remotely' to mean 'slightly', as in 'remotely interested', which is not standard American usage.
Confusing 'not remotely' with 'not remote', which changes the meaning.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: Synonym of pay back in all senses.
senses.example: I finally repaid my student loans, just before sending my kids to college.

senses.definition: To make worthwhile; to yield a result worth the effort; to pay off.
To give in return; requite.
To pay (cover with tar, pitch, etc.) again.

core.definition: To pay back money you owe someone, or to give something back in return for a favor, kindness, or harm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PAY, which is a long diphthong. The first syllable is a reduced vowel, so avoid saying 'ree' as in 'ree-PAY'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when you repay a kindness or debt, and it can be negative when you repay an insult or harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use repay for money, loans, and favors, as in 'I'll repay you Friday.' Repaying a favor is often done by doing something nice in return rather than by paying money. For casual talk, pay back is equally common, so the two are interchangeable in most everyday contexts.

distinctions.note: Pay back is more informal and common in speech, while repay sounds slightly more formal and is common in writing and finance.
Reimburse means an organization pays you back for money you already spent for them, such as work expenses.
A refund is money returned to you by a store or company, usually for goods or services you did not keep.

examples.everyday: Thanks for covering my lunch yesterday, I'll repay you on Friday.
examples.professional: The company must repay the bridge loan within ninety days of closing.
examples.analytical: Paul argues that a Christian cannot repay evil with evil, since vengeance belongs to God.

nuance.analogy: Repay is like returning a borrowed book to the library, giving back exactly what you received.
nuance.etymology: From Old French repaier, from re- 'back' plus paier 'to pay'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'repay to' the person instead of 'repay' the person directly, as in 'I will repay you' not 'repay to you'.
Confusing repay with reply or respond, which mean answering rather than giving back.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, repay refers both to human obligation and to God's justice.
