Romans 12:19 (RSV) says that vengeance belongs to God, who will repay, so believers should not take revenge themselves. Luke 14:14 (RSV) says that those who cannot repay a host will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. The Greek word behind repay in Romans 12 is apodidōmi, meaning to give back or render.

repay.etymology: From Old French *repaier* (“to pay back”), from *re-* + *paiier* (“to pay”), from Latin *paco* (“to settle, to make peaceful”), from *pāx* (“peace”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: One who reproves; a rebuker.

core.definition: A person who reproves or scolds someone for a fault or wrong, often in a serious or disapproving way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, REP. The final -er is a reduced, unstressed American r-colored vowel, so say it as 'ver,' not 'vair.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. The word suggests someone who criticizes with authority, and it can sound judgmental depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in casual speech; they say someone who 'criticizes' or 'calls people out.' You will meet it in essays, sermons and older literature. The verb 'reprove' has the same tone, so it is best kept for writing and formal speech.

distinctions.note: A critic judges quality in art, work or ideas, while a reprover rebukes behavior or a moral fault.
Scold is more informal and often suggests nagging or shrill anger, while reprover sounds more measured and formal.

examples.professional: As the team lead, I try not to act as a reprover in code reviews; I'd rather explain what went wrong.
examples.analytical: The prophet is cast as a reprover of the nation's injustice, whose authority rests on the moral law rather than on personal anger.

nuance.analogy: A reprover is like a referee who blows the whistle on a foul: the call is about the rule that was broken, not about the player's character.
nuance.etymology: From 'reprove' (from Old French reprover, from Latin reprobare, 'to disapprove') plus the agent suffix '-er.'
common_mistakes: Using 'reprover' as a casual synonym for 'critic' of art or ideas; it refers to rebuking behavior or faults.
Stressing the second syllable (re-PROH-ver) instead of REP-roh-ver.

senses.definition: To rank again; to rank in a different order.
senses.example: After the new data arrived, the team decided to rerank the search results by relevance.

core.definition: In search and machine learning, to reorder a list of results using a new, usually more accurate, score.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RANK, with a lighter stress on the prefix re-. Don't pronounce it REE-rank; the nasal ng sound at the end is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a process rather than a judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rerank mainly in technical settings such as search engines, recommendation systems, and AI pipelines. A first-stage system retrieves candidate results, and then a reranker reorders them using a more expensive model. Outside technical work, people say 'sort again' or 'put in a new order'.

distinctions.note: Sort orders items by a simple field or key; rerank usually means applying a new scoring model to an existing candidate list.
Rescore changes the scores; rerank changes the order that results from those scores.

examples.everyday: Our music app reranks the playlist whenever you skip a song.
examples.professional: We'll rerank the top 100 search candidates with a cross-encoder before showing them to users.
examples.analytical: A reranker can reorder candidates using query-document interactions that the first-stage retriever cannot compute cheaply.

nuance.analogy: Reranking is like a teacher reading a stack of essays once to pick a shortlist and then reading the shortlist carefully to set the final order.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' plus rank, from Old French ranc 'row, line'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as REE-rank; the main stress belongs on RANK.
Writing 'rerank' and 'reranking' inconsistently; both 'rerank' and 're-rank' appear, but the unhyphenated form is standard in technical writing.

senses.definition: A soldier who is assigned as reserved: after training, no longer on full active duty.

core.definition: A member of a military reserve force who trains part-time and can be called to active duty when needed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, ZUR. The final -ist is a short 'ist', not 'eest', and the v is voiced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to respectful: the word describes someone who serves part-time and is respected for that commitment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'reservist' for someone in the Army Reserve, Navy Reserve, Air Force Reserve or similar, not for a full-time soldier. People say 'my brother is a reservist' or 'reservists were called up.' National Guard members are a related but separate category, and the word is standard in news and everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Guard members serve under state governors and can be called for local emergencies; reservists serve under federal military branches.
Active-duty soldiers serve full time, while reservists train part-time, usually one weekend a month and two weeks a year.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a reservist, so he's away one weekend a month for training.
examples.professional: Our project lead is a naval reservist, so her schedule may change if she is called up for training.
examples.analytical: The reservist occupies an ambiguous civic role, combining civilian identity with military obligation.

nuance.analogy: A reservist is like a volunteer firefighter on call: trained, committed and ready, but living a civilian life most of the time.
nuance.etymology: From reserve plus -ist, from Latin reservare, 'to keep back'.
common_mistakes: Using 'reservist' for any soldier; it refers only to part-time members of a reserve force.
Putting the stress on the first syllable (RE-servist); the stress is on ZUR.

senses.definition: To shuffle something again, especially playing cards.
senses.example: Before the next hand, she reshuffled the deck to make sure nobody had an advantage.

senses.definition: To reorganize or rearrange something, especially government posts.
senses.example: The prime minister reshuffled his cabinet after two ministers resigned unexpectedly.

senses.definition: An instance of reshuffling, a reorganization.
senses.example: The latest reshuffle moved three senior engineers into the new data science group.

core.definition: To rearrange people or things, such as jobs or assignments, into new positions or roles.

pronunciation.tip: In the verb, stress falls on SHUF, and the final syllable is a light 'uhl'. As a noun Americans usually say RE-shuf-uhl, with stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is common in business and politics and can suggest instability or a shake-up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'reshuffle' for organizational change, such as a company reshuffling its leadership team or a president reshuffling the cabinet. In card games it is literal. For small changes, say 'rearrange' or 'move things around', and for a dramatic change, 'shake-up' is more informal.

distinctions.note: Rearrange is neutral and can describe small moves; reshuffle often implies moving several people or roles at once.
Shake-up is more dramatic and informal, suggesting disruption; reshuffle is more neutral and organizational.

examples.everyday: We moved the couch, reshuffled the bookshelves, and the living room finally feels bigger.
examples.professional: The VP reshuffled the analytics teams so that data engineers now report directly to the platform group.
examples.analytical: Political scientists often read a cabinet reshuffle as a signal about shifting power, not only about competence.

nuance.analogy: Reshuffling is like shuffling a deck and dealing new hands: the cards haven't changed, but the game does.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' and shuffle (verb).
common_mistakes: Using reshuffle for small furniture moves; it sounds like a major organizational change.
Mispronouncing the last syllable as 'fuhl' with a strong vowel; it is a light 'uhl'.

senses.definition: Shining brilliantly; gleaming; radiant.
senses.example: The resplendent sun rose over the horizon.

senses.definition: Shiny and colorful, and thus pleasing to the eye; splendid in appearance.
senses.example: The peacock displayed its resplendent plumage.

senses.definition: Magnificent; glorious; splendid; marked by extraordinary excellence or beauty.
senses.example: The queen appeared in resplendent majesty.

senses.definition: Exhibiting the property of resplendency in Peano arithmetic.
senses.example: The logician proved that the countable model was resplendent, which simplified the argument considerably.

core.definition: Very bright, shining and beautiful, in a way that is impressive and eye-catching.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SPLEN. The final -ent is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'unt', and the ending does not rhyme with 'dent'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests splendor and admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'resplendent' mainly in writing, speeches or descriptions, such as in wedding toasts, church writing or literary prose. In casual talk, people say 'gorgeous', 'stunning' or 'dressed up'. Use it sparingly, because it can sound grand or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Splendid' is more general and can mean simply excellent; 'resplendent' stresses glowing appearance.
'Gorgeous' is casual and common; 'resplendent' is formal and suggests a more ceremonial beauty.

examples.everyday: Mom looked resplendent in her blue dress at the family reunion.
examples.professional: The conference hall was resplendent with the new brand colors, though the budget was tight.
examples.analytical: The poem describes the cathedral as resplendent, a word that makes its beauty a sign of divine order.

nuance.analogy: Like a stained-glass window with the sun behind it: the light makes the whole thing glow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin resplendere, 'to shine brightly', from re- 'again' and splendere 'to shine'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: say rih-SPLEN-dunt.
Using 'resplendent' in very casual speech, where it can sound overdone.

resplendent.etymology: From the obsolete sense of the English verb *splendish* (“to shine”), from Latin *splendere* (“to shine”), or from *resplend* + *ent*, from Latin *resplendere* (“to shine back, glitter”).

senses.definition: In a restrictive manner.

core.definition: In a limiting or narrow way; so as to restrict or confine what is allowed or included.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRICT, the second syllable, not on the first. The -ive ending is a short 'iv' and the final -ly is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes how narrowly a rule, license, or term is applied, and can signal frustration when the limit seems unfair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mostly in legal, policy and academic writing, for example when a license or statute is read narrowly. In casual speech they usually say 'strictly' or 'narrowly' instead. Its tone is neutral, so it fits a formal critique as well as a plain description.

distinctions.note: Strictly means exactly and without exception; restrictively means in a way that cuts down what is allowed.
Narrowly stresses a small scope; restrictively stresses a limiting effect produced by a rule or term.

examples.everyday: The landlord's pet policy is written so restrictively that even a goldfish needs approval.
examples.professional: The license is worded restrictively, so it covers only internal use and not resale.
examples.analytical: The court read the statute restrictively, excluding cases the legislature probably meant to include.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence with very narrow gates, the rule lets only a few things through.
nuance.etymology: From restrictive plus -ly; restrictive comes from Late Latin restrictivus, from restringere, to draw back tightly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (RES-trictively) instead of the second, STRIK.
Using it to mean 'strictly' in casual talk, where people expect the simpler word.

senses.definition: To rise again; to go through a period of renewed vigor or vitality.
A resurgence.
senses.example: A resurge of interest in vinyl records surprised many music store owners.

core.definition: To rise again with renewed strength, energy or popularity after a period of decline.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SURJ, which rhymes with 'urge'. The final sound is the soft 'j' of 'judge', not 'zh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it describes a return of strength, but it can also describe the return of unwanted things like violence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use resurge mostly in news writing, essays and literary prose, and less often in speech. In everyday talk people say 'make a comeback' or 'come back strong.' Interest, demand and nationalism often resurge. For an unwanted return, use resurface or flare up instead.

distinctions.note: Resurface means to come back into view; resurge means to rise again in strength, energy or popularity.
Rebound often means recovering quickly after a fall, such as stock prices; resurge suggests a renewed rise in strength or interest.

examples.everyday: Interest in vinyl records has resurged, and my son now wants a turntable.
examples.professional: Demand for our product resurged after the price cut, and the sales team had to hire.
examples.analytical: Nationalist sentiment resurged in the decades after the empire's collapse, reshaping borders and identities.

nuance.analogy: Like a tide that goes out and then comes back with force, the interest rises again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin resurgere, to rise again, from re- plus surgere, to rise.
common_mistakes: Using 'resurge' as a noun for the process; the noun is 'resurgence'.
Stressing the first syllable, as in RE-surge, which weakens the meaning.

senses.definition: A believer in a future bodily resurrection.
One who resurrects an abandoned idea, practice, etc. a revivalist.
senses.example: The consultant was a resurrectionist who revived outdated management fads that everyone had forgotten.

senses.definition: (historical) One who sells cadavers to anatomists, surgeons, etc. especially by exhuming corpses from graves; a graverobber.
senses.example: Victorian resurrectionists robbed fresh graves and sold the bodies to anatomy lecturers in London.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A person who believes in a future bodily resurrection of the dead, when God will raise the dead to life in renewed bodies.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -REK-, and the final -ist has a short ih sound, not a long ee. Many learners stress the first syllable or add an extra syllable after the k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theology and church history. In older writing it can carry a skeptical or mocking tone.
nuance.usage_note: This term appears mainly in theological, historical and academic writing. Christians who believe in the resurrection of the body would more often say 'I believe in the resurrection of the dead' than call themselves resurrectionists. Be careful, because the historical sense (a grave robber) is very different, so context matters.

distinctions.note: An annihilationist believes the wicked are destroyed rather than kept alive forever; a resurrectionist affirms bodily rising, which an annihilationist may or may not accept.
An immortalist hopes for indefinite life, sometimes through medicine or technology; a resurrectionist holds a specific religious belief in God raising the dead.
A revivalist seeks to restore religious fervor or old ideas; a resurrectionist is someone who believes in literal bodily resurrection.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study leader calls herself a resurrectionist, so she believes God will raise our bodies someday.
examples.professional: In my seminar, we compare how early Christian writers and later resurrectionist thinkers described the risen body.
examples.analytical: Irenaeus is often read as a resurrectionist who insisted that the flesh, not merely the soul, would be raised.

nuance.analogy: Like a builder who insists the old house will be rebuilt on its own foundation, not replaced with a new one.
nuance.etymology: From resurrection, from Latin resurrectio ('a rising again'), plus -ist, a suffix for a person holding a belief.
common_mistakes: Confusing the theological sense with the historical grave-robber sense
Stressing the first syllable, saying REZ-uh-rek-shuh-nist instead of rez-uh-REK-shuh-nist
nuance.biblical_note: The underlying Greek word is anastasis (ἀνάστασις, 'a standing up again, rising'). Acts 23:6–8 describes Paul's trial, where the Pharisees affirm the resurrection and the Sadducees deny it. Mark 12:18–27 records Jesus answering Sadducees who question the resurrection. John 11:23–26 records Jesus telling Martha that her brother will rise, and that he himself is the resurrection and the life.

senses.definition: To return to an earlier, simpler or worse condition; to regress.
To go backwards; to retreat.
To return to bad behavior; to relapse.
senses.example: After months of sobriety, he began to retrogress and returned to drinking every weekend.

senses.definition: A retrogression.
senses.example: The sudden retrogress in her test scores worried her parents and tutors.

core.definition: To return to an earlier, simpler or worse state; to regress or move backward.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second half, -GRESS, with a weaker stress on the first syllable. The final s is a hard s, not z.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests loss or failure to progress and is used mainly in formal, analytic or policy writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use retrogress mostly in formal writing, reports, or discussions of progress in health, science or development. In everyday talk they say go backward, slide back or backslide. Official reports on health or social indicators sometimes say a measure has retrogressed.

distinctions.note: Regress and retrogress are close; regress is more common in general and psychological use, while retrogress sounds more formal and often describes a condition.
Backslide is informal and often describes relapse in habits or morals; retrogress is formal and neutral.

examples.everyday: After a great week, my dad's back pain retrogressed, so he went back to the chiropractor.
examples.professional: If the new model retrogresses on the holdout set, we will not deploy it until the regression is fixed.
examples.analytical: Any reform that depends on the same institutions risks retrogressing into the patterns it was meant to end.

nuance.analogy: Retrogress is like a train that backs up the track instead of moving toward its station.
nuance.etymology: From Latin retrogressus, stepped back, from retro, backward, and gradi, to step.
common_mistakes: Using retrogress as a noun in place of retrogression.
Pronouncing the final s as z, or using retrogress in casual speech where go backward sounds more natural.

retrogress.etymology: From Latin *retrōgressus*, perfect active participle of *retrōgradior* (“retrograde”).

senses.definition: A method of producing effective tones in the printing of etchings by skillful treatment of the ink in certain parts.
senses.example: The printmaker used retroussage to wipe ink from the plate, leaving soft gray halos around the lines.

core.definition: A printmaking technique in which the printer wipes and lightly redistributes ink on an etching plate to create soft, subtle tones.

pronunciation.tip: This is a French word, so the stress falls on the second syllable, TROO. The final syllable sounds like the 's' in 'measure' and is not pronounced like 'sage'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise studio term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Printmakers and art teachers in American studios and universities use this word, usually while demonstrating an etching process. Outside printmaking circles most Americans will not know it, so it is best to explain it briefly if you use it in conversation. A natural reply from another artist would be 'Oh, how does that change the tones?'

distinctions.note: Wiping in general means removing ink from the plate surface. Retroussage deliberately leaves and redistributes ink to create soft, tonal effects.
Chine collé is a method of bonding thin paper to the print during pressing. Retroussage is a way of handling ink on the plate itself.

examples.everyday: My friend who makes etchings explained retroussage to me over coffee, and it sounded like magic.
examples.professional: In the print workshop, we use retroussage to bring out the soft gradations in the sky of the plate.
examples.analytical: Retroussage makes the tonal range depend on the printer's hand, so no two impressions of the same plate are identical.

nuance.analogy: Like softening a pencil line by lightly rubbing it with a fingertip, so the darkest marks fade into the paper.
nuance.etymology: From French retrousser 'to tuck up or roll back', from re- and trousser 'to truss'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with English stress as RET-roo-sage.
Confusing it with the French adjective retroussé, which describes something turned up, such as a nose.

senses.definition: The sound made by a telephone when ringing.
senses.example: My phone's ringtone is a cheerful xylophone melody that always startles people in meetings.

senses.definition: A customizable tone used to indicate an incoming call on a telephone, especially a mobile phone.
senses.example: I set my favorite song as my ringtone.

senses.definition: Of a telephone: to play a ringtone.
senses.example: My old phone ringtones every time a telemarketer calls, which drives me up the wall.

core.definition: A sound or melody a phone plays to signal an incoming call, which the owner can usually choose or change.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light 'tone' that rhymes with 'phone.' Keep the 'ng' clean without adding a /g/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a casual, everyday word about personal phones.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ringtone' for both the sound and the act of choosing it. People often talk about changing a ringtone, and the word is common in casual speech and in phone settings. It is not used for landlines in most cases.

distinctions.note: 'Ring' can refer to the ringing sound itself, while 'ringtone' refers to the specific chosen sound on a phone.
A notification sound signals a text or alert, while a ringtone is specifically for incoming calls.

examples.everyday: My ringtone is so loud that people in the coffee shop turn around when I get a call.
examples.professional: Please put your phone on vibrate or silence your ringtone during the meeting.
examples.analytical: A ringtone is a small cultural marker that tells others something about the owner's taste and values.

nuance.analogy: A ringtone is like a doorbell that you choose yourself, so your home sounds like you.
nuance.etymology: Ring from Old English hringan and tone from Greek tonos, tension or pitch.
common_mistakes: Saying 'ring tone' as two words in formal writing, when 'ringtone' is standard.
Using 'ringtone' for a text alert sound, which is a different thing.

conversation.text: I changed my ringtone so I know when it's my wife.
Everyone checked their phones when the ringtone went off.
Your ringtone is so loud; can you turn it down?

senses.definition: An instance of wandering.
senses.example: The dog's roaming through the neighborhood worried the family every evening.

senses.definition: The ability to use a cell phone outside of its original registering zone.
senses.example: Roaming charges made the phone bill jump after our flight landed in Mexico.

senses.definition: The use of a network or service from different locations or devices.
senses.example: Enterprise roaming lets employees keep the same connection as they move between offices.

senses.definition: Using the OS service of manipulating folders and documents from different PC devices by a registered user.
senses.example: With profile roaming enabled, my desktop documents follow me to any computer I log into.

core.definition: Using your cell phone service in another area, city or country, often with extra fees from your provider.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, ROH. The ending -ing is a short i sound, so it is 'ROH-ming' not 'ROH-meeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. In everyday use, it usually refers to extra charges that can be surprising.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear roaming when traveling abroad or when a phone signal switches to another carrier. Phrases such as 'roaming charges' and 'turn off data roaming' are common. Ask your carrier 'Does my plan include roaming?' A natural reply is 'Yes, but it's a few dollars a day.' It is mainly used in phone and data contexts.

distinctions.note: Wandering is physically moving around, while phone roaming is a technical service that connects your device to another network.
International calling is making calls to another country, while roaming is using your phone on a foreign network, which can apply to calls, texts and data.

examples.everyday: Turn off data roaming before we land, or the phone bill will be a shock.
examples.professional: Our travel policy covers roaming costs for approved trips, so submit receipts within thirty days.
examples.analytical: Roaming shows how mobile networks depend on interconnection agreements, which make a signal from one carrier usable on another.

nuance.analogy: Phone roaming is like a guest using a neighbor's Wi-Fi: it works, but the host may charge for it.
nuance.etymology: Derived from roam (verb), from Middle English romen, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'roaming fees' in casual speech when Americans more often say 'roaming charges'.
Confusing roaming with wandering, since the phone sense is technical and has nothing to do with walking.

conversation.text: Turn off data roaming before you land in Mexico, or you'll get a huge bill.
I got charged for roaming even though I barely used my phone.
My plan includes free roaming in Canada.

senses.definition: To move about on the ground while rotating and turning one's body.
senses.example: Pigs like to roll around in the mud.

senses.definition: To be considered, without much coherence, in someone's mind.
senses.example: I'm going to write a book because I've got all these crazy ideas rolling around in my head.

senses.definition: To indulge in sexual intercourse (with).
senses.example: I know a girl who's fun to roll around with, but can't have a conversation.

senses.definition: To laugh very heartily.
senses.example: We rolled around laughing when Dad tried to explain the group chat.

senses.definition: Of a time or event: to come up; to happen.
senses.example: By the time Friday rolls around, I'm ready for the weekend.

core.definition: To keep thinking about an idea or question again and again in your mind without reaching a clear conclusion.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'around', the particle, in this phrasal verb. The first syllable of 'around' is a weak schwa, so don't say 'a-ROUND' with a full 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests restless or unresolved thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'roll around' in casual talk about thoughts that keep returning, as in 'That idea keeps rolling around in my head.' Physically, it means to move on the ground by turning over, as with children on grass. The slang sexual sense exists but is crude, so avoid it at work or in front of others. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I've been thinking about it too.'

distinctions.note: Think about is neutral and general; roll around suggests returning to the idea repeatedly without settling it.
Mull over suggests deliberate, careful thought; roll around can suggest restless or unresolved thoughts.
Ruminate is formal or literary; roll around is conversational.

examples.everyday: I've been trying to decide on a new car, and the question keeps rolling around in my head.
examples.professional: The team has been rolling around the idea of automating the reports, but nobody wants to own it yet.
examples.analytical: The question of free will keeps rolling around the seminar without any agreed answer.

nuance.analogy: Like a pebble tumbling in a jar, bumping into the same thoughts over and over.
nuance.etymology: From roll (verb) and around (adverb).
common_mistakes: Using 'roll around' only for physical motion; the mental sense is just as common in American speech.
Saying 'roll round', which is more typical of British English; Americans say 'around'.

core.definition: A citizen of ancient Rome or of the Roman Empire, a person whose status and rights were important in the New Testament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ROH, and reduce the second syllable to a schwa, 'mun.' Do not pronounce the final syllable as 'man' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in religious or historical contexts it names a people or citizen without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech Roman usually refers to a person from ancient Rome or from the Roman Empire, and it is common in history classes, Bible study, and museums. It may also describe modern people from Rome, Italy, but Americans usually say 'Italian' or 'someone from Rome.' Capitalize it as a proper noun.

distinctions.note: Italian refers to modern people of Italy, while Roman in this sense refers to the ancient Empire.
Latin is a language, while Roman refers to a citizen or person of the Roman state.

examples.everyday: My kid is doing a project on the Romans, so we visited the Roman ruins in town.
examples.professional: The grant proposal describes the infrastructure built by Roman engineers in the first century.
examples.analytical: Paul's status as a Roman citizen shapes the narrative in Acts, where his legal rights are repeatedly emphasized.

nuance.analogy: A Roman was like a citizen of a powerful empire whose passport protected them across the entire Mediterranean world.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Romanus, from Roma, the city of Rome.
common_mistakes: Using lowercase roman for the people, which is a different word meaning a type of font or numeral.
Confusing Roman in the Bible with Romance or modern Italian identity.
nuance.biblical_note: In Greek, the word is Rhōmaios, used in the New Testament for a citizen of Rome or a member of the Roman state. Acts 22:25-29 describes Paul's claim to Roman citizenship, which changes how the officers treat him. John 11:48 uses the word 'Romans' to describe the authorities who feared the crowds would bring Roman intervention. Romans 1:7 addresses the letter to believers in Rome, the city at the center of the empire.

senses.definition: Having a round, spherical or curved shape; circular; orbicular.
senses.example: The rotund little pumpkin sat on the porch, bright orange and nearly round.

senses.definition: Having a round body shape; portly or pudgy; obese.
Full and rich; orotund; sonorous; full-toned.
senses.example: The bass singer's rotund tone filled the hall without any strain.

core.definition: Round in shape, or having a round, plump body. Also used for a full, deep, resonant voice.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -TUND. The vowel in the second syllable is the short 'uh' of 'cut'. The final d is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative when describing a person's body, since it can sound like a polite word for fat. For a voice or round shape it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rotund in writing and formal speech, sometimes humorously, to describe a plump person or a round object. Saying it directly about a person can sound stiff or unkind, so 'heavyset' or 'round' is more common in conversation.

distinctions.note: Round is everyday and neutral for shapes, while rotund is more formal and can describe plump bodies.
Plump is usually gentle and used for cheeks or fruit, while rotund is more formal and can sound more critical.

examples.everyday: The old barber was a rotund man with a big laugh, and everyone liked him.
examples.professional: The design team wants a rotund shape for the handle so it fits the hand better.
examples.analytical: The author's rotund style gives his sentences a full and resonant sound that rewards slow reading.

nuance.analogy: A rotund object is like a well-filled balloon: full, round and broad.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rotundus, round, from rota, wheel.
common_mistakes: Calling a person 'rotund' in casual conversation, where it can sound rude or stiff.
Confusing it with 'rotary', which relates to turning rather than shape.

rotund.etymology: Latin *rotundus* (“round”), from Latin *rota* (“wheel”), from Proto-Indo-European **Hreth₂-* (“to run, to roll”).

senses.definition: The action of the verb to row.
senses.example: Rowing across the lake at dawn is my favorite way to clear my head.

senses.definition: The action of propelling a boat with oars.
The rowing of boats as a competitive sport.
The act of having a row, or argument.
senses.example: The rowing between the two roommates over dishes kept the whole apartment awake.

core.definition: The sport of racing boats propelled by oars, usually in teams or pairs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ow' is a long 'oh' sound. The ending '-ing' is short, so avoid stretching it into 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests teamwork, discipline and endurance.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, the sport is often called 'crew' in college and high school programs, so you may hear 'crew team' or 'I rowed crew in college'. 'Rowing' is the general name for the sport and for the act of moving a boat with oars. Americans use 'rowing' for leisure rowing too, such as rowing around a lake.

distinctions.note: Crew is the common American name for the sport in college and high school settings, while rowing is the general term.
Sculling uses two oars per rower, while sweep rowing uses one oar per rower.
Paddling uses a single blade pushed by hand, as in canoes and kayaks, not oars fixed in place.

examples.everyday: My daughter started rowing this year, so we're up at 5 a.m. on weekends to get her to practice.
examples.professional: Our rowing team trains on the river from 6 to 8 every morning during the season.
examples.analytical: Rowing reveals the paradox of collective effort: each rower must match the stroke of the whole boat to make any progress at all.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay of heartbeats: every stroke must sync up so the whole boat moves as one.
nuance.etymology: From 'row' (to propel with oars), from Old English rōwan, plus the '-ing' form.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'row' with the 'cow' vowel, which turns the sport into a different word
Calling the sport 'boat racing' in American English; the sport is rowing, and the event is a regatta or race

senses.definition: Of or relating to a monarch or his (or her) family.
Having the air or demeanour of a monarch; illustrious; magnanimous; of more than common size or excellence.
senses.example: The mayor received the visiting dignitary with royal courtesy and a lavish banquet.

senses.definition: Used as an intensifier.
senses.example: a royal pain in the neck

senses.definition: In large sailing ships, of a mast right above the topgallant mast and its sails.
senses.example: royal mast; royal sail

senses.definition: Free-for-all, especially involving multiple combatants.
senses.example: The bar fight turned into a royal brawl that spilled out onto the sidewalk.

senses.definition: Describing a piece which, if captured, results in loss of game.
senses.example: Maharajah and the Sepoys pits a single royal amazon for white against a standard chess army for black.

senses.definition: A royal person; a member of a royal family.
senses.example: The royals waved from the balcony while the crowd cheered below in the square.

senses.definition: A standard size of writing paper, measuring 24 by 19 inches.
senses.example: The printer asked whether we wanted letter or royal sheets for the annual report.

senses.definition: Any of various lycaenid butterflies.
senses.example: The entomologist pinned a rare royal butterfly collected from the coastal meadows.

senses.definition: The fourth tine of an antler's beam.
senses.example: The hunter noted the royal on the antler, the fourth point from the base.

senses.definition: A stag with twelve points (six on each antler).
senses.example: The buck we saw at dawn was a royal with twelve points, the biggest we'd ever seen.

senses.definition: An old English gold coin, the rial.
senses.example: The collector showed us an old royal, a gold coin from Elizabethan England.

senses.definition: In auction bridge, a royal spade.
senses.example: I held the royal spade, so I was sure we would make the slam.

senses.definition: A tuft of beard on the lower lip.
senses.example: His royal, a small tuft on his lower lip, gave him a distinguished look.

senses.definition: Bell changes rung on ten bells.
senses.example: The ringers spent the evening practicing royal on ten bells in the old tower.

senses.definition: A standard size of printing paper, measuring 25 by 20 inches.
senses.example: The printer recommended royal for the posters, since the brochure needed a larger sheet.

senses.definition: In large sailing ships, square sail over the topgallant sail.
senses.example: The crew set the royal above the topgallant as the wind freshened over the bow.

senses.definition: A small mortar.
senses.example: The garrison fired a royal, a small mortar, across the harbor at dusk.

senses.definition: (dated) The Australian decimal currency intended to replace the pound in 1966; was changed to "dollar" before it was actually circulated.
senses.example: The 1966 plan to replace the pound with the royal was scrapped before any coins circulated.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Relating to a king or queen or their family; also very fine or splendid.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable is one diphthong, like 'boy', not two separate syllables. The final syllable is a reduced 'uhl', so say 'ROY-uhl', not 'roy-AL' or 'loyal'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests prestige, honor and high quality, though in news it can be neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'royal' for the British monarchy and for other kingdoms when talking about history, news or celebrity events. In everyday American speech it appears in phrases such as 'royal blue' and 'the royal treatment'. As a noun, 'royal' is less common than 'royalty' in American conversation, and people often say 'a member of the royal family' instead.

distinctions.note: Regal describes a stately, dignified appearance, while royal refers to monarchy or the family of a monarch.
Noble can mean aristocratic rank or moral dignity, while royal refers specifically to a king, queen or their family.
Imperial relates to an empire or emperor, while royal relates to a kingdom and its monarch.

examples.everyday: My grandmother still uses her royal blue china for holiday dinners.
examples.professional: Our brand guidelines require the royal blue logo on all client-facing materials.
examples.analytical: The royal family's role in modern Britain is largely symbolic, yet its ceremonies still signal the nation's continuity.

nuance.analogy: Like a crown on a flag: a symbol of authority that shapes how the whole thing is seen.
nuance.etymology: From Old French reial, from Latin regalis, from rex (king).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (roy-AL) instead of the first
Confusing royal with loyal, which is pronounced LOY-uhl

royal.etymology: From Middle English *royal*, from Old French *roial* (Modern French *royal*), from Latin *rēgālis*, from *rēx* (“king”).

senses.definition: A noisy, sometimes violent disturbance; noise and confusion; a noisy quarrel or brawl.
senses.example: The kids' rumpus in the backyard woke the whole neighborhood before sunrise.

senses.definition: To cause a noisy disturbance or commotion.
senses.example: Don't rumpus around the house while your father is trying to sleep.

core.definition: A noisy commotion, uproar, or quarrel, often caused by children or a heated argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -us is a weak, unstressed syllable that sounds like 'uhs', not 'oos'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative, but often humorous or affectionate when describing children's noise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rumpus for a noisy fuss, often with kids (the kids are making a rumpus upstairs) or a heated argument among adults. It is informal and a bit old-fashioned, like something a grandparent might say. Calling a situation a rumpus usually signals mild disapproval, sometimes with humor.

distinctions.note: Commotion is general and neutral; rumpus is informal and suggests noisy playfulness or a quarrel.
Uproar is stronger and more public, often an outburst of anger or outrage; rumpus is more everyday.
Ruckus is a close synonym common in American informal speech, usually about a loud fight or disturbance.

examples.everyday: The kids made such a rumpus during naptime that I had to go upstairs and settle them down.
examples.professional: The vendor escalation caused a rumpus in the team channel, so we moved the discussion to a call.
examples.analytical: Once the audience joined in, the debate turned into a rumpus, and the original argument was lost.

nuance.analogy: A rumpus is like a kitchen full of pots clattering to the floor at once, loud and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in English in the 18th century.
common_mistakes: Using rumpus for a quiet disagreement; the word implies noise and commotion.
Confusing it with romp, which means a playful run or active game.

senses.definition: Something that has been run out.
senses.example: The landslide had a long runout.

senses.definition: A relatively flat portion at the end of a ski run to slow down, or to connect trails.
Slowing down at the end of a ski run, skiing on a runout.
senses.example: After the jump, I finished with a long runout that let my legs recover.

senses.definition: The end portion of the groove of a phonographic record, after the recorded sound.
senses.example: The needle hissed through the runout groove after the final song ended.

senses.definition: A supposed auction employing shill bidders in order to convince legitimate buyers to purchase worthless articles.
senses.example: The online auction turned out to be a runout, with fake bidders driving up prices.

senses.definition: Deviation of the axis of rotation of a rotating object (especially a milling cutter or workpiece) relative to that object's centerline; the specific amount of deviation.
senses.example: We determined that inaccuracy was caused by a large amount of tool runout.

senses.definition: A sudden tension between two coupled railcars when the fore one is moving faster than the hinder one.
senses.example: The freight train lurched as a runout jolted the coupler between the two cars.

senses.definition: The method of getting out (dismissed from play) in which a batsman, in making a run, has not reached the popping crease when a fielder breaks his wicket with the ball.
senses.example: The batsman was given out on a runout after the fielder broke the stumps.

core.definition: A flat or gently sloping section at the bottom of a ski trail where skiers slow down and stop safely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce out as owt, a single diphthong. Do not separate the two parts with a pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical term, and it becomes important when skiers are tired or the slope is icy.
nuance.usage_note: Skiers and resort staff use runout for the flat area at the end of a run where you glide to a stop. Ski instructors may say 'Take the runout slowly' or 'Meet me at the runout.' Outside skiing, run-out has other meanings, such as the cricket dismissal, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Runout is a flat stretch of snow on a ski trail; runoff is water or an election, and the two words sound very similar.
Run-out with a hyphen is common in cricket and in older writing, where it means a runner being put out; in skiing, runout is the usual spelling.

examples.everyday: Stay left on the blue trail and you'll hit the flat runout right by the lift.
examples.professional: The resort crew packed the runout after the storm so skiers could stop safely at the bottom.
examples.analytical: A poorly designed runout turns the final section of a race course into a hazard, because skiers cannot slow down in time.

nuance.analogy: A runout is like the gravel lot at the bottom of a hill where a bicycle rolls to a gentle stop.
nuance.etymology: From the verb run out, used in the sense of coming to the end of a course.
common_mistakes: Using runout for a simple exit or escape in everyday English, where American speakers would say 'way out' or 'exit.'
Mixing up runout with runoff when speaking quickly, since the first syllables sound the same.

senses.definition: A deliberate action aimed at weakening someone (or something, a nation, etc) or preventing them from being successful, through subversion, obstruction, disruption, and/or destruction.
senses.example: Investigators suspected sabotage when the power plant shut down during the storm.

senses.definition: To deliberately destroy or damage something in order to prevent it from being successful.
senses.example: The railway line had been sabotaged by enemy commandos.

core.definition: Deliberate damage or disruption to a machine, system, or plan, done secretly to stop it from succeeding, often by a rival or enemy.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, SAB. The final syllable is pronounced like the 'zh' in 'measure', not like 'tahj' or 'tah-ZHAY' in English speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies secret, intentional harm and usually suggests that someone is acting in bad faith.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sabotage for physical damage, such as cutting cables, and also for deliberate efforts to ruin a project, a campaign, or a relationship. Accusing someone of sabotage is serious, so use it when you have evidence of intent. As a verb, 'sabotage' is also common in news and office talk: 'They sabotaged the launch'.

distinctions.note: To undermine someone is to weaken their authority or position gradually, often without visible damage; sabotage is more direct and usually involves a specific act of damage.
To obstruct is to block progress, for example by refusing to vote; sabotage implies deliberate damage or destruction, not just interference.
Vandalism is damage done for its own sake or out of random mischief; sabotage is strategic damage meant to stop a specific goal.

examples.everyday: I think my brother sabotaged my fantasy team by trading away my best player right before the playoffs.
examples.professional: The deployment failed because someone sabotaged the migration script, so the nightly job corrupted the customer table.
examples.analytical: Historians still debate whether the minister's resignation was sabotage by rival factions or simply the collapse of a fragile coalition.

nuance.analogy: Sabotage is like someone quietly loosening the bolts on a bridge before the parade, so the damage looks like an accident until it is too late.
nuance.etymology: From French saboter, 'to botch work' or 'to clatter in wooden shoes', from sabot, 'wooden shoe'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (sab-uh-TAHZH) instead of the first.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'tahj' rather than with the 'zh' sound.
Using 'sabotage' for simple mistakes or accidents; it requires intent.

senses.definition: Someone who sacrifices, one who makes a sacrifice.
senses.example: The sacrificer lit the fire at dawn and offered the lamb on the stone altar.

core.definition: A person who gives up something valuable for a larger purpose or a religious offering.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, then say 'fy' as a clear diphthong. The final '-er' is a reduced, rhotic 'ur,' not 'sa-KRIF-ice-er.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises self-giving, though the word itself is rare and can sound stiff.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use sacrificer in everyday speech. They more often say someone who sacrifices, or call a person selfless or self-giving. The word appears mainly in literary, religious, or historical writing about people who offer or give up things.

distinctions.note: A martyr dies or suffers for a cause, often for faith, while a sacrificer may give up time, money, or comfort without that extreme cost.
A volunteer chooses to help, often with little cost, while a sacrificer gives up something of real value.

examples.everyday: My mom was the real sacrificer in our family, working two jobs so we could all go to college.
examples.professional: She's a true sacrificer on this team, since she gave up her promotion to keep the project on schedule.
examples.analytical: In Abraham's story, the sacrificer is tested not by the loss itself but by the willingness to give what is most valued.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse keeper who gives up sleep and comfort so ships can find safe passage, the sacrificer gives up something for others.
nuance.etymology: From sacrifice, from Latin sacrificium, from sacer (sacred) and facere (to make).
common_mistakes: Using sacrificer as a synonym for victim, when it refers to someone who chooses to give.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sak-ruh-FY-sur.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the Hebrew word zebach (sacrifice, an offering) and the Greek word thysia (sacrifice). The word sacrificer itself is not biblical, but priests who offered sacrifices are the closest biblical figures. Romans 12:1 urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice. Hebrews 9:26 says Christ appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Psalm 51:17 says God desires a broken spirit rather than mere offerings.

traditions.view: The Divine Liturgy is understood as the offering of Christ's sacrifice, and the priest offers the Eucharist within the liturgical life of the Church.
The Eucharist is understood as the sacramental re-presentation of Christ's one sacrifice on Calvary, and the priest acts in persona Christi in offering it.
Most Protestants hold that Christ's sacrifice was once for all and complete, and they understand the Lord's Supper as a memorial or thanksgiving rather than a repeated offering.

senses.definition: The act of something that sags.
senses.example: The sagging of the old bridge's cables worried the engineers, who scheduled inspections.

senses.definition: A manner of wearing pants or shorts below the waist, revealing some or all of the underwear.
senses.example: The school banned sagging, so students had to wear belts that kept waistbands up.

senses.definition: Worn low on the waist, or wearing pants or shorts low on the waist.
Hanging down loosely.
senses.example: The sagging porch roof leaned toward the yard after years of heavy snow.

core.definition: Drooping or bending downward from weight or lost firmness, or worn low on the hips, as pants or shorts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable with a short 'a' as in 'cat'. The final '-ing' is a reduced, unstressed 'ing' with no strong 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes something that has lost its shape, support, or strength.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sagging' for furniture, roofs, skin, bridges, and economic or market trends. The fashion sense of 'sagging pants' is informal and sometimes controversial, often linked to youth culture and criticized by older adults. In everyday talk 'saggy' is a more casual variant for objects.

distinctions.note: 'Drooping' describes limp hanging, often plants or heads, while 'sagging' suggests weight or pressure causing a dip or loss of firmness.
'Saggy' is informal and often used for skin or clothing, while 'sagging' is more general and neutral in tone.

examples.everyday: That old couch is sagging, so we need a new one before the guests arrive.
examples.professional: Morale is sagging after the reorganization, so we should schedule more team check-ins.
examples.analytical: The argument has a sagging middle section, where the claims stop supporting the conclusion they were meant to carry.

nuance.analogy: Like a clothesline that bows under wet laundry, something sagging has lost the tension that kept it straight.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'sag', probably of Scandinavian origin, from Middle English saggen.
common_mistakes: Spelling it with one g, as 'sagging' requires a double g before -ing.
Using 'sagging' for a temporary dip in mood without knowing whether a negative tone is appropriate.

senses.definition: Relating to saliva.
A salivary gland.

core.definition: Relating to saliva or to the glands that produce it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ary ending is an unstressed 'air-ee' with a clear r. Do not drop the r or say 'SAL-uh-var-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a clinical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use salivary mainly in medicine, dentistry, and biology, as in 'salivary glands' or 'salivary flow'. In everyday talk people say 'the glands in your mouth' or just 'saliva'. Using it casually can sound clinical, so save it for a doctor's visit or a science class, where a typical reply might be 'Your salivary glands look healthy.'

distinctions.note: Salivary is an adjective describing things connected with saliva or its glands, while salivate is a verb meaning to produce saliva, often in anticipation.
Oral means relating to the mouth in general, while salivary is specific to saliva and the glands that produce it.

examples.everyday: My dentist says my salivary glands aren't making enough moisture, so I should drink more water.
examples.professional: The study measured salivary cortisol at several points during the workday to track stress.
examples.analytical: Salivary biomarkers offer a noninvasive window into hormonal and immune responses, though interpreting them requires careful controls.

nuance.analogy: The salivary glands are the mouth's small water pumps, keeping it moist.
nuance.etymology: From Latin salivarius, of saliva, from saliva, spittle.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as suh-LIV-uh-ree
Dropping the r, as in SAL-uh-vee

senses.definition: Promoting health or well-being; wholesome, especially relating to food or air.

core.definition: Good for health; wholesome, especially describing air, climate, or food that promotes well-being.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LOO. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final syllables are reduced to -bree-us, not -bree-oos.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as healthful or pleasant, often a place or climate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use salubrious mainly in writing, travel descriptions, or formal speech, and rarely in casual talk. Saying 'healthy' or 'good for you' is more natural in everyday conversation. It can sound pompous if used about ordinary food.

distinctions.note: Healthy is common and general, while salubrious is formal and often describes an environment or climate.
Wholesome often suggests moral or emotional goodness as well as health, while salubrious is mostly about physical well-being.

examples.everyday: My doctor says the mountain air up here is salubrious, so I should spend more weekends hiking.
examples.professional: The clinic's new site was chosen for its salubrious environment, away from the highway and its pollution.
examples.analytical: Early nineteenth-century writers often praised a region as salubrious, linking moral character to the quality of its air.

nuance.analogy: Like a fresh morning breeze that seems to clear the mind and body.
nuance.etymology: From Latin salubris, healthful, from salus, health.
common_mistakes: Confusing salubrious with salutary, which means beneficial in effect rather than healthful.
Stressing the first syllable as SAL-oo-brus, which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Capable of being salvaged, saved or repaired. Worth rescuing and keeping rather discarding or replacing.
senses.example: The car wasn't salvageable after the engine fire. The insurance company totalled it and I bought a new one.

core.definition: Able to be rescued, repaired, or used again, so that it is worth saving instead of throwing away or replacing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAL, and the -age syllable reduces to a short ij sound. Do not say sal-VAJ; the middle vowels are almost silent in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or hopeful when describing something worth keeping. It can be negative when describing a badly broken situation that barely survives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for cars, furniture, data, documents, and even projects or relationships, as in The car is badly damaged but salvageable. It is common in insurance, repair, and business talk. In a meeting, you might say The draft is salvageable to suggest that some of the work can be kept.

distinctions.note: Repairable means it can be fixed; salvageable adds that it is also worth keeping, even if only parts of it can be used.
Usable means it works now; salvageable means it is damaged but can be rescued.

examples.everyday: The water ruined the carpet, but the hardwood floors still look salvageable.
examples.professional: Half the dataset is corrupted, but the timestamps are salvageable, so we can rebuild the rest from backups.
examples.analytical: Many arguments in the old essay are weak, yet its central intuition seems salvageable if we reframe it in terms of consent.

nuance.analogy: Like a dented can of soup, the outside looks bad, but the food inside can still be eaten.
nuance.etymology: From salvage, from Old French salvage, safety, from Latin salvare, to save, plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sal-VAJ-uh-bul.
Using it for people; it is mostly used for things, projects, or situations.

senses.definition: Wearing a sandal or sandals.

core.definition: Wearing sandals on your feet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle syllable to a quick uh. Do not say sand-DAHL-ed or add a second l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; describes what someone is wearing and can suggest relaxed dress or a plain, simple look.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sandaled mainly to describe clothing, as in 'sandaled feet' or 'sandaled tourists', and mostly in writing. In speech people more often say 'wearing sandals' or 'in flip-flops'. The double-l spelling sandalled is British and looks wrong in American writing.

distinctions.note: Barefoot means having no shoes or sandals at all, while sandaled means wearing sandals.
Sandalled is the British spelling with a double l; Americans write sandaled, with the same meaning.

examples.everyday: I can't hike that gravel road in sandaled feet, so grab your sneakers.
examples.professional: The client said the event is casual, but I'd still skip the sandaled look for the board presentation.
examples.analytical: The sandaled friar in the painting signals the order's vow of poverty, since the detail marks a rejection of leather shoes.

nuance.etymology: From sandal, from Latin sandalium and Greek sandalion, plus the adjective ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Spelling it sandalled, the British form, in American writing.
Stressing the second syllable as sand-DAHL-ed, as if the word had a long a.

senses.definition: Involving bloodshed.
Eager to shed blood; bloodthirsty.
Consisting of, covered with, or similar in appearance to blood.
senses.example: The surgeon wiped the sanguinary residue from the steel tray.

senses.definition: A bloodthirsty person.
senses.example: The old pirate was a sanguinary who relished every battle.

senses.definition: The plant common yarrow, or herba sanguinaria (Achillea millefolium).
senses.example: She picked sanguinary from the meadow edge to brew a tea for her cut.

core.definition: Involving or marked by bloodshed, or fiercely eager to kill.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'gw' is a clear consonant cluster, and the final syllable is an American 'air-ee', with the r pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes violence, slaughter or a bloodthirsty attitude, and it is usually used in historical or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sanguinary' mostly in formal history, literature and journalism, for battles, massacres or wars. In everyday speech, people say 'bloody' or 'violent' instead. Calling a person sanguinary is an unusual and strong accusation, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Bloody is common and informal in speech; sanguinary is formal and mainly used for battles, wars or violent history.
Sanguine means cheerful or optimistic, though its root means blood; sanguinary means involving bloodshed.

examples.everyday: That war movie was too sanguinary for me, so I had to look away during the battle scenes.
examples.professional: The report describes a sanguinary outbreak of violence at the protest, which the board must review urgently.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the sanguinary character of the civil war reflected ideology, economics or both.

nuance.analogy: A sanguinary battle is like a storm that leaves its mark on the land: the damage is visible for years.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sanguinarius, from sanguis, 'blood'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sanguinary' with 'sanguine', which means optimistic in English.
Using 'sanguinary' in casual speech where 'bloody' or 'violent' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Of or relating to health.
Clean and free from pathogens; hygienic.
Sanitary towel.
senses.example: The pharmacy shelf stocked sanitary napkins in the same aisle as bandages.

core.definition: Clean and free from germs or harmful bacteria, so that it is safe for health, especially in food, medical or home settings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAN, and the final -ary is a weak syllable pronounced 'air-ee' with a clear r. Do not say 'san-ih-TARE-ee' or drop the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: it signals cleanliness and safety, so it is reassuring in food, medical and home contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sanitary as an adjective for clean and free from germs, especially for kitchens, restrooms and medical settings. The noun sense, sanitary towel, is mainly British; Americans say sanitary napkin or sanitary pad for that product. In everyday talk, clean or hygienic is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Clean means free of visible dirt, while sanitary is stronger and means free of germs or harmful bacteria.
Sterile means completely free of all living microorganisms, a much stricter standard than sanitary.
Hygienic is close in meaning and more general, used for habits and conditions that prevent disease.

examples.everyday: Let's wash our hands and make sure the kitchen is sanitary before the guests arrive.
examples.professional: The restaurant inspector checked that the prep area was sanitary and that all food was stored at safe temperatures.
examples.analytical: In the history of public health, a sanitary environment was treated as the first line of defense against epidemic disease.

nuance.analogy: A freshly wiped countertop is not sterile like a lab bench, but it is clean enough that you feel safe eating off it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sanitas 'health,' from sanus 'healthy.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as sa-NIT-ary; the main stress is on SAN.
Asking for a sanitary towel in an American store, where sanitary napkin or pads is the normal term.

sanitary.etymology: 19th century, borrowed from French *sanitaire*, formed from Latin *sanitas* (“health”).

senses.definition: Of human behavior: to make a choice that suffices to fulfill the minimum requirements to achieve an objective, without special regard for utility maximization or optimization of one's preferences.

core.definition: To choose the first option that meets your minimum requirements, rather than searching for the best possible option.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ice is pronounced like the word ice (/aɪs/), not like the -iss in kiss.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a decision strategy and carries no judgment, though some readers hear it as settling for less.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in economics, decision science, artificial intelligence and psychology, where Herbert Simon's bounded rationality is discussed. In everyday talk people say settle, go with the first option that works, or just take what's good enough. Using satisfice at a restaurant or in a meeting would sound overly technical, unless you are deliberately joking about it.

distinctions.note: Optimizing means searching for the single best outcome, while satisficing means stopping once an option is good enough.
Settle is everyday and can sound like giving up, while satisfice is a precise technical term with no negative feeling.

examples.everyday: We didn't compare every hotel in Denver, so we just satisficed and booked the first one with a decent rating and parking.
examples.professional: Given our deadline, the team will satisfice on the vendor shortlist and pick the first option that meets the security requirements.
examples.analytical: Simon argued that real decision makers satisfice because their information and computational capacity are limited, so optimal choice is an unrealistic model of human behavior.

nuance.analogy: Like grabbing the first apartment that fits your budget and commute instead of touring every building in the city.
nuance.etymology: Revived by economist Herbert Simon in the 1950s, blending satisfy and suffice.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as -ISS instead of -ICE (/aɪs/).
Using satisfice to mean simply satisfy or please someone, when it means choosing a minimally acceptable option.

satisfice.etymology: 1560, Northern alteration of *satisfy*, probably influenced in form by.

senses.definition: The condition of being a savant.

core.definition: The condition of being a savant, meaning having an exceptional ability in one area, often alongside significant developmental or mental disability.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, as in savant. The first vowel is a reduced 'uh' and the final syllable is a weak 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use, but the older term can sound dated or stigmatizing.
nuance.usage_note: Clinicians and writers now mostly prefer savant syndrome, which sounds more precise and less like a label for a person. You will still see savantism in older books, in literary writing, and in some popular articles. Use savant syndrome in professional or medical settings.

distinctions.note: Savant syndrome is the current clinical term; savantism is an older, more general word that can sound like a personal label.
A prodigy is exceptionally talented without a disability, so savantism specifically implies a disability alongside the skill.

examples.everyday: I read a novel about a boy with a kind of savantism for train schedules, and he could recite any timetable from memory.
examples.professional: Our literature review found that most published case studies of savantism rely on small samples and lack proper controls.
examples.analytical: The term savantism carries a historical weight that the clinical phrase savant syndrome was meant to shed.

nuance.analogy: Like an old map with a familiar name, the word still points to the same territory but carries outdated assumptions.
nuance.etymology: From savant, from French savoir, to know, with the English suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using savantism as if it were the usual professional term instead of savant syndrome.
Stressing the first syllable (SAV-un-tiz-um) instead of the second.

senses.definition: To run with quick light steps, to scamper.
A dash.
senses.example: The mouse made a quick scurry across the kitchen floor.

senses.definition: Bustle.
senses.example: The lobby filled with a noisy scurry of commuters rushing to catch the early trains.

core.definition: To move quickly with short, light, hurried steps, like a small animal or a person trying not to be noticed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and use the r-colored vowel of bird, so do not say SKOO-ree or SKAH-ree. The final y sounds like a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests hurry or nervousness and often evokes small creatures in a playful way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scurry mainly for small animals such as mice, squirrels and crabs, and for people hurrying in a fussy or nervous way. You might say the kids scurried off to the bus. For ordinary walking, say hurry or rush. The noun is less common and mostly literary.

distinctions.note: Scamper suggests playful, lively running, often by children or pets, while scurry suggests quick, hurried movement, often from urgency or fear.
Scramble means to move hurriedly using hands and feet or in disorder, and it implies difficulty or a struggle.
Scatter means that things or people move apart in different directions, not that the moving person hurries.

examples.everyday: When the thunder started, everyone at the picnic scurried for the car.
examples.professional: Before the board meeting, the team scurried to finish the slides and fix the broken chart.
examples.analytical: Rather than face the data, the report's authors scurry from one unverified claim to the next, hoping no one notices the gaps.

nuance.analogy: Like mice that dart across a kitchen floor when the light comes on.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using scurry for ordinary walking; it suggests quick, hurried, small movements.
Confusing it with scurvy, a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency, which is pronounced differently.

senses.definition: Skill in, and knowledge of, the work of navigating, maintaining, and operating a vessel at sea.

core.definition: The practical skill of navigating, handling and maintaining a boat or ship at sea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEE, with a lighter secondary stress on the final syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced muhn, not man, and the ship ending uses a short i.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises skill, judgment and competence on the water.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seamanship in sailing, maritime and naval contexts, and to praise someone's skill with boats. In everyday talk people more often say he really knows boats or he's a good sailor. The word is also used figuratively in leadership writing for skill under pressure.

distinctions.note: Navigation is finding and following a route; seamanship is broader and includes handling the vessel, knots and safety.
Boatmanship refers mainly to handling small boats, such as rowing or paddling; seamanship covers larger vessels at sea.
Sailing is the activity itself; seamanship is the skill and judgment that make the activity safe and competent.

examples.everyday: Her father taught her knots and basic seamanship before she turned ten.
examples.professional: Our training manual covers radio protocol and basic seamanship for new crew members.
examples.analytical: Seamanship in the age of sail depended on reading wind and swell, a body of knowledge that modern instruments have partly replaced.

nuance.analogy: Seamanship is like driving skill on water: knowing the vehicle, the route and how to respond when conditions change.
nuance.etymology: From seaman plus -ship, a suffix forming nouns of skill or state; seaman comes from Old English sǣ and mann.
common_mistakes: Confusing seamanship with seamen, the plural of seaman; seamanship is the skill, not the people.
Pronouncing the middle syllable with a full man vowel; it is reduced to muhn.

senses.definition: The act of secluding, shutting out or keeping apart.
senses.example: The monks' seclusion from the outside world was meant to deepen their prayer.

senses.definition: The state of being secluded or shut out, as from company, society, the world, etc. solitude.
A secluded, isolated or private place.
senses.example: They retreated to a seclusion in the hills where no tourists ever came.

senses.definition: The mature phase of the extratropical cyclone life cycle.
senses.example: warm seclusion

core.definition: The state of being private and away from other people, often for rest or concentration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable. The zh sound is like the s in measure, and the final syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests privacy, but can sound lonely in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seclusion in formal writing, religious or literary contexts, and descriptions of retreats, such as living in seclusion. In casual talk people more often say privacy, time alone or getting away. It can sound dramatic if used for a short break, so use it for longer or deliberate withdrawal.

distinctions.note: Solitude is being alone, often chosen and peaceful, while seclusion emphasizes being shut away from society or the world.
Privacy is about keeping personal matters hidden, while seclusion describes living apart in a quiet place.

examples.everyday: After the long week, I just want a little seclusion on the porch with a book.
examples.professional: During the product launch crunch, the engineers worked in seclusion to avoid interruptions.
examples.analytical: The mystic argued that spiritual growth requires a measure of seclusion from the noise of the world.

nuance.analogy: Seclusion is like closing a door on a busy house so you can hear your own thoughts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin seclusio, a shutting off, from secludere.
common_mistakes: Using seclusion for a short break or a single moment alone; it usually describes a longer or deliberate state.
Pronouncing the middle sound as s instead of zh, as in sek-loo-shun.

seclusion.etymology: From Medieval Latin, from Latin *seclusio*, from *secludere*.

senses.definition: Having an inclination to secrecy.
senses.example: She's a secretive girl, not giving away much about her life.

senses.definition: Relating to secretion.
senses.example: The gland's secretive activity increases during digestion, releasing enzymes into the small intestine.

core.definition: Inclined to hide information, feelings or activities from others, or keeping things private and unannounced.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEE, and the middle syllables are reduced to a shortih sound. The r is clearly pronounced in American English, and the ending -tive sounds like tiv.

nuance.connotation: Negative or wary. Calling someone secretive suggests they are hiding something, so it can sound like criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for people who keep plans, feelings or money to themselves, such as 'He's been secretive about the new job.' It is a mild judgment, so say it carefully about a friend or coworker. A softer alternative is 'private' or 'closed-off'.

distinctions.note: Private is neutral and describes a boundary you set for your own life, while secretive suggests you are actively hiding something.
Seclusive describes withdrawing from people, while secretive describes concealing information even if you are around others.

examples.everyday: Why are you being so secretive about your birthday plans?
examples.professional: Leadership has been secretive about the reorganization, so the team is starting to speculate in the hallway.
examples.analytical: Institutions that are secretive about their methods make it harder for the public to evaluate their claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a locked diary with no key on the shelf: the contents exist, but nobody is meant to read them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin secretus, 'set apart, hidden', from secernere, 'to separate'.
common_mistakes: Using secretive when you mean 'secret', as in 'a secretive plan'; a plan is secret, while a person is secretive.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable, SEE.

senses.definition: The property of being sedentary.
The habit of spending most of one's time physically at rest, sitting or lying down, etc. (Includes circumstances of being mentally busy but not physically busy).
The state of being mostly or entirely motionless, stationary.

core.definition: The state of spending most of your time sitting or lying down and getting little physical activity.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable and a secondary stress falls on the -tair syllable. The final -ness is weak, so say it as nus, not nes.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it is usually discussed as a health risk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sedentariness mostly in health, medical, and public-health writing and in formal discussion. In everyday speech people say sitting all day, being inactive, or a sedentary lifestyle. Saying sedentariness in casual conversation can sound stiff or like a doctor's report.

distinctions.note: Inactivity is a general lack of activity, while sedentariness describes a long-term pattern of sitting or lying down.
Laziness is a moral judgment about someone's character, while sedentariness is a neutral description of behavior.
Immobility means being unable to move, often because of injury or illness, whereas sedentariness is a habit that a person can change.

examples.everyday: My doctor pointed to my sedentariness and told me to walk at least thirty minutes a day.
examples.professional: Our wellness committee wants to address sedentariness among staff, since many of our engineers spend most of the day at their desks.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers of technology argue that modern sedentariness is not only a bodily condition but a cultural habit that shapes how we think.

nuance.analogy: Like a car left idle in the driveway, a body that rarely moves gradually loses its readiness.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sedentarius, sitting, from sedere, to sit.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the -tair syllable, as in sed-un-TAIR-ih-nus.
Using sedentariness where a sedentary lifestyle would sound more natural in everyday speech.

senses.definition: To beguile or lure (someone) away from duty, accepted principles, or proper conduct; to lead astray.
senses.example: He was seduced by the promise of easy money and abandoned his principles.

senses.definition: To entice or induce (someone) to engage in a sexual relationship.
senses.example: The novel's narrator describes how the charming stranger tried to seduce her at the party.

senses.definition: To have sexual intercourse with.
senses.example: He had repeatedly seduced the girl in his car, hotels and his home.

senses.definition: To win over or attract.
senses.example: He was seduced by the bright lights and glamor of the city.

core.definition: To lead someone away from what is right or sensible, or to persuade them into a sexual relationship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, DOOS. Americans often make the 'yoo' glide weak or drop it, so it sounds close to 'sih-DOOS'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; often implies manipulation, deception or moral corruption, though it can be used playfully.
