senses.example: The plates were stacked waiting to be cleaned.

senses.definition: Having large breasts.
senses.example: That girl at the party was really stacked.

senses.definition: Having large muscles; buff.
senses.example: He was so stacked from years of lifting that his shirts barely fit.

senses.definition: Wealthy.
senses.example: Her uncle was stacked after selling his software company.

senses.definition: Having a large advantage as a result of accumulating many items and upgrades.
senses.example: By the late game, she was stacked with upgrades and far ahead of everyone.

senses.definition: Unfairly constructed; rigged.
senses.example: a stacked deck of cards

senses.definition: Measured stacked or organized (such as of firewood when in neat stacks), but with gaps between individual pieces.
senses.example: The firewood was stacked loosely along the fence, with gaps between the logs.

senses.definition: Having many skilled players.
senses.example: The indoor soccer league is stacked, so our weekend team barely wins.

core.definition: Arranged in a neat pile or stack, one on top of another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the single syllable. The final -ed is silent in sound, so say 'stakt' with a t sound, not 'stack-ed' with two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the everyday sense. In slang senses, 'stacked' can be a compliment or can sound crude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stacked' for plates, boxes and lists on a table, and in sports and business as in 'a stacked lineup' meaning a very strong team. The slang sense for large breasts or muscular build is informal and can sound rude or sexual, so avoid it at work. For a strong group, 'loaded' is often a safer everyday synonym.

distinctions.note: Piled suggests an unordered heap, while stacked suggests a neat, orderly arrangement.
Loaded can mean full or strong in many senses; stacked emphasizes things placed one on another or a deep roster.

examples.everyday: The dishes are all stacked on the counter, so I need to wash them before dinner.
examples.professional: The stacked bar chart shows monthly revenue split by region, which makes the trend easy to read.
examples.analytical: Stacked ensembles combine the predictions of several base models through a separate meta-learner.

nuance.analogy: Stacked is like pancakes on a plate: each one sits on top of the last, and the pile is neat.
nuance.etymology: From stack plus -ed, from Old Norse stakkr 'haystack'.
common_mistakes: Using the slang meaning ('large breasts') in polite or professional conversation without realizing it can sound rude.
Pronouncing it as two syllables, 'stack-ed'.

senses.definition: Synonym of standard language.
senses.example: Students learning English are taught standard dialect, though many speak regionally.

core.definition: The prestige variety of a language that is taught in schools and used in government, news media, and formal writing.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on DY in 'dialect', and the second word is only lightly stressed. The 'ia' in dialect is usually reduced to a quick 'uh' and not pronounced as two full syllables 'dee-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in linguistics, but in everyday talk it can sound like a judgment that other varieties are less correct.
nuance.usage_note: This is mainly a term in linguistics and education. Americans rarely use it in casual speech, where they would say 'proper English' or simply 'standard English.' Linguists prefer the term to avoid implying that other dialects are defective.

distinctions.note: Standard dialect is the term most often used for the variety in a language, while standard language is the broader term for a codified official form.
A regional accent concerns only pronunciation, while a dialect includes grammar and vocabulary as well.

examples.everyday: Her grandmother speaks a regional dialect at home, but at work she switches to standard dialect.
examples.professional: The style guide asks all external reports to be written in standard dialect, with no slang or regional grammar.
examples.analytical: Calling a variety the standard dialect often reflects the speech of educated urban elites rather than any inherently superior grammar.

nuance.analogy: Think of a standard dialect as the formal dress code of a language: everyone can wear their own clothes, but this one is expected at official events.
nuance.etymology: Standard comes from Anglo-Norman estaundard; dialect comes from Greek dialektos, 'way of speaking'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'dialect' on the first syllable; the stress is on DY.
Using standard dialect to mean 'correct' in a way that implies other dialects are wrong.

senses.definition: Despite the preceding.

core.definition: Nevertheless; even so, despite what was just said.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'all', and 'and' reduces to a quick 'un'. Say it as one smooth phrase, linking the l of 'still' into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it signals a concession before a contrasting point.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in conversation and informal writing to admit a drawback before adding a positive point, as in 'It was expensive; still and all, it was worth it.' It sounds folksy and is more common in the South and in older speech. In formal writing, use 'nevertheless' or 'even so.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I guess so.'

distinctions.note: Nevertheless is more formal and suits writing; still and all is conversational and folksy.
Even so is neutral and common in speech and writing; still and all has a more homespun flavor.

collocations: still and all, I'm glad we went
still and all, it was fun

examples.everyday: The restaurant was crowded and the service was slow; still and all, the pasta was great.
examples.professional: The migration ran over budget and two weeks late; still and all, the new pipeline has cut our reporting errors in half.
examples.analytical: The author's exegesis is often strained; still and all, the book forces readers to confront the text's uncomfortable claims.

nuance.analogy: A tie-breaker added to a sentence to say, 'Okay, but...' and then turn the point around.
nuance.etymology: From the adverb still, meaning nevertheless, with the idiomatic addition and all.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word or as 'still n all'; it is three words.
Using it in very formal writing, where 'nevertheless' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A pain in the abdomen, often caused by indigestion, usually lower than the stomach and related to the intestines.
senses.example: After eating the entire pizza alone, I had a terrible stomachache all night long.

core.definition: A pain in the belly, often from indigestion, eating too much, or a stomach bug.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, STUM. The second syllable is a reduced 'uk', and the word ends with a strong 'ayk' like 'ache'. Do not pronounce the 'ch' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a common, minor ailment and is used casually in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say stomachache for any pain in the belly, and they often say I have a stomachache in casual conversation, especially with children. For a more serious pain, Americans might say stomach pain or abdominal pain. The word is usually spelled as one word in American English.

distinctions.note: Stomachache is the everyday term for a common ache, while stomach pain sounds more medical and can describe more serious or lasting pain.
Nausea is the feeling of wanting to vomit, while a stomachache is a pain in the belly that may or may not come with nausea.

examples.everyday: I ate too much pizza last night and now I have a stomachache.
examples.professional: If you have a stomachache during the flight, please let the flight attendant know.
examples.analytical: Medical notes often describe a child's recurring stomachache as a symptom rather than a diagnosis, which requires further evaluation.

nuance.analogy: A stomachache is like a warning light on the dashboard: it signals that something in the system needs attention.
nuance.etymology: From stomach, from Greek stomachos, plus ache, from Old English æce.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words (stomach ache), which is less common in American spelling.
Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly (STUM-ah-kayk).

conversation.text: I have a stomachache from eating too much candy.
He stayed home from school with a stomachache.
Spicy food sometimes gives me a stomachache.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being stout.
(rare) The result or product of being stout. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The stoutness of the new bridge's pilings reassured engineers after the flood tested the foundation.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The quality of being sturdy or thick in build, or firm and brave in character or resolve.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and use the "ow" of "out." The ending -ness is a weak, reduced syllable, so say "nus" quickly, not as a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when describing a person's body, since it can sound like a polite way of saying "heavy"; positive when describing courage or steadiness of character.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use "stoutness" in everyday speech. For objects, they say "sturdiness" or "solidity"; for a person's body, they would normally say "heavyset" or "big-boned," and for character, "toughness" or "firmness" is more natural. You will mostly meet "stoutness" in older writing or in careful, formal descriptions.

distinctions.note: "Sturdiness" stresses solid strength and durability of physical things; "stoutness" can also describe a person's build or firm character.
"Fatness" is blunt and often hurtful; "stoutness" is gentler and more formal, but still refers to a heavy build.

examples.everyday: Grandpa's stoutness has always made him look like a friendly bear when he hugs us.
examples.professional: The stoutness of the new steel frame lets the rack carry twice the load of the old design.
examples.analytical: Her stoutness of conscience under institutional pressure is the central example in the essay's account of moral courage.

nuance.analogy: Like a thick stone wall: solid, hard to push over, and not easily moved.
nuance.etymology: From stout (adjective) with the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing "stoutness" with "stoutly," the adverb.
Pronouncing the "ou" as "oo" or "oh" instead of the "ow" in "out."

senses.definition: A long, narrow, pliable strip of leather, cloth, or the like.
A strap worn on the shoulder.
senses.example: The strap of her purse kept slipping off her shoulder during the long walk home.

senses.definition: A strip of thick leather used in flogging.
Something made of such a strip, or of a part of one, or a combination of two or more for a particular use. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The backpack's chest strap and hip strap work together to keep the load stable.

senses.definition: A piece of leather, or strip of wood covered with a suitable material, used to hone the sharpened edge of a razor; a strop.
senses.example: My grandfather still sharpened his razor on a leather strap every morning.

senses.definition: A narrow strip of anything, as of iron or brass.
senses.example: The old wooden crate was reinforced with iron straps at each corner.

senses.definition: A band, plate, or loop of metal for clasping and holding timbers or parts of a machine.
senses.example: Metal straps bolted across the rafters held the old barn's frame together.

senses.definition: A gun, normally a personal firearm such as a pistol or machine pistol.
senses.example: The kid in the alley pulled a strap from his jacket and told us to freeze.

senses.definition: A strap-on.
senses.example: Her sex-positive workshop covered toys, lubricant, and how to fit a strap for beginners.

senses.definition: Synonym of strapline.
senses.example: The brand's new strap, Live Brighter Every Day, now appears on every package.

senses.definition: A championship belt, or by extension, the title.
senses.example: He won the heavyweight strap after knocking out the defending champion in round nine.

senses.definition: An investment strategy involving simultaneous trade with one put and two call options on the same security at the same strike price, similar to but more bullish than a straddle.
senses.example: She placed a strap on the stock, buying one put and two calls at the same strike.

senses.definition: A piece of rope or metal passing around a block and used for fastening it to anything.
senses.example: The sailor ran a strap around the pulley block and secured it to the mast.

senses.definition: The flat part of the corolla in ligulate florets, as those of the white circle in the daisy.
senses.example: In the daisy, each white strap of the ray florets is actually a single petal.

senses.definition: The leaf, exclusive of its sheath, in some grasses.
senses.example: In this grass, the strap extends well beyond the sheath that wraps the stem.

senses.definition: To beat or chastise with a strap; to whip, to lash.
senses.example: His father would strap him with a belt whenever he lied.

senses.definition: To fasten or bind with a strap.
senses.example: I strapped my son into the back seat.

senses.definition: To sharpen by rubbing on a strap; to strop.
senses.example: to strap a razor

senses.definition: To slap or stroke the muscled areas of a horse with a cloth or pad, a form of massage meant to improve muscle tone.
senses.example: Before the show, the groomer straps the horse's neck to loosen the muscles.

core.definition: A narrow strip of leather, cloth or nylon used to hold, fasten or carry something.

pronunciation.tip: One short syllable. The r is clear, and the vowel is the short a of 'cat'. Do not add a vowel after the p.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names an everyday object and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use strap for watches, bags and car seats: 'The strap on my watch broke.' As a verb, 'strap in' is common for buckling a child into a car seat or an airplane seat. The sense of beating someone with a strap is rare and historical.

distinctions.note: A belt goes around the waist to hold pants; a strap is a narrower band for bags, watches or harnesses.
A band is usually a continuous loop or wider piece, like a watch band or rubber band; strap is often adjustable.

examples.everyday: Hold on, my bag strap just snapped.
examples.professional: Please check the strap connector before you mount the sensor.
examples.analytical: The strap of the bag becomes a symbol of the traveler's burden.

nuance.analogy: A strap is like a thin ribbon of leather that holds things together, like a belt for a backpack.
nuance.etymology: Middle English strappe, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'strap' for a long belt for pants; use belt for waist wear.
Confusing strap with stripe, which has a different vowel and meaning.

strap.etymology: From a variant of earlier *strope* (“loop on a harness”), from Middle English *strope*, *stroppe*, from Late Old English *strop*, *stropp* (“a band, thong, strap; oar-thong”) and Old French *estrope* (“strap, loop on a harness”), both from Latin…

senses.definition: The science and art of military command as applied to the overall planning and conduct of warfare.
senses.example: The general's strategy relied on surprising the enemy at dawn.

senses.definition: A plan of action intended to accomplish a specific goal.
senses.example: Oftentimes, the very simple strategies pay very great dividends.

senses.definition: The act of strategizing; the development of effective strategies.
senses.example: Our team spent the afternoon on strategy for next quarter's product launch.

core.definition: A carefully planned, overall approach designed to reach an important goal, rather than a single action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, STRAT. The second and third syllables are reduced, and the final 'y' sounds like a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It implies thoughtful planning, though it can sound like jargon in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it everywhere, from business and sports to family life, as in 'our strategy for saving money'. In casual talk people might say 'plan' or 'approach' instead. A strategy is the big picture; a single step within it is usually called a tactic or move.

distinctions.note: A tactic is a specific method or move used within a strategy; a strategy is the overall plan that guides the tactics.
A plan is any set of intended steps; a strategy is a plan built around a large goal and the choices needed to reach it.
A goal is what you want to achieve; a strategy is how you intend to achieve it.

examples.everyday: Our strategy for the kids is to keep bedtime boring and quick, and it actually works.
examples.professional: Our go-to-market strategy depends on partnering with regional distributors in the first year.
examples.analytical: Kant rejected the strategy of judging actions by their likely results, insisting instead on the moral law.

nuance.analogy: Like a route on a map, while tactics are the turns you make along the way.
nuance.etymology: From Greek strategia, 'generalship', from strategos, 'general', from stratos, 'army' + agein, 'to lead'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'strategy' with 'tactic', which is a single method inside a larger strategy.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress falls on STRAT, not on 'jee'.

strategy.etymology: Latin *stratēgia*, from Ancient Greek *στρατηγία* (“office of general, command, generalship”), from *στρατηγός* (“the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from *στρατός* (“army”) + *ἄγω* (“to lead, conduct”).

senses.definition: Formed, as in opinions, based upon a person's feelings or intuition, rather than upon observation or purely logical reasoning; coming more from within the observer than from observations of the external environment.
senses.example: Her decision to leave the job was subjective, based on a feeling rather than any data.

senses.definition: Pertaining to subjects as opposed to objects (A subject is one who perceives or is aware; an object is the thing perceived or the thing that the subject is aware of.)
senses.example: Philosophers distinguish the subjective self, which perceives, from the objective world it perceives.

senses.definition: Resulting from or pertaining to personal mindsets or experience, arising from perceptive mental conditions within the brain and not necessarily or directly from external stimuli.
senses.example: The migraine caused subjective sensations of light that no scanner could detect.

senses.definition: Lacking in reality or substance.
senses.example: The dreamlike city in his novel felt subjective, a place without any real substance.

senses.definition: As used by Carl Jung, the innate worldview orientation of the introverted personality types.
senses.example: In Jung's typology, an introvert's subjective orientation turns attention inward toward the self.

senses.definition: Mind-dependent.
senses.example: Some philosophers argue that color is subjective, existing only as a property of minds.

senses.definition: Experienced by a person mentally and not directly verifiable by others.
senses.example: Her memory of the accident is subjective, so the investigators relied on other witnesses.

senses.definition: Describing conjugation of a verb that indicates only the subject (agent), not indicating the object (patient) of the action. (In linguistic descriptions of Tundra Nenets, among others.)
senses.example: In this linguistics paper, the verb form is subjective, marking only the agent of the action.

senses.definition: The subjective case.
senses.example: The textbook explains that the subjective is used for the doer of an action.

senses.definition: A noun or pronoun in the subjective case.
senses.example: The pronoun they is a subjective in that sentence, not an object.

core.definition: Based on personal feelings, opinions, or experience rather than on facts that can be checked or measured.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JEK. The final syllable is a short tiv, with the vowel close to the i in sit, and the word does not end in a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It often implies that a judgment may be biased, but it is a normal word in professional and academic talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subjective often in meetings, reviews, and debates to say that an opinion depends on personal taste or interpretation. It is not rude, but calling someone's view subjective can imply it lacks objective support. A natural reply is that it is a fair point or that the data can help settle it.

distinctions.note: Objective refers to facts independent of personal feelings, while subjective refers to what comes from the observer's own mind.
Personal describes something belonging to a person, while subjective describes a judgment shaped by personal perception.

examples.everyday: Which movie is better is pretty subjective, so I think it depends on what you like.
examples.professional: The design review is subjective, so let's add measurable criteria before we pick the final layout.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that our experience of space and time is subjective in origin, yet still universally structured.

nuance.analogy: Like tasting a dish: the flavor is real, but how it tastes depends on the person eating it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin subjectivus, from subjectum, the thing placed under, as in the subject of thought.
common_mistakes: Confusing subjective with subjected; subjective is an adjective about personal judgment.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying suhb-JEK-tiv with a weak middle or a long final ee.

senses.definition: The party acting on behalf of the subrogor in a subrogation.

core.definition: The party, usually an insurer, that pays a claim and takes over the right to recover the amount from a third party responsible for the loss.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GEE, the last syllable, and the r is clearly pronounced. The middle syllables reduce to a light 'ruh,' so avoid making the word sound like 'sub-ro-GAY.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise legal and insurance term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subrogee in insurance, law, and claims settlement, especially in discussions of auto or property claims. Adjusters and lawyers say it to explain who may pursue recovery. In everyday talk people say 'the insurance company can go after the other driver's insurance.'

distinctions.note: The subrogee is the party who steps into another's rights and pursues recovery; the subrogor is the party whose rights are transferred.
An assignee receives rights by voluntary transfer; a subrogee acquires rights by law or by paying a debt on another's behalf.

examples.everyday: The adjuster said that since they paid for my car, they are now the subrogee and can chase the other driver's insurance for the money.
examples.professional: As subrogee, our carrier can pursue the at-fault party's insurer for the full amount we paid under the policy.
examples.analytical: A subrogee takes no greater rights than the subrogor possessed, so any defense good against the subrogor is equally good against the subrogee.

nuance.analogy: The subrogee is like a friend who pays your bill and then takes over your place in line to ask the store for a refund.
nuance.etymology: From subrogate, from Latin subrogare, 'to choose as a substitute,' with the -ee ending for the one who receives the right.
common_mistakes: Confusing subrogee with subrogor, since the two words look alike and have opposite roles.
Stressing the first syllable and pronouncing the word as SUB-ruh-jee.

senses.definition: Real being; existence.
senses.example: Medieval theologians debated whether evil has any true subsistence or is merely the absence of good.

senses.definition: The act of maintaining oneself at a minimum level.
senses.example: Many farmers in the region barely earned enough for subsistence after paying rent and seed costs.

senses.definition: Inherency.
senses.example: the subsistence of qualities in bodies

senses.definition: Something (food, water, money, etc.) that is required to stay alive.
Embodiment or personification or hypostasis of an underlying principle or quality.
senses.example: In the Trinitarian debate, the Council defined the Son as a distinct subsistence within the one divine essence.

core.definition: The condition of having just enough food, money, or resources to stay alive, with little or nothing left over.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SIS. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -ence is reduced to 'uns', not 'ents'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somber. It describes a basic, often difficult level of existence, sometimes with sympathy for those who live that way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subsistence most often in economics, geography, and development discussions, as in subsistence farming or subsistence living. In everyday speech they might say barely getting by or living paycheck to paycheck. The word is somewhat formal, and it carries a sense of hardship, so avoid it when describing a comfortable lifestyle.

distinctions.note: Survival is the general fact of staying alive, while subsistence specifically refers to the minimum resources needed to keep going day to day.
Livelihood means the way someone earns a living, while subsistence means the minimal level of support needed to survive, often without surplus.

examples.everyday: After the factory closed, my uncle's family lived on a bare subsistence until he found new work.
examples.professional: The report shows that many rural households depend on subsistence farming and have little access to markets.
examples.analytical: Marx distinguished between wages that cover mere subsistence and those that reflect the value a worker truly produces.

nuance.analogy: Subsistence is like a boat with just enough fuel to reach the next shore, with no spare to waste.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subsistere, meaning to stand firm or remain, from sub- (under) and sistere (to stand).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Using subsistence to mean existence in general rather than minimal survival.

subsistence.etymology: From Middle English *subsistence*; partly from Middle French *subsistence* and partly from its etymon Late Latin *subsistentia* (“substance, reality, in Medieval Latin also stability”), from Latin *subsistēns*, present participle of *subsistō* (“to…

senses.definition: A person or animal that sucks, especially a breast or udder; especially a suckling animal, young mammal before it is weaned.
senses.example: The farmer's piglet was the smallest sucker in the litter and needed extra feeding.

senses.definition: An undesired stem growing out of the roots or lower trunk of a shrub or tree, especially from the rootstock of a grafted plant or tree.
senses.example: The gardener cut off every sucker growing from the base of the rose bush.

senses.definition: A parasite; a sponger.
senses.example: That cousin is a sucker who has lived off his brother's paycheck for years.

senses.definition: An organ or body part that does the sucking; especially a round structure on the bodies of some insects, frogs, and octopuses that allows them to stick to surfaces.
senses.example: The octopus used each sucker along its arms to grip the smooth glass wall.

senses.definition: A thing that works by sucking something.
senses.example: The shop vacuum's sucker clogged with wet sawdust during the basement cleanup this weekend.

senses.definition: The embolus, or bucket, of a pump; also, the valve of a pump basket.
senses.example: Replace the worn sucker in the well pump before winter sets in and the water freezes.

senses.definition: A pipe through which anything is drawn.
senses.example: A long sucker ran from the storage tank down into the sump in the basement.

senses.definition: A small piece of leather, usually round, having a string attached to the center, which, when saturated with water and pressed upon a stone or other body having a smooth surface, adheres, by reason of the atmospheric pressure, with such force as to enable a considerable weight to be thus lifted by the string; formerly used by children as a plaything.
senses.example: As kids we played with a leather sucker that stuck to the kitchen tiles.

senses.definition: An animal such as the octopus and remora, which adhere to other bodies with such organs.
senses.example: Divers spotted a remora, a sucker clinging to the belly of a passing shark.

senses.definition: Any fish in the family Catostomidae of North America and eastern Asia, which have mouths modified into downward-pointing, suckerlike structures for feeding in bottom sediments.
senses.example: Anglers in the river often catch a sucker feeding along the muddy bottom.

senses.definition: A lollipop; a piece of candy which is sucked.
senses.example: She licked the cherry sucker slowly while watching cartoons on Saturday morning.

senses.definition: A person who is easily deceived, tricked or persuaded to do something; a naive or gullible person.
senses.example: One poor sucker had actually given her his life’s savings.

senses.definition: A person irresistibly attracted by something specified.
senses.example: I'm a sucker for ghost stories.

senses.definition: Any thing or object.
senses.example: See if you can get that sucker working again.

senses.definition: A person.
To strip the suckers or shoots from; to deprive of suckers.
senses.example: to sucker maize

senses.definition: To produce suckers; to throw up additional stems or shoots.
senses.example: The old apple tree began to sucker after the hard winter pruning.

senses.definition: To move or attach oneself by means of suckers.
senses.example: The octopus suckers onto the rock and waits patiently for crabs to pass by.

senses.definition: To fool someone; to take advantage of someone.
senses.example: The salesman suckered him into signing an expensive maintenance contract.

senses.definition: To lure someone.
senses.example: Those ads are designed to sucker shoppers into buying overpriced extended warranties.

core.definition: A person who is easily fooled or cheated; a gullible person who pays too much or falls for a trick.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak, r-colored schwa, so don't say 'suck-ah' with a strong vowel. Keep the final 'k' crisp.

nuance.connotation: Negative and mildly insulting; it implies someone was naive. Used playfully among friends it can be a joke about yourself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sucker' in casual talk when someone was taken advantage of, as in 'I paid full price for that, what a sucker.' Calling another person a sucker to their face is an insult, so use it about yourself or about a situation. The word also means a lollipop, and 'I'm a sucker for...' means you really love something, as in 'I'm a sucker for chocolate.'

distinctions.note: A dupe is someone deliberately tricked, a more formal word; a sucker is a casual, slangy word for someone who is easily taken in.
A pushover is someone who gives in easily to others; a sucker is someone who gets cheated or pays too much.

collocations: fall for it like a sucker

examples.everyday: I paid forty dollars for that gadget and it broke in a day, what a sucker I was.
examples.professional: We were suckers to sign that vendor contract without reading the penalty clause.
examples.analytical: A sucker is usually someone who accepts a bad deal because the terms seem to reward him, and that appearance is what makes the con work.

nuance.analogy: Like a fish that bites the hook because the bait looks too good to pass up.
nuance.etymology: From suck (verb) plus -er; 'suck' comes from Old English sūcan, to draw in with the mouth.
common_mistakes: Using 'suckers' as a verb form; 'sucker' is a noun, so say 'it sucks', not 'it suckers'.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'er' with a strong vowel instead of a reduced American r-schwa.

senses.definition: Acquiescence or tacit compliance with some circumstance, behavior, or instruction.
senses.example: The landlord tolerated the noisy tenants only on sufferance, never out of real approval.

core.definition: Reluctant tolerance; permission to stay or act granted grudgingly, without real approval.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'er' is a quick, weak vowel, and the ending is a soft 'uns' rather than a full 'ance' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cool; it implies that someone is tolerated rather than welcomed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'sufferance' outside the phrases 'on sufferance' and 'by sufferance,' which mean tolerated reluctantly or allowed without real approval. At work, someone might joke, 'I'm here on sufferance until the audit ends.' It sounds formal and a little literary, so in everyday speech people say 'tolerated' or 'put up with.'

distinctions.note: Tolerance is a general willingness to accept differences; sufferance is a grudging allowance of something that might otherwise be forbidden.
Suffering means pain or distress; sufferance is about permission or toleration, not pain.
Permission is formal approval; sufferance is allowance without approval.

examples.everyday: My brother lets me borrow his truck, but only on sufferance, so I always fill the gas tank.
examples.professional: The new manager accepted the old team's process only on sufferance until the audit is finished.
examples.analytical: Many of the early women scholars were admitted to the seminar on sufferance rather than as full participants.

nuance.analogy: Sufferance is like a guest who is allowed into the house but never given a key.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'suffrance,' from Latin 'sufferre,' meaning to endure.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sufferance' with 'suffering'; sufferance means tolerance, not pain.
Misspelling it as 'sufference'; the correct spelling is 'sufferance.'

sufferance.etymology: From Middle English *sufferaunce*, from Anglo-Norman *suffraunce*, from Late Latin *sufferentia*.

senses.definition: A statement P in relation to statement Q such that P implies Q.
senses.example: In logic, being a square is a sufficient condition for being a rectangle.

core.definition: A condition whose truth guarantees that a given outcome holds: if P is a sufficient condition for Q, then P implies Q, though Q may hold without P.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FISH in sufficient and on DISH in condition, and both final syllables are reduced. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', and the first syllable is not stressed as in 'suf-FI-cient'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge, used in logic, mathematics and philosophy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in logic, math, computer science and philosophy courses, and in proofs or research papers. It is not used in casual conversation. In everyday speech, Americans say 'enough' or 'is all you need' instead. Do not confuse it with 'necessary condition' when explaining an argument.

distinctions.note: If P is necessary for Q, then Q implies P. If P is sufficient for Q, then P implies Q. A necessary and sufficient condition is a biconditional.
Enough is an everyday word for having what is needed. Sufficient condition is a technical term for a logical relationship between statements.

collocations: show that P is a sufficient condition

examples.everyday: Having a valid ticket is a sufficient condition for getting into the concert, so you don't need anything else.
examples.professional: In our fraud model, a balance change over fifty thousand dollars is a sufficient condition for flagging the transaction for review.
examples.analytical: If P is a sufficient condition for Q, then whenever P holds, Q must hold, although Q may hold in cases where P does not.

nuance.analogy: A key that opens a particular door is a sufficient condition for entering that room, but it is not the only way in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sufficiens, from sufficere, 'to be enough'.
common_mistakes: Confusing sufficient condition with necessary condition, which reverses the direction of implication.
Saying 'sufficient condition is required', when a sufficient condition guarantees the result but is not required for it.

senses.definition: A category in accounting records for irregular or miscellaneous items not otherwise classified.
senses.example: The accountant booked the $340 in office supplies and parking fees under sundries.

core.definition: Small miscellaneous items sold in a store, such as toiletries, household goods, and personal products.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SUN, and the final syllable is the diphthong of 'dries', not 'dree'. Keep the r clear after d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes ordinary store merchandise and, in accounting, a miscellaneous catch-all line.
nuance.usage_note: In American stores, sundries is a practical word for small household or personal items sold at drugstores, convenience stores, and hotel shops. In accounting, sundries is a catch-all line for minor or unclassified items. Americans usually say 'the sundries aisle' in stores and 'miscellaneous expenses' in formal financial reports.

distinctions.note: Sundry is an adjective meaning various or miscellaneous, while sundries is the plural noun for those items.
Toiletries names one specific group of items, while sundries is a broader store category.
Notions is an American term for small sewing supplies, a narrower category than sundries.

examples.everyday: I stopped at the drugstore for a few sundries: shampoo, batteries, and a birthday card.
examples.professional: The sundries line on the income statement grew after we added the new retail channel.
examples.analytical: Accounting treats sundries as a catch-all category, so auditors often review that line closely for misclassified expenses.

nuance.analogy: Sundries are like the junk drawer of a store's accounts, holding the useful things that do not fit anywhere else.
nuance.etymology: From sundry, from Old English syndrig, meaning separate or various.
common_mistakes: Using sundries as a singular noun, as in 'a sundries'; it is normally plural.
Confusing the noun sundries with the adjective sundry, which describes things.

senses.definition: A high-level class that passes attributes and methods down the hierarchy to subclasses.
senses.example: In our code, the Vehicle superclass defines methods that every Car and Truck subclass inherits.

senses.definition: A taxon ranking below a phylum and above a class.
senses.example: Biologists classify the mammals within the superclass Tetrapoda, which also includes amphibians and reptiles.

senses.definition: To create a superclass of.
senses.example: The team decided to superclass the existing Shape class so that circles and squares could share code.

core.definition: In object-oriented programming, a class from which other classes inherit attributes and methods; a parent class.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SUP, and the second syllable is a reduced er. The final syllable is the short a of 'cat', so say 'klass', not 'klahs'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In American software engineering, people say superclass in Java and C++ discussions, but Python developers more often say base class or parent class. In biology, superclass is a taxonomic rank, but in everyday speech it is rare. When a colleague asks about inheritance, a natural reply is 'The subclass inherits from the superclass.'

distinctions.note: Base class is common in Python and C++, while superclass is the typical term in Java and in general object-oriented writing; both mean the parent class.
A subclass inherits from a superclass, so the two terms describe opposite positions in the hierarchy.

examples.everyday: My cousin is learning to code, and she keeps asking about superclasses.
examples.professional: Let's move the shared validation logic into the superclass so each subclass doesn't repeat it.
examples.analytical: Designing a superclass requires a clear abstraction, because a poorly chosen parent class forces subclasses to inherit behavior they do not need.

nuance.analogy: A superclass is like a family recipe that each child adapts, so every version shares the core steps but adds its own changes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin super, above, and class, from Latin classis, a division or group.
common_mistakes: Using superclass in Python conversations, where base class is more common.
Stressing the second syllable; the main stress is on SU, as in SOO-per.

senses.definition: To go beyond or exceed (something) in an adjudicative or literal sense.
senses.example: The former problem student surpassed his instructor's expectations and scored top marks on his examination.

core.definition: To be better than or greater than something or someone else, to exceed a standard or expectation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PASS, with the short "a" as in "cat". The first syllable is a reduced, rhotic "ur".

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone or something for exceeding a standard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use surpass in business reports, reviews and praise, and it sounds natural in everyday speech too. For casual talk, beat or top is more common. Surpass works especially well with abstract nouns like expectations, goals or records.

distinctions.note: Beat is informal and often used for competitions; surpass suggests exceeding a standard or expectation.
Exceed is very close in meaning and is slightly more neutral and measurable.

examples.everyday: Her lasagna surpasses anything we've ever ordered from that Italian place.
examples.professional: Our new model surpassed the baseline accuracy by five points in the final evaluation.
examples.analytical: The argument surpasses earlier theodicies in its precision, though it still leaves the central question unresolved.

nuance.analogy: To surpass someone is like passing a runner on a track: you move ahead of them and keep going.
nuance.etymology: From Old French surpasser, from sur- ("over") and passer ("to pass").
common_mistakes: Using surpass with a preposition such as "to"; say surpass someone directly.
Pronouncing the vowel as "sir-PAHS" instead of the short "a" in "cat".

senses.definition: In a swift manner; quickly; with quick motion or velocity; fleetly.
senses.example: The ambulance arrived swiftly, and the paramedics stabilized her before the ride to the hospital.

core.definition: Quickly and with speed; in a fast, prompt and efficient manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ly is a light, reduced ee sound, not a long i like in lie.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Suggests efficiency and grace, often in news or formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say quickly or fast in everyday talk. Swiftly sounds formal or literary, as in The police acted swiftly. Use it in a letter, a report or a sermon, not in casual chats with friends.

distinctions.note: Quickly is the everyday word; swiftly is more formal and suggests smooth, graceful speed.
Rapidly often describes change or growth over time; swiftly usually describes action or movement.

examples.everyday: Thanks for answering so swiftly, I was really worried.
examples.professional: Our security team acted swiftly to contain the breach and notify customers.
examples.analytical: The psalmist pictures God's word running swiftly across the earth, a sign of its unhindered and effective action.

nuance.analogy: Like a swift bird that cuts through the air without effort, it moves quickly and cleanly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English swift, moving quickly, with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using swiftly in casual conversation where quickly is natural
Stressing the second syllable, saying swift-LEE instead of SWIFT-lee
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind the idea of rapid movement is ruts, meaning to run or hasten. Psalm 147:15 says God's word runs swiftly over the earth, describing the speed and effectiveness of his command rather than defining the adverb itself.

swiftly.etymology: From Middle English *swiftly*, *swyftely*, *swiftliche*, from Old English *swiftlīċe* (“swiftly”), equivalent to *swift* + *-ly*.

senses.definition: One who or that which synchronizes.
senses.example: As the lead engineer, she served as the synchronizer for all three development teams.

senses.definition: Part of a synchromesh manual transmission that allows the smooth engagement of gears.
senses.example: The worn synchronizer made second gear grind every time I shifted on cold mornings.

senses.definition: A device that permits an automatic weapon to fire between the blades of a revolving propeller.
senses.example: The synchronizer let the fighter's machine guns fire cleanly between the spinning propeller blades.

senses.definition: A kind of arbiter.
senses.example: Her role as synchronizer between the union and management kept negotiations from collapsing.

senses.definition: A device for aligning multiple film strips in a replay or editing device.
senses.example: The projectionist used a synchronizer to line up the sound and picture reels before splicing.

senses.definition: An algorithm that can be applied to a synchronous distributed algorithm to produce a version that operates in asynchronous networks.
senses.example: The researchers applied a synchronizer to convert their protocol so it runs on asynchronous networks.

core.definition: A device or part that brings two moving things to the same speed or timing, such as the gear-matching part in a manual transmission.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SINGK, and reduce the middle syllable to ruh. The -er ending is a rhotic American r, not a separate ah sound. Keep the -nyz- part as one clear syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term for a mechanical or electronic part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use synchronizer in car repair, auto shops and mechanical engineering, where it refers to the part in a manual transmission that matches gear speeds. People in car talk also say synchro as a short form. In computing or media work the word refers to any system that aligns timing.

distinctions.note: Synchro is an informal short form of synchronizer that is common among mechanics and drivers.
The clutch disconnects the engine from the transmission so you can shift; the synchronizer matches gear speeds so the gears engage smoothly.
A timer measures or triggers events by time, while a synchronizer makes two or more moving things match in speed or timing.

examples.everyday: The gears grind when I shift into second, so the mechanic says the synchronizer is worn.
examples.professional: The firmware acts as a synchronizer between the sensor feeds, so every frame shares one timestamp.
examples.analytical: In this framework a synchronizer is a construct that aligns independent event streams so that causal order can be inferred.

nuance.analogy: Like a brake that slows two spinning wheels to the same speed so they can lock together without a jolt.
nuance.etymology: From synchronize, from Greek syn-, 'together,' and chronos, 'time,' plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as sin-kruh-NY-zer.
Confusing synchronizer with synchronicity, which refers to a meaningful coincidence or a concept in the work of Carl Jung.

senses.definition: An archetypal pairing of contrasexual opposites, symbolizing the communication of the conscious and unconscious minds.
senses.example: Jung's theory of syzygy describes the paired contrasexual figures that mediate between conscious and unconscious.

senses.definition: A relation between generators of a module.
senses.example: We computed the syzygies among the generators of the module using a computer algebra system.

senses.definition: The pairing of chromosomes in meiosis.
senses.example: During prophase I, each homologous chromosome finds its partner in a precise syzygy.

senses.definition: Complementary female–male pairings of the emanations known as Eons.
senses.example: In Valentinian Gnosticism, each Aeon's syzygy completes the divine pleroma as a male-female pair.

senses.definition: An alignment of three celestial bodies (for example, the Sun, Earth, and Moon) such that one body is directly between the other two, such as occurs at an eclipse.
The fusion of some or all of the organs.
senses.example: Botanists described the syzygy of the sepals as a single fused cup in the specimen.

senses.definition: The association of two protozoa end-to-end or laterally for the purpose of asexual exchange of genetic material.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the paramecia formed a syzygy, exchanging genetic material side by side.

core.definition: An alignment of three or more celestial bodies in a straight line, such as the Sun, Earth, and Moon during a full or new moon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SIZ. The g is pronounced like the j in judge, and the final syllable is a light ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term, and it is rarely used outside astronomy or specialized writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in astronomy classes, science writing, or discussions of eclipses and tides. Outside science it is rare, though in Jungian psychology it names a paired inner and outer principle. In everyday talk, people usually say 'lining up' or 'alignment.'

distinctions.note: A conjunction in astronomy means two bodies appear close together in the sky, while a syzygy specifically means three or more bodies lined up.
Alignment is a general word for things in a line, while syzygy is a precise astronomical term.

examples.everyday: The tides are unusually high this week because the Sun and Moon are in syzygy.
examples.professional: Our tide model needs to be recalibrated during syzygy, when the gravitational pull combines.
examples.analytical: In astronomy, syzygy marks the moments when the Sun, Earth, and Moon form a line, which explains the strongest tides.

nuance.analogy: A syzygy is like three people standing in a perfectly straight line with a flashlight, so the shadow falls on one person behind them.
nuance.etymology: From Greek suzugia, 'yoking together,' from sun, 'together,' and zugon, 'yoke.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'sigh-zee' with a long i; the first vowel is short, as in SIZ.
Using it as a synonym for any kind of pairing or relationship in everyday English.

syzygy.etymology: From Late Latin *sȳzygia* (“a conjunction”), from Ancient Greek *συζυγία* (“a union, a yoke, a pair”).

core.definition: A Canaanite city in the plain of Esdraelon, assigned to the tribe of Manasseh, near the city of Megiddo.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TAY. The middle syllable is a reduced uh, and the final ch is pronounced as a k sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical place name used in scholarly and religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name in Bible study, historical geography, or archaeology. It is not used in everyday conversation. In a sermon or Bible class, speakers pronounce it TAY-uh-nak.

distinctions.note: Megiddo is a nearby city, and Taanach is a separate Canaanite site, though the two are often mentioned together in the Old Testament.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got stuck on the name Taanach, so we looked it up on a map.
examples.professional: In the seminar, I'll present a short overview of Taanach and its role in the Manasseh allotment.
examples.analytical: The reference to Taanach beside Megiddo in Judges 5:19 suggests that the battle was fought in the plain controlled by both cities.

nuance.analogy: Taanach is like a small town on a map of the old Israelite territories, important mainly because it sits near the larger city of Megiddo.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ta'anakh, a Canaanite place name whose meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tah-AHN-ack' with the stress on the second syllable.
Confusing Taanach with Megiddo, which is a more famous nearby city.
nuance.biblical_note: Taanach (Hebrew Ta'anakh) is a Canaanite royal city in the north, within the territory allotted to the half-tribe of Manasseh. Joshua 12:21 lists its king among the Canaanite kings defeated under Joshua. Joshua 17:11 counts Taanach among Manasseh's towns that were inside Issachar and Asher's borders, though Manasseh could not fully take them. Judges 5:19 places the battle of Deborah and Barak near the waters of Megiddo, with the kings of Taanach fighting against Israel, showing its strategic role.

senses.definition: The state of being tabescent.

core.definition: The state of wasting away gradually, becoming thin and weak, often from illness or prolonged decline.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, BES. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, so do not say 'tab' with a clear a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes decline and loss of flesh, so it sounds grave and clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Rare in everyday American speech. It appears in literary criticism, older medical writing and formal essays about illness, decay or mortality. Americans would normally say wasting away, emaciation or decline, which are more natural in conversation.
word_family: tabes (noun, Latin root, medical term for wasting)

distinctions.note: Emaciation is the common medical term for extreme thinness; tabescence is a more literary word for the gradual process of wasting away.
Atrophy refers to a specific organ or muscle shrinking from disuse or disease; tabescence describes the whole body or person wasting away.

examples.professional: The clinical report describes a six-month tabescence of muscle mass that the team attributed to the disease.
examples.analytical: Her essay reads the tabescence of the body as a figure for mortality, tracing how decay becomes a moral image.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle slowly burning down until only a stub remains, tabescence is a gradual wasting that leaves less and less behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tabescere, to waste away or melt, related to tabes, wasting.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'tab-ESS-cence' with stress on the first syllable instead of the second.
Using it for quick weight loss; it implies gradual, progressive wasting over time.

related: tabes (noun, Latin root, medical term for wasting)

senses.definition: To go about something slowly and carefully or at one's own pace.
senses.example: Take your time — there's no need to rush.

senses.definition: To take more time to do something than is considered acceptable.
senses.example: You sure took your time getting here!

core.definition: To do something slowly and carefully at your own pace, without rushing, and without feeling pressure to finish quickly.

pronunciation.tip: Your is weak in speech and often sounds like yer. Stress falls on time, and the final m should be clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reassuring when meant kindly; it can sound sarcastic if someone is being slow and frustrating.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to reassure someone who is working, reading, or deciding, as in 'Take your time, there's no rush.' If you say it with an edge, it sounds sarcastic about someone being slow. A natural reply is 'Thanks, I'll be quick' or 'Thanks, I appreciate it.'

distinctions.note: Casual reassurance that stresses there is no deadline, while take your time more directly invites slow, careful work.
A formal adjective describing a slow pace; Americans rarely use it in casual talk.

collocations: take your time reading the contract

examples.everyday: Take your time with the dishes; I'm not going anywhere.
examples.professional: Take your time reviewing the draft; the client deadline isn't until Friday.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of patience argue that real understanding requires that we take our time with a text rather than skim it for conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Like walking through a quiet museum with no closing bell in sight.
nuance.etymology: Time comes from Old English tīma, meaning a point or period of time.
common_mistakes: Making time plural or dropping your, as in take times, which sounds unnatural.
Using take your time as a command when someone is already late; it sounds sarcastic in that situation.

senses.definition: A bathing suit composed of a tank top and the lower half of a bikini.

core.definition: A women's two-piece swimsuit with a loose tank-top style top and bikini-cut bottoms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, KEE. The n before the k changes to an 'ng' sound, so start with 'tang', not 'tan'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests practical, modest coverage and comfort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans wear tankinis at pools, beaches, and resorts, especially for more coverage than a bikini gives. Stores often sell the top and bottoms separately, so ask for 'a tankini top' or 'a tankini set'. It is a women's term; men usually wear swim trunks or board shorts. Saying 'tankini' in a store is natural and easily understood.

distinctions.note: A bikini has two small pieces with minimal coverage; a tankini adds a longer top that covers the midriff.
A one-piece is a single garment; a tankini has two pieces, but the top overlaps the bottoms for fuller coverage.

examples.everyday: I wore a tankini to the lake because I didn't want to deal with sunburn on my stomach.
examples.professional: The swimwear buyer says tankini sales rose in our midsize stores this spring.
examples.analytical: The rise of the tankini reflects a modest-swimwear trend that balances fashion, religious custom, and personal comfort.

nuance.analogy: Like a tank top and bikini bottoms combined into one swim outfit.
nuance.etymology: A blend of tank top and bikini.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (TAN-kee-nee); the stress is on KEE: tang-KEE-nee.
Asking for a 'tank' or 'bikini top' in a store; ask for a tankini top or a tankini set.

senses.definition: An Aramaic translation of the Tanakh written or compiled between the Second Temple period and the early Middle Ages.
senses.example: Our seminar read a targum of Isaiah alongside the Hebrew text to see how early readers interpreted it.

core.definition: An Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible, prepared for synagogue reading and explanation in Jewish communities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TAR, with a hard g and a reduced final syllable. The Hebrew plural is Targumim, so do not add a plural s when speaking about several Targums.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a scholarly term used in religious and historical study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Targum mainly in academic Bible study, Jewish studies, and religious history. Speakers usually refer to a particular Targum, such as Targum Onqelos. In general conversation people would say 'Aramaic translation' instead, which is clearer for non-specialists.

distinctions.note: The Septuagint is a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible; a Targum is an Aramaic translation or paraphrase.
The Vulgate is Jerome's Latin translation used in the Roman Catholic Church; a Targum is Aramaic and Jewish in origin.

examples.everyday: My friend in the Jewish studies class said the Targum was read aloud in synagogues where people did not speak Hebrew.
examples.professional: Our seminar compared the Targum with the Septuagint to see how each rendered difficult Hebrew passages.
examples.analytical: The Targum often expands the Hebrew with interpretation, so the translator's theology shows in the choice of words.

nuance.analogy: Like a live interpreter at a conference who translates a speech and adds clarifying explanations as they go.
nuance.etymology: From Aramaic and Hebrew targum, meaning translation or interpretation.
common_mistakes: Using Targum as a plural; the Hebrew plural is Targumim, though English speakers often say Targums.
Confusing Targum with the Septuagint or Vulgate, which are different translations.
nuance.biblical_note: The Targum connects with Nehemiah 8:8, where Ezra and the Levites read the law and gave the sense so that the people understood the reading. Jewish tradition sees this as the start of the practice of translation and explanation. Ezra 4:8 through 6:18 and Ezra 7:12-26 are written in Aramaic, the language of the Targum. The Targum is not part of the Christian canon but is important for understanding the Hebrew Bible's reception.

senses.definition: A woman who assigns tasks; a female overseer.

core.definition: A woman who assigns tasks to others and oversees how they are done, often in a demanding or bossy way.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on TASK, with a weaker stress on mis. The final -ess is an unstressed schwa-s sound, not the full ess of less.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly teasing; it suggests strictness and an eagerness to give orders.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly say taskmaster for both men and women, so taskmistress sounds old-fashioned or playful. Use it for a woman who keeps everyone busy, but avoid it at work, where it can sound condescending. Taskmaster is the natural, neutral choice.

distinctions.note: Taskmaster is the standard gender-neutral American term; taskmistress is the female form and sounds more dated.
Supervisor is a neutral job title; taskmistress suggests someone who pushes others hard and enjoys giving orders.

examples.everyday: Our mom was a real taskmistress on Saturdays, and nobody watched TV until the yard was done.
examples.professional: Our project lead becomes a bit of a taskmistress near deadlines, tracking every open ticket.
examples.analytical: In the novel, the governess becomes a taskmistress who controls the household by assigning every chore.

nuance.analogy: A taskmistress is like a stage manager who calls every cue and keeps the whole show moving on schedule.
nuance.etymology: Task from Anglo-Norman tasche; mistress from Old French maistresse, from maistre, from Latin magister.
common_mistakes: Using taskmistress as a neutral job title; the word carries a hint of bossiness.
Stressing the second syllable of mistress; say MIS-tress, with a weak final syllable.

senses.definition: In a tawdry manner.

core.definition: In a cheap, showy way that looks flashy but has little real value, taste or quality.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel is the aw sound of caught, which Americans with the cot-caught merger make like the a in father. The middle syllable is a reduced dri, and the ending is a light ee.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something cheap, gaudy or shabby in a way that suggests poor taste or a lack of genuine worth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this adverb in writing, reviews, or literary and critical prose. In casual speech people would say cheap, tacky or gaudy instead. It is a strong word, so using it about a friend's decorating can sound harsh.

distinctions.note: Gaudily stresses bright, excessive ornament, while tawdrily adds the idea of cheapness and shabbiness beneath the show.
Cheaply means inexpensively or of low quality in general, while tawdrily describes a showy, flimsy look that tries to seem valuable.

examples.everyday: The hotel lobby was tawdrily decorated, with plastic flowers and gold paint everywhere.
examples.professional: The packaging looked tawdrily cheap, so the client asked us to redesign it from the start.
examples.analytical: The novel shows a city whose public ceremonies are tawdrily staged, exposing a moral emptiness beneath the glitter.

nuance.analogy: Like costume jewelry that sparkles from across the room but turns green when you look closely, something tawdrily made looks rich from a distance and cheap up close.
nuance.etymology: From tawdry, which comes from St. Audrey, whose fair sold cheap lace and trinkets; the name was shortened to tawdry.
common_mistakes: Using tawdry as an adverb in formal writing, when the correct form is tawdrily.
Confusing tawdry with tardy, which means late, and the two words sound somewhat alike.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being tenebrose or tenebrous.

core.definition: The state of being dark, gloomy or murky, either literally or in a figurative, spiritual sense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the BRAH syllable. The vowel in that syllable is the American 'ah' from the cot-caught merger, and the final -ty is a light 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting gloom, dread or obscurity.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word found mostly in literary criticism, Gothic fiction, poetry and some religious writing about darkness. Everyday Americans would say darkness, gloom or murk. Tenebrous is the more common adjective and is easier to use in writing.

distinctions.note: Gloom often names a mood or sadness, while tenebrosity is a literal or sublime quality of darkness.
Obscurity can mean being unknown or hard to understand, while tenebrosity refers to darkness itself.

examples.everyday: Once the power went out, the whole house sank into a tenebrosity that made us feel our way to the flashlight.
examples.professional: The safety report describes the tunnel's tenebrosity as a hazard, since lighting failed on two sections.
examples.analytical: Mystics have often described the soul's passage through spiritual tenebrosity, a darkness that becomes a place of purification rather than despair.

nuance.analogy: Tenebrosity is like a closet with the door shut and no light switch.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tenebrosus, full of darkness, from tenebrae, darkness.
common_mistakes: Confusing tenebrosity (darkness itself) with tenebrism (a painting style).
Putting the stress on the final syllable instead of BRAH.

tenebrosity.etymology: From Middle English *tenebrosite*, from Old French *tenebrosité*, ultimately from Latin *tenebrae* (“darkness”).

senses.definition: The property of being tepid.

core.definition: The quality of being lukewarm; a lack of warmth, enthusiasm, or energy in feeling, response, or temperature.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PID, and reduce the first e to a schwa, since the stress shifts from the first syllable in tepid. The final -ity is a flapped t that sounds like a soft d.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a lack of warmth, interest, or commitment, often with a note of disappointment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tepidity mainly in formal or literary writing, where it describes a mild or half-hearted reaction. In everyday speech they say 'lukewarm' or 'half-hearted'. Tepidity is rarely used for water temperature in conversation.

distinctions.note: Lukewarm is the common everyday word for both temperature and enthusiasm; tepidity is more formal and literary.
Indifference means not caring at all; tepidity means caring a little, but without warmth or energy.

examples.everyday: The tepidity of the applause made the speaker look uncomfortable.
examples.professional: The tepidity of the client's response suggests they are not convinced by the proposal.
examples.analytical: The Revelation to the church at Laodicea warns against a tepidity that is neither hot nor cold.

nuance.analogy: Like a cup of coffee left on the table too long: not hot enough to warm your hands, and not cold enough to throw away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tepidus 'lukewarm', from tepere 'to be warm'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as TEE-pid instead of tuh-PID.
Using tepidity for ordinary water temperature in casual speech.
Confusing tepidity with tepid, which is the adjective.
nuance.biblical_note: Tepidity appears in the New Testament letter to the church at Laodicea. The Greek word chliaros means 'lukewarm' or 'tepid', and it describes a church neither hot nor cold. Revelation 3:15-16 describes the church's lukewarm condition and its sharp rejection. Revelation 3:19 calls the church to be zealous and to repent.

senses.definition: One of the two parts to the scriptures of the Christian religion: the New Testament, considered by Christians to be a continuation of the Hebrew scriptures, and the Hebrew scriptures themselves, which they refer to as the Old Testament.
senses.example: She reads a chapter of the New Testament every morning before she starts work.

senses.definition: A tangible proof or tribute.
senses.example: The ancient aqueducts are a testament to the great engineering skill of the Roman Empire.

senses.definition: A credo, expression of conviction.
senses.example: The prime minister's speech was a glowing testament to the cabinet's undying commitment to the royal cause.

senses.definition: A solemn, authentic instrument in writing, by which a person declares his or her will as to disposal of his or her inheritance (estate and effects) after his or her death, benefiting specified heir(s).
senses.example: His testament left the family farm to his daughter and the house to his son.

senses.definition: To make a will.
senses.example: Before the surgery, my grandfather decided to testament his savings to the church.

senses.definition: To bequeath or leave by will.
senses.example: He testamented his library collection to the university after his death.

core.definition: One of the two main divisions of the Christian Bible (Old Testament, New Testament); also, clear proof or evidence of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TES; the last two syllables are reduced to 'tuh-munt.' Don't pronounce the final syllable as 'ment' with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive when meaning tribute ('a testament to her courage'); neutral in the biblical sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say 'a testament to' to mean evidence or proof. 'Old Testament' and 'New Testament' are standard terms. The legal sense 'last will and testament' is old-fashioned but still used in legal documents.

distinctions.note: Testimony is a spoken or written statement of witness, while testament is the proof itself or a document.
A covenant is a binding agreement; in Scripture, 'testament' translates the Greek diatheke, which can mean covenant or will.
A testament to something is more moving than neutral proof.

examples.everyday: That old farmhouse is a testament to how well people used to build things.
examples.professional: The team's flawless launch is a testament to months of careful planning.
examples.analytical: The empty tomb is, for the Gospel writers, not merely a fact but a testament to God's act in history.

nuance.analogy: A testament stands like a witness whose very existence proves a claim.
nuance.etymology: From Latin testamentum, 'a will, a covenant,' from testari, 'to bear witness.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'a testament of' instead of 'a testament to.'
Putting stress on the last syllable.
Confusing testament with testimony.
nuance.biblical_note: 'Testament' in 'Old Testament' and 'New Testament' comes from Latin testamentum, which translated the Greek diatheke, 'covenant' (also 'will'), and Hebrew berit, 'covenant.' Jeremiah 31:31 promises a new covenant. Luke 22:20 reports Jesus speaking of the new covenant in his blood. Hebrews 9:15-17 plays on both senses, covenant and will.

testament.etymology: From Middle English *testament*, from Old French *testament*, from Latin *testāmentum* (“the publication of a will, a will, testament, in Late Latin one of the divisions of the Bible”), from *testor* (“to be a witness, testify, attest, make a will”), from…

senses.definition: A testis: the male sex and endocrine gland, found in most types of animals, that produces sperm and male sex hormones, including the steroid testosterone.
senses.example: Biology class explained that the testicle produces sperm and testosterone in most animals.

senses.definition: Either half of the structure that contains the testes: one side of the scrotum and its contents, considered as one object (one half of the ballsack, including its ball).
senses.example: The doctor checked the left testicle for swelling during the routine exam.

core.definition: One of the two male reproductive glands, located in the scrotum, that produce sperm and the hormone testosterone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final syllable a weak 'kul,' with no strong vowel. The 'c' is a hard k sound, and the word has three syllables, not two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical in medical settings; in casual speech, people more often use slang, which can sound crude.
nuance.usage_note: In doctor's offices, health classes, and medical conversations, 'testicle' is the normal neutral term. In everyday talk, Americans often say 'balls' or 'nuts,' which are informal and can sound crude in polite company. The word 'testis' is the technical term and is more common in biology.

distinctions.note: Testis is the technical biological term for the gland in all animals, while testicle is the everyday word for the human organ.
The scrotum is the pouch of skin that holds the testicles, not the glands themselves.

examples.everyday: The doctor said I should see a specialist if I notice any pain in a testicle.
examples.professional: The health and safety form asks whether the employee has any history of testicular injury.
examples.analytical: The Leydig cells of the testicle produce testosterone in response to luteinizing hormone.

nuance.analogy: The testicles are like a factory that makes sperm and male hormones, housed in a protective outer case.
nuance.etymology: From Latin testiculus, diminutive of testis 'testicle, witness,' a reference to the paired glands.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable or adding an extra syllable, such as 'TES-tih-cull-ar'.
Using 'testicle' as a casual joke word in polite conversation, which can sound odd.

senses.definition: To make a declaration, or give evidence, under oath.
To make a statement based on personal knowledge or faith.
senses.example: She agreed to testify that she saw the defendant leave the store shortly after noon.

senses.definition: To be evidence of.

core.definition: To give evidence as a witness, usually under oath, or to state something you personally know or believe to be true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the last syllable rhyme with 'sky.' The middle syllable is a weak vowel, so do not say 'TES-tee-fy.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal settings; positive or serious in religious or personal contexts, where it means speaking openly about one's faith or experience.
nuance.usage_note: In courtrooms and hearings, Americans say 'testify' for giving sworn evidence, and they say 'to take the stand' for the same event. In everyday talk, people use it for speaking out about personal experiences, such as 'she testified about her recovery.' In church, it often means sharing one's faith publicly.

distinctions.note: Witness can be a noun for a person who sees something, or a verb meaning to see an event; testify specifically means giving a formal statement, usually in court.
Testimony is the noun for the statement itself, while testify is the action of giving it.

examples.everyday: My neighbor had to testify about the accident at the trial last week.
examples.professional: Our engineer will testify to the system's performance at the compliance hearing on Thursday.
examples.analytical: The Gospel of John presents John the Baptist as one who came to testify to the light.

nuance.analogy: To testify is to step forward and say what you saw, like a referee calling out a foul that everyone else missed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin testificari, to bear witness, from testis 'witness' and facere 'to make.'
common_mistakes: Using 'testify' without a clear object: say 'testify against' or 'testify to,' not just 'testify about the crime' in a formal setting.
Confusing 'testify' with 'testimony' in sentences: 'give testimony' is the usual phrase for the statement.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is martyreō, meaning 'to bear witness.' John 1:6-8 (RSV) says John the Baptist came to bear witness to the light. John 15:26-27 describes the Spirit and the disciples bearing witness about Jesus. Acts 1:8 promises that the disciples will be Christ's witnesses to the ends of the earth.

testify.etymology: From Middle English *testifien*, borrowed from Old French *testifier*, from Latin *testificor* (“to bear witness”), from *testis* (“a witness”) + *facere* (“to make”).

senses.definition: Reply to a text message.
senses.example: I'll text you back as soon as I finish the meeting.

core.definition: To reply to someone's text message by sending a text of your own.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BACK, the particle. In fast speech the k of text links into back, so it sounds almost like 'teks-BAK' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. It implies that a reply is expected, so it can sound pushy if used to chase someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'll text you back' or 'Text me back' in casual conversation when they will answer later. It is for phone texting specifically. At work, say 'I'll get back to you' or 'I'll reply by email' instead. A natural reply is 'Sounds good, I'll text you back.'

distinctions.note: Call back means phoning someone again; text back means replying by text message.
Reply is general and works in email or formal writing; text back is casual and specific to phones.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I was driving. I'll text you back when I park.
examples.professional: I'm in a workshop until noon, but I'll text you back before lunch.
examples.analytical: Users who text back quickly tend to sustain conversations longer, which suggests that reply speed is itself a signal of engagement.

nuance.analogy: It is like returning a serve, but from your pocket.
nuance.etymology: Text from Latin textus; back from Old English bæc.
common_mistakes: Saying 'text back to her' instead of 'text her back'.
Saying 'answer back' for texting; answer back means to reply rudely.

conversation.text: I texted her an hour ago, and she hasn't texted back.
Text me back when you get a chance.
Sorry I didn't text back; I was driving.

senses.definition: A brief electronic message sent between mobile phones.
To transmit a text message.
senses.example: I told him to text message you when he's finished.

core.definition: A brief electronic message sent from one mobile phone to another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TEKST and give message a lighter secondary stress. The second syllable has a short i, so it is MES-ij, not MES-ayj.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is the standard everyday term and carries no social weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'text message' or simply 'text' in everyday talk, and 'text' is standard as a verb ('I texted her'). In formal writing, use 'text message' at first mention. A natural reply to a message is 'Got it, thanks for the text.'

distinctions.note: SMS is the technical name for the standard phone text service, which is limited in length.
Instant messages go through apps such as Slack or WhatsApp over the internet, while standard text messages use the phone network.

examples.everyday: I sent you a text message about dinner. Did you see it?
examples.professional: Please send a text message to the on-call engineer if the alert fires.
